item.title: An OpenSSH bug lets attackers skip the password on some Linux servers. CISA’s deadline is November 12.
item.description: CISA added CVE-2026-123158 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on November 9, with a due date of November 12. It affects sshd built without PAM on systems using the musl C library, such as Alpine Linux. Update to OpenSSH 10.6p2 or your distribution’s fixed package and restart sshd, or turn password logins off.
item.author: circuits50capital@circuits.fit (Emilio Santos)
item.content:encoded:
On November 9, 2026, the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency added an OpenSSH flaw, CVE-2026-123158, to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog. The federal due date is November 12. On affected servers, an attacker who can reach the SSH port can log in to some accounts without knowing the password.

OpenSSH says the bug affects “some Linux systems,” not every server. It applies when OpenSSH is built and run without PAM, the pluggable authentication modules framework, on a system that uses the musl C library. Alpine Linux, a lightweight distribution whose advisory covers servers, containers and cloud images, is the named example. If you run SSH on Alpine, update today and restart the SSH service, or turn password logins off.

What happened

The OpenSSH project released portable OpenSSH 10.6p2 on November 5. Its release notes describe “a critical security workaround that affects Linux systems that use the musl libc and PAM disabled.” The project says it considers the root cause to be outside sshd, the SSH server, but that the bug is exploitable through sshd and can be avoided there. The notes credit Özgün Kültekin of Wakefield with the report.

The National Vulnerability Database entry, published November 5, says sshd before 10.6p2 on Linux, when musl is used without PAM, lacks a workaround for a password authentication bypass, and that for some account configurations any password between 256 and 1024 characters succeeds. The CVSS 3.1 score supplied by the CVE assigner is 8.1, rated High.

Alpine’s security team published its own advisory the same day, and it explains the mechanism in plain terms. Without PAM, sshd checks a password by hashing the attempt with the C library’s crypt() function and comparing the result to the stored password field. musl’s crypt() returns the string * as an error when the input is over 256 bytes. * is also exactly what the stored field contains for an account with no password set. The two match, and the login succeeds. Alpine says it takes one connection, works every time, and needs no retries.

CISA added the CVE on November 9, based on evidence of active exploitation, alongside three other flaws. Its catalog entry is marked for forensic triage, which means agencies are expected to check whether a system was compromised, not only patch it. CISA lists known ransomware use as unknown.

Who is affected

Alpine lists three conditions, and all three must be true:

  • sshd runs without PAM. That is the default Alpine openssh-server package, or openssh-server-pam with UsePAM no. openssh-server-pam with UsePAM yes is not affected.
  • Password logins are on. PasswordAuthentication yes is the OpenSSH default unless someone changed it.
  • The machine has an account whose password field is *, and at least one other account with a $5$ or $6$ password hash. Accounts with * include root on Alpine base images since about 3.16, any key-only user created without a password, and users that come from a directory service through musl-nscd. One account with a real password is enough to make every account without one reachable.

OpenSSH’s default PermitRootLogin prohibit-password protects root itself. Alpine warns that this does not help if another account that can log in is able to become root, for example through doas. The official Alpine tiny-cloud images from 3.18.11 through 3.24.3 ship an alpine user with a * password field and passwordless doas. Alpine says those images are safe on first boot and become exploitable as soon as any $6$ hash exists on the machine, for example when an admin sets a console password.

Alpine says every release it checked is affected, 3.21 through 3.24 and edge, plus the older 3.16 to 3.20 releases. It is not affected where containers do not run sshd, where password authentication is off, where no account has a $-style hash, and on cloud images configured through cloud-init, which writes PasswordAuthentication no.

What it means for owners and CISOs

This is a narrow bug with a severe outcome. The population is small compared with a flaw in every OpenSSH install, but the machines that fit it tend to be the ones nobody inventories: a container someone gave an SSH port for debugging, a small Alpine virtual machine a contractor set up, an appliance or edge box built on Alpine. If your provider says “we don’t run Alpine,” ask how they know.

The fix is cheap. Updating a package and restarting a service is minutes of work per machine. The expensive part is the follow-up on any machine that was exposed with password logins on, because a successful login leaves the attacker with a shell, and on tiny-cloud images a route to root. That is why CISA marked the entry for forensic triage, and why “we patched it” is not the end of the conversation.

The release notes also carry a wider signal. The OpenSSH team says it has received a large number of security reports, many from AI models or made with AI assistance, and has seen bugs found by AI tools later found independently by other researchers. For now it will make more frequent releases rather than batching fixes. Plan on more small OpenSSH updates, and make sure someone owns them.

What to do this week

  1. List every machine and container that runs sshd on Alpine or another musl-based system. Include anything a provider manages for you. Write down the answer and who gave it.
  2. Update and restart. On Alpine, run apk upgrade -U -a. Alpine’s fixed packages include 10.6_p2-r0 on edge, 10.3_p1-r2 on 3.24, 10.2_p1-r1 on 3.23 and 10.0_p1-r11 on 3.22, with fixes published back to 3.16. Then restart sshd with rc-service sshd restart. Alpine stresses that upgrading the package does not replace the running daemon.
  3. If you cannot update yet, turn password logins off. Confirm key login works first and keep your current session open. Set PasswordAuthentication no, run sshd -t, restart sshd, and check that sshd -T | grep -i passwordauthentication prints passwordauthentication no. Alpine says either step closes the hole.
  4. Rebuild images. Alpine says images built from 3.21.10, 3.22.8, 3.23.8, 3.24.4 and later include the fixed package. Older point releases do not, so update running instances and rebuild base images and containers.
  5. Check for a past login on exposed machines. Alpine’s advice: look in /var/log/messages for sshd lines reading “Accepted password for” an account that has no password, such as alpine, root or any key-only user. Review doas use and recently created users, files and authorized keys. If you cannot rule out a login, treat the machine as compromised.

Also added to KEV November 9 (due November 12)

CISA added three other flaws the same day, all with the same November 12 due date and all marked for forensic triage: GPUStack CVE-2026-102895, an improper authentication flaw that CISA says could allow unauthenticated administrative access; SignalWire FreeSWITCH CVE-2026-116779, a code injection flaw; and IBM Aspera Faspex CVE-2026-123218, an incorrect authorization flaw that could let an authenticated user escalate privileges. If you run any of them, follow the vendor advisory linked from CISA’s catalog entry.

What to watch next

  • Other musl-based images. The advisories name Alpine. If a product you use ships on a musl-based system with its own SSH build, ask the vendor whether it is affected.
  • More OpenSSH point releases. The project has said it will release more often for now. Track the release notes page rather than waiting for a distribution bulletin.
  • Post-incident detail. CISA has not published who was attacked or how. If vendors or researchers publish indicators, run them against any machine that had password logins on before you patched.

Not sure whether one of your servers, containers or providers fits the conditions above? Our $29 Quick Answer service covers one question like that, in writing.

Sources

  • OpenSSH, release notes for OpenSSH 10.6p2, released November 5, 2026 (critical security workaround for Linux systems using musl libc with PAM disabled; root cause outside sshd; reported by Özgün Kültekin of Wakefield; more frequent releases)
  • Alpine Linux, “Security advisory: openssh-server password authentication bypass”, November 5, 2026 (conditions, affected releases, fixed package versions, tiny-cloud images, detection advice, root cause in musl crypt())
  • CISA, “CISA Adds Four Known Exploited Vulnerabilities to Catalog”, November 9, 2026 (CVE-2026-102895, CVE-2026-116779, CVE-2026-123158, CVE-2026-123218)
  • CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog, checked November 11, 2026, catalog version 2026.11.10 (all four added November 9, due November 12, forensic triage Yes, known ransomware use Unknown)
  • NIST National Vulnerability Database, CVE-2026-123158, published November 5, 2026 (description; CVSS 3.1 base score 8.1 from the CVE assigner)
  • OpenSSH portable, commit “avoid password authn bypass” (the fix)

Related: Barracuda appliances are on CISA’s exploited list, this week’s patch calendar, and Security and vulnerabilities, every security briefing, guide and tool in one place.

item.title: Cisco BroadWorks is on CISA’s exploited list. Ask your phone provider if they patched.
item.description: CISA added CVE-2026-20320 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on November 10, with a due date of November 24. Cisco fixed the unauthenticated file-read flaw in August in release RI.2026.07, with no workaround. A security firm reported that an AI agent used it to break into a European telecom. Ask your provider, and check your own default passwords.
item.author: circuits50capital@circuits.fit (Emilio Santos)
item.content:encoded:
On November 10, 2026, the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency added a Cisco BroadWorks flaw, CVE-2026-20320, to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog, with a federal due date of November 24. Cisco fixed it on August 19. Two days before CISA’s listing, a security firm reported that an AI agent directed by a human operator had used it to break into a European telecommunications provider.

Most small businesses will never log in to a BroadWorks server. The security firm’s report describes BroadWorks as Cisco’s carrier-grade platform for hosted voice and unified communications services, the kind of system a phone or hosting provider runs. If your phones, or your servers, are hosted by a provider, the patch is theirs to apply and the risk is partly yours. The job this week is to ask them, in writing, and to check your own default passwords.

What happened

Cisco’s advisory, first published August 19, describes an XML external entity flaw in the Open Client Interface (OCI) XML parser of Cisco BroadWorks. An unauthenticated, remote attacker can send a crafted XML message to the OCI provisioning service and read sensitive files from the system with the privileges of the BroadWorks software. Cisco rates it High, with a CVSS base score of 7.5. Four products are affected if they run a vulnerable release, regardless of configuration: BroadWorks Application Delivery Platform, Application Server, Profile Server and Xtended Services Platform.

The first fixed release for all four is RI.2026.07. Cisco says there are no workarounds. Its advisory, still at version 1.0 when we checked it on November 11, says Cisco’s security team is not aware of malicious use. CISA’s catalog says otherwise: it added the CVE on November 10, based on evidence of active exploitation, as one of six additions that day. CISA lists known ransomware use as unknown.

What the security firm reported

On November 8, Malbear Labs, a threat research group, published a report it calls “Operation Snowball.” It says it found an exposed open directory holding the live workspace of an autonomous intrusion tool: more than 70 session transcripts of a jailbroken DeepSeek agent, directed by a Chinese-speaking operator, running more than two weeks of largely unsupervised attacks against a European telecommunications provider and organizations hosted in its data centers and cloud.

According to the report, the entry point was CVE-2026-20320 on the provider’s BroadWorks Xtended Services Platform, release 23.0.1.1075. From there, the report says, the agent recovered private keys and credentials, moved through internal networks using older flaws, and compiled a list of 13 organizations hosted on the provider’s infrastructure, drawn from public registry records. Among the access it claims, the report lists millions of patient records reached through a TrakCare Oracle database that still used default database credentials.

These are the firm’s findings, based on the attacker’s own transcripts and reports. Infosecurity Magazine, writing up the research, noted that the post does not say whether Malbear checked the claims with any victim, what was taken rather than staged, or whether all 13 organizations were breached. Malbear did not name the provider and says it withheld the directory’s address to protect the affected organizations.

Who is affected

Directly, any organization running one of the four BroadWorks products on a release earlier than RI.2026.07. In practice, that is mainly service providers that sell hosted calling and collaboration. Indirectly, it is their customers. The report says the provider’s BroadWorks provisioning server holds subscriber configuration for every user on the platform, and it describes an attacker using one provider as a route to the organizations hosted on it.

What it means for owners and CISOs

This is the vendor-inventory problem again. You cannot patch a provider’s platform, and you probably do not know what it runs. What you can do is ask a clear question, get a dated answer, and keep it with your vendor records. Three months passed between Cisco’s fix and CISA’s listing. A provider that patched in August has nothing to worry about and can say so in one line. A provider that cannot answer is telling you something.

The second lesson costs nothing. In the report’s account, the most damaging step was not a sophisticated exploit but a database that still had its default password. Every business has a list of devices and systems that shipped with one: printers, network gear, cameras, phone handsets, admin consoles. A tool that tries default passwords on everything it can reach is cheap to run, and the report describes an agent doing exactly that.

What to do this week

  1. Find out who hosts your phones and servers. List the provider for hosted voice, unified communications and any hosted servers or data center space.
  2. Send one written question to each. “Do you run Cisco BroadWorks for our service? If so, are all BroadWorks Application Delivery Platform, Application Server, Profile Server and Xtended Services Platform systems on release RI.2026.07 or later, and on what date did you upgrade? Given CISA’s November 10 listing of CVE-2026-20320, have you reviewed those systems for signs of compromise?”
  3. Record the answer. Put the provider, the answer, the date and the person who replied in your vendor or risk register. Our free risk exception register works for this if the answer is “not yet.” The Renewal & Risk Operator Pack ($29) includes a spreadsheet version of that register.
  4. Change default passwords you own. Walk your own list: routers, firewalls, printers, cameras, desk phones, database and admin accounts. Anything still on its factory password gets changed this week, or taken off the network.
  5. If you run BroadWorks yourself, upgrade to RI.2026.07 or later. There is no workaround. Review OCI provisioning exposure and logs, since the flaw is reachable without a login.

What to watch next

  • Cisco’s advisory. It still said “not aware of any public announcements or malicious use” on November 11. Watch for an update that reflects CISA’s listing or adds detail.
  • Victim confirmation. The report’s access claims have not been confirmed by the organizations involved, as far as public reporting shows. Treat the patient-record figure as a claim until someone confirms it.
  • Provider notices. If your provider runs BroadWorks and was behind on patches, you may get a notice. Read it for dates, the systems involved and what data they held about you.

Not sure how to word the question for your provider, or what a good answer looks like? Our $29 Quick Answer service covers one question like that, in writing.

Sources

  • Cisco, “Cisco BroadWorks Out-of-Band Blind XML External Entity Injection Vulnerability”, cisco-sa-bworks-xxe-uwUd7CEt, first published August 19, 2026, version 1.0, checked November 11, 2026 (CVE-2026-20320, CVSS 7.5, affected products, first fixed release RI.2026.07, no workarounds, not aware of malicious use)
  • CISA, “CISA Adds Six Known Exploited Vulnerabilities to Catalog”, November 10, 2026
  • CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog, checked November 11, 2026, catalog version 2026.11.10 (CVE-2026-20320 added November 10, due November 24, known ransomware use Unknown)
  • Malbear Labs, “Operation Snowball: Inside an Autonomous AI Intrusion Campaign”, November 8, 2026 (the security firm’s report; entry through CVE-2026-20320; 13 organizations; default database credentials)
  • Infosecurity Magazine, write-up of Operation Snowball (notes the claims were not confirmed with victims)

Related: PHP2Shell and the vendor inventory, the OpenSSH password bypass due November 12, and Security and vulnerabilities, every security briefing, guide and tool in one place.

item.title: Copilot usage billing moved to early 2027. Set your spending limit before you buy.
item.description: Microsoft now says new Microsoft 365 Copilot Business purchases through resellers will switch on usage-based billing by default in January to March 2027, not December 1. The default is 4,000 Copilot Credits per user per month, it applies across the tenant, and it can be capped at zero but not turned off.
item.author: circuits50capital@circuits.fit (Emilio Santos)
item.content:encoded:
Microsoft has moved the date when new Microsoft 365 Copilot Business purchases through resellers switch on usage-based billing by default. In a Partner Center announcement dated November 3, 2026, it said the change now arrives during its fiscal 2027 third quarter, January to March 2027, instead of December 1, 2026.

The date moved. The design did not. When it lands, a new Copilot Business purchase through the Cloud Solution Provider (CSP) program will set up usage billing for the whole tenant, with a default limit of 4,000 Copilot Credits per user per month. If you buy Microsoft 365 through a reseller, the useful step this quarter is to agree, in writing, what that limit should be before anyone adds a seat.

What happened

Microsoft’s November 3 update says usage-based billing “is now enabled by default for new Microsoft 365 Copilot Business subscriptions purchased in Cloud Solution Provider (CSP) during Microsoft’s FY27 Q3 (January-March 2027), instead of December 1, 2026, as previously announced.” Microsoft says it heard partner feedback and wanted to give partners extra time to prepare. The same update moved a Partner Center sandbox date that had been set for November 2. Microsoft says it will announce a new sandbox date, and that sandbox testing will be available for at least 30 days before general availability.

The rest of the announcement is unchanged in substance:

  • Scope. New purchases of Microsoft 365 Copilot Business licenses in CSP, including standalone offers and bundles.
  • Whole tenant. “New purchases enable usage-based billing by default for existing Microsoft 365 Copilot Business licenses in the tenant.” One new purchase turns it on for the Copilot Business users you already have.
  • Default limit. 4,000 Copilot Credits per user per month, which admins can adjust. Microsoft’s own example: a customer with 100 Copilot Business users could consume up to 400,000 credits a month under the default.
  • Billing. Pay-as-you-go is the default configuration. Microsoft names Copilot Cowork, Work IQ APIs and GitHub Copilot Harness as eligible usage-based experiences.
  • Markets. The updated timelines apply in all markets, including several, such as Australia, Brazil, France, Germany and India, where Microsoft had not expected these capabilities to be available at first.

How the switch works

Microsoft’s Partner Center documentation for the feature fills in detail that matters to a buyer. It covers Copilot Business only. Microsoft 365 Copilot for enterprise is out of scope, and so are education, nonprofit and GCC low tenants. The page also says some of what it describes is not yet released and that API details may change before general availability.

  • No separate opt-in. The reseller uses the same add-to-cart flow as today. Partner Center creates the Azure resources and a default spending policy at checkout.
  • What triggers it. A new subscription purchase, adding seats to an existing Copilot Business subscription through the Partner Center portal, or a Copilot trial converting to a paid license.
  • Existing policies win. Partner Center creates the default policy only if the tenant has no spending or billing policy from any channel or partner.
  • It can be capped, not removed. “Usage-based billing can’t be fully turned off once configured.” Partners set the spending limit to zero, which stops further spend while leaving the policy in place. Microsoft also warns that disabling usage-based billing might limit access to some AI experiences.
  • Two limits. When a partner creates a policy by hand, the documented defaults are 1,200,000 credits for the tenant and 4,000 per user.

A worked example

Take an illustrative ten-person firm that buys Copilot Business for all ten staff through its reseller in February 2027. These are example inputs, not a real customer.

  • Seat cost. Microsoft’s public pricing page lists the Copilot Business add-on at $21.00 per user per month, shown as $18.00 under a promotion that runs from July 1 to December 31, 2026, applies to the first year only and requires an annual commitment. A February 2027 purchase falls after that window, so budget at list unless your reseller confirms otherwise, and note that a reseller’s price can differ from Microsoft’s own page: 10 × $21.00 = $210 a month, or $2,520 a year.
  • Usage ceiling under the default. 10 users × 4,000 credits = 40,000 Copilot Credits a month that the firm could consume before the limit stops it. That is a ceiling, not a forecast. Actual charges depend on actual usage.
  • The dollar value of that ceiling. We have not found a per-credit price on a Microsoft page we could verify, so we are not putting a dollar figure on 40,000 credits. Ask your reseller to show the per-credit rate on the quote.

The limitation is the point: the seat price is fixed and published, the usage side is not, and the default is set by Microsoft, not by you.

What it means for owners and CFOs

For a small business, this turns Copilot from a fixed per-seat line into a fixed line plus a metered one. The metered part starts with a ceiling you did not choose, applies to staff you licensed before the change, and cannot be switched off afterward, only capped. None of that is a reason to avoid Copilot. It is a reason to treat the spending limit as a purchasing decision, like a seat count.

The other change on the calendar is earlier. Microsoft’s October Partner Center announcements say that from December 1, 2026, new Microsoft 365 Copilot and Copilot Business offers can be bought without a qualifying Microsoft 365 base subscription, and the current add-on offers reach end of sale in CSP that day. Existing customers can keep renewing them. Expect your reseller’s quote to change names around then, so check that the line items match what you agreed.

What to do this week

  1. Ask your reseller one written question. “If we buy or add Copilot Business seats after usage billing turns on by default, what spending limit will you set, per user and for the tenant, and will you set it before checkout?”
  2. Pick a number. Zero is a valid answer if you do not plan to use metered features yet. If you do, set a per-user limit you can explain and a tenant limit you can afford in a bad month.
  3. Name an owner. Someone should check the usage view in Partner Center or the Microsoft 365 admin center monthly, and the reseller should tell you if it changes a limit.
  4. Check your renewal date. If your Microsoft 365 renewal falls between now and March 2027, read Your Microsoft 365 renewal price, line by line first. It covers the July 1 list prices with 10- and 25-seat examples.

What to watch next

  • A firm date. “January to March 2027” is a plan. Microsoft has said it will announce the sandbox date in advance. Watch the Partner Center announcements page for the general availability date.
  • A published per-credit price. Until it is on a Microsoft page, any dollar ceiling on the 4,000-credit default is an estimate.
  • December 1 offer changes. The base-subscription requirement goes away for new offers that day. Confirm your quote uses the offer and promotion you expect.

If you want a second pair of eyes on a Microsoft 365 quote or renewal, including the Copilot lines and spending limits, our $79 Microsoft 365 Renewal Check covers it.

If Microsoft 365 is one of several renewals coming up, the Renewal Audit reviews up to 25 for a fixed $199. If you would rather track them yourself, the Renewal & Risk Operator Pack ($29) includes a renewal scorecard spreadsheet, and the free software renewal scorecard runs in your browser.

Sources

  • Microsoft Partner Center, November 2026 announcements, “Availability update: Updates to usage-based billing for new Microsoft 365 Copilot Business licenses and Partner Center sandbox environments,” dated November 3, 2026 (FY27 Q3 instead of December 1, 2026; tenant-wide effect; 4,000-credit default; 100-user example; all markets; sandbox date moved)
  • Microsoft Learn, usage-based billing for Microsoft 365 Copilot Business in Partner Center, checked November 11, 2026 (scope, purchase events, default policies, cannot be fully turned off, limit to zero, 1,200,000 and 4,000 credit defaults, pre-release notice)
  • Microsoft Partner Center, October 2026 announcements (new Copilot offers without a base subscription from December 1, 2026; add-on offers end of sale in CSP December 1)
  • Microsoft, Copilot for business pricing, checked November 11, 2026 (Copilot Business add-on $21.00, shown at $18.00 per user per month paid yearly under a July 1 to December 31, 2026 promotion)

Related: Your Microsoft 365 renewal price, line by line, software renewal scorecard, and Renewals and SaaS spend, every renewal briefing, guide and tool in one place.

item.title: Barracuda appliances are on CISA’s exploited list. Check firmware this week.
item.description: CISA added two Barracuda flaws to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on November 10, with a due date of November 13. Barracuda has identified exploitation activity affecting a small number of organizations. Confirm the latest firmware and patches, keep the admin interface off the internet, and review the device if that page was reachable.
item.author: circuits50capital@circuits.fit (Emilio Santos)
item.content:encoded:
On November 10, 2026, the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency added two Barracuda flaws to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog. The federal due date is November 13. The night before, Barracuda updated its advisory to say it had identified exploitation activity affecting a small number of organizations.

If your business uses a Barracuda Email Security Gateway, or one of several other Barracuda appliances, treat it as a job for this week: confirm the latest firmware and patches are on, turn automatic patching back on if it was turned off, and keep the administrative interface off the public internet.

What happened

Barracuda published the advisory on November 2. It describes two vulnerabilities. CVE-2026-116606 is a pre-authentication authorization bypass in the Email Security Gateway, with a CVSS score of 9.3. CVE-2026-111560 is a command injection flaw, with a CVSS score of 8.6.

On November 5, Barracuda clarified that CVE-2026-116606 does not require a login. It does require that the attacker can reach the administrative user interface. Mandiant’s disclosure for that flaw, MNDT-2026-0042, says an unauthenticated attacker can invoke a configuration-import function and restore a crafted backup archive, which can change the appliance’s global configuration. Mandiant lists Email Security Gateway versions earlier than 9.4.0.030 as affected.

CVE-2026-111560, described in Mandiant’s MNDT-2026-0041, is an operating-system command injection in the timezone configuration field. An authenticated administrator can inject commands that then run with root privileges. Barracuda and CISA both say the two flaws can be chained. Used together, Barracuda says, they could let an attacker bypass authorization controls and obtain root access to the device. In all cases, Barracuda says successful exploitation requires access to the administrative interface.

On November 9 at 9:00 p.m. EST, Barracuda updated the advisory: “We have identified exploitation activity affecting a small number of organizations.” It has not said how many organizations were affected, or what the attackers achieved. On November 10, CISA added both identifiers to the catalog, based on evidence of active exploitation, and set a due date of November 13. Both entries are marked for forensic triage. CISA lists known ransomware use as unknown.

Those due dates bind federal civilian agencies. A private firm is not under the same mandate, but a three-day window is a useful priority signal, and the forensic-triage mark is a reason to look for compromise rather than only installing a patch.

Who is affected

CVE-2026-116606 affects the Barracuda Email Security Gateway only. CVE-2026-111560 also affects the Email Security Gateway, and it affects five other products: the Load Balancer Application Delivery Controller (ADC), Message Archiver, WAF Control Center, Web Application Firewall, and Web Security Gateway.

Mandiant lists these affected version ranges for the command-injection flaw: Email Security Gateway 9.4.0.27 and earlier, Load Balancer ADC 6.4.0 and earlier, Web Application Firewall 11.0.1 and earlier, Web Security Gateway 16.1.100.100 and earlier, Message Archiver 5.5.4.0 and earlier, and WAF Control Center 2.2.1 and earlier. Barracuda’s own advice is to install the latest firmware and the security patches it lists, rather than to stop at a single build number.

The patch identifiers in Barracuda’s advisory are BNSF-40425 for Email Security Gateway 9.4.017 and later, BNSF-40430 for older Email Security Gateway builds, BNADC-16586 for the Load Balancer ADC and the Web Application Firewall, BNMA-32468 for the Message Archiver, BNWF-60060 for the WAF Control Center, and BNYF-24789 for the Web Security Gateway.

What to do this week

  1. Find out if you have one of these appliances. Ask your IT provider whether you use a Barracuda Email Security Gateway, Load Balancer ADC, Message Archiver, WAF, WAF Control Center, or Web Security Gateway, including any unit they manage for you. Write down the answer.
  2. Confirm the latest firmware and patches are on. Barracuda says customers should verify that systems are on the latest firmware and have received all security patches. If automatic patching was turned off, turn it back on. A device that is several versions behind may need more than one update. Contact Barracuda Support if you need help applying a patch.
  3. Keep the admin interface off the internet. Barracuda recommends restricting administrative interfaces to trusted internal networks. Organizations whose admin pages are not reachable from the public internet are less exposed to this attack path.
  4. If the admin page was exposed, do a forensic review. Installing a patch does not undo a change an attacker may already have made. CISA’s catalog entries for both flaws are marked for forensic triage. Ask your provider to look for unexpected configuration changes, unexpected backup restores, timezone changes, and unusual administrator activity, then follow Barracuda’s current guidance.

Questions to ask your IT provider

  • Do we run a Barracuda Email Security Gateway, Load Balancer ADC, Message Archiver, WAF, WAF Control Center, or Web Security Gateway, including any appliance you manage for us?
  • Is the administrative interface reachable from the public internet? If it was, when was that closed, and what did you review afterward?
  • Are we on the latest firmware, and have the patches Barracuda lists for CVE-2026-116606 and CVE-2026-111560 been applied? Is automatic patching turned on?
  • If the admin page was exposed, have you looked for unexpected configuration changes, backup restores, timezone changes, and administrator activity?

If you want a second opinion on what to ask your provider, our $29 Quick Answer service covers that question.

Sources

  • Barracuda, “Pre-Authentication Authorization Bypass and Command Injection Vulnerabilities in Certain Barracuda Products”, published November 2, 2026; updated November 5, 2026, 2:30 p.m. EST (authentication not required for CVE-2026-116606, administrative UI access required) and November 9, 2026, 9:00 p.m. EST (exploitation activity affecting a small number of organizations); CVSS 9.3 and 8.6; affected products and patch identifiers
  • CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog JSON feed, version 2026.11.10, released November 10, 2026, at 2:03 p.m. Eastern time (CVE-2026-116606 and CVE-2026-111560 added November 10, due November 13, forensic triage marked Yes, known ransomware use Unknown; both entries note the flaws can be chained)
  • CISA, “CISA Adds Six Known Exploited Vulnerabilities to Catalog”, November 10, 2026 (additions based on evidence of active exploitation)
  • Mandiant, MNDT-2026-0042 (CVE-2026-116606, Email Security Gateway versions earlier than 9.4.0.030, CVSS 9.3)
  • Mandiant, MNDT-2026-0041 (CVE-2026-111560, command injection in the timezone field, affected products and versions, CVSS 8.6)

item.title: N-able took N-central offline. Ask your MSP if they use it.
item.description: A researcher published 33 unpatched flaws, with exploit code, in the tool many managed service providers use to run client computers. N-able has taken hosted N-central down and told on-premises customers to leave servers off until a hotfix lands.
item.author: circuits50capital@circuits.fit (Emilio Santos)
item.content:encoded:
On Monday, November 9, 2026, N-able took its hosted N-central service offline in the Americas, Europe and Asia-Pacific. It also told customers who run N-central on their own servers to shut those servers down and leave them off until N-able says they can come back. The move followed a researcher’s public release of 33 unpatched flaws, with working exploit code, in the remote monitoring tool many managed service providers use to run their clients’ computers.

If an IT provider manages your office computers, ask them today whether they use N-able N-central.

What happened

Late Sunday, November 8, security researcher Sean Bales published a set of flaws he called Able2Shell, including proof-of-concept exploits, according to BleepingComputer. Huntress, which reviewed the research, counts 33 flaws that can be chained into four attacks: three that can run code on the N-central server and one that can raise privileges to root. The researcher tested them against N-central Appliance 2026.4.0.31 and said earlier versions are likely affected.

N-able then announced a critical security incident. In a statement to BleepingComputer it said it took hosted N-central offline on November 9 as a precaution and told on-premises customers to take their servers offline until further notice. At that time it said it had not observed active exploitation.

As of mid-morning November 10, Eastern time, N-able’s status page still listed the incident as a major outage under investigation, with no end time. Hosted N-central remained offline in all three regions, and the on-premises N-central rows were marked the same way. N-able said it is seeing scanning tied to the published exploit code, but has no evidence that any customer environment has been successfully exploited. It is still working on a hotfix, with a target of midday November 10, Eastern time, and it continues to recommend that N-central stay offline until that hotfix is available and the server has been upgraded. A check of N-able’s N-central release notes found no new hotfix for this incident; the latest security hotfix listed there is still 2026.4 HF1, dated November 2, which addresses a separate issue.

What to do

  1. Ask your provider. If an MSP or IT firm runs your computers, ask whether they use N-able N-central, hosted or on-premises, and write down the answer.
  2. Upgrade before turning it back on. An on-premises server should be upgraded to N-central 2026.4 Hotfix 2 (build 2026.4.1.26) before it comes back online; N-able upgrades hosted servers itself. Then upgrade Agents first and Probes second, in both hosted and on-premises setups, as the release notes direct.
  3. Check logins and new admin accounts since November 8. Ask your provider to review login activity and any new administrator accounts from November 8 onward, and to look for unexpected remote sessions or new scripts, before they turn N-central back on. Huntress recommends that review because earlier N-central incidents saw attackers create admin accounts and push tools into client networks.
  4. Watch N-able’s status page for the all-clear. Hosted N-central comes back when N-able says so. The official page is uptime.n-able.com.

When this piece first ran, no CVE identifiers had been assigned, according to SecurityWeek. N-able’s Hotfix 2 release notes now list seven, including CVE-2026-125882 (code execution through a file repository upload path traversal) and CVE-2026-125878 (OGNL injection). The flaws were not on CISA’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog as of feed version 2026.11.09. That does not change the advice. Follow N-able’s current direction rather than waiting for a catalog entry.

If you want a second opinion on what to ask your provider, our $29 Quick Answer service covers that question.

Sources

  • N-able status page (official incident 202580, checked mid-morning November 10, 2026, Eastern time: status Investigating, severity Major Outage, hotfix ETA midday November 10 EST, hosted and on-premises N-central still offline; N-able reports scanning tied to the published exploit code and no evidence of successful exploitation in a customer environment)
  • BleepingComputer, “N-able takes cloud platform offline after 30+ ‘zero-days’ published”, November 9, 2026, including N-able’s statement
  • Huntress, “N-able Disables Cloud Services Following Disclosure of ‘Able2Shell’ Exploit Chains”, November 9, 2026
  • SecurityWeek, “N-able Takes N-central Offline as Researcher Drops Over 30 Zero-Days”, November 10, 2026 (no CVE identifiers assigned yet)
  • CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog JSON feed, version 2026.11.09 (no Able2Shell or new N-central identifiers for this incident)
  • N-able, “N-central 2026.4 HF2 Release Notes”, posted November 10, 2026, 3:48 PM ET (build 2026.4.1.26, upgrade guidance, CVE list, known issues)

item.title: Four AI spending reports in one week. The budget is outrunning the measurement.
item.description: Menlo puts enterprise AI spend at $176.8 billion. Only 10% of CFOs in an RGP survey see significant returns. What the four reports agree on, and what to do before FY2027 locks.
item.author: circuits50capital@circuits.fit (Emilio Santos)
item.content:encoded:
Four surveys on enterprise AI spending landed between November 2 and November 5, 2026. Read together, they say the same uncomfortable thing: AI budgets are rising faster than finance teams can measure what the money does. For anyone setting FY2027 numbers this month, that gap is the part worth acting on.

Here is what each report found, what the sources have at stake, and how to use the numbers at your own budget table and at your next software renewal.

The four reports

Menlo Ventures: spending up 5.4 times

Menlo Ventures’ 2026 State of Enterprise AI report, released November 3, puts enterprise AI spending at $176.8 billion by September 2026, up from $33 billion in 2025. The share of enterprises paying for AI rose only from 55% to 65%, so most of the growth is existing buyers spending more, not new buyers arriving.

Two other findings matter for budget owners. New budgets funded 55% of incremental enterprise AI spending and 22% came from existing software budgets, mostly staying with incumbents as they convert licenses, such as Microsoft Office to Copilot. And Anthropic, OpenAI and Google together took 69% of deployment spending, up from 50% in 2025. Menlo says companies budgeted nearly twice what they spent in 2025 and still ended up spending 2.5 times what they budgeted.

Read it with care. The market-size figures are Menlo’s own estimates from a bottom-up model, and Menlo discloses that it is an investor in Anthropic and OpenRouter, both of which appear in its findings. The survey covered nearly 400 U.S. enterprise decision-makers.

West Monroe: 74% now put more than a tenth of IT into AI

West Monroe’s The New Rules of Enterprise Software & AI Spend, released November 5, found that the share of buyers putting more than 10% of their IT budget into AI rose from 23% in 2025 to 74% in 2026. The online survey ran in Q3 2026 among 300 U.S. executives; buyers came from organizations with at least $100 million in revenue.

The useful finding is about pricing. Buyers prefer predictable models: enterprise subscriptions (33%) and usage-based pricing (24%). Yet 36% of sellers think buyers prefer hybrid pricing that includes outcome-based components. Sellers also underestimate how often buyers simply buy: 42% of buyers say they mainly buy AI rather than build it, while only 22% of sellers think so.

RGP via CFO.com: 10% see significant returns today

CFO.com reported on November 3 that consulting firm RGP surveyed 400 finance chiefs in September at companies with at least $250 million in revenue across North America, Europe and Asia Pacific. Only 10% said they see “significant positive” ROI from AI today; 54% expect it within 24 months. At companies under $1 billion in revenue, just 1% reported significant AI ROI, against 17% at companies of $5 billion or more. RGP’s own framing: “The 24-month AI promise is now on the record, and boards will hold CFOs to it.”

CloudZero: raising budgets they cannot justify

CloudZero, which sells cloud cost software, published a survey of 252 senior finance leaders on November 2. It is a vendor survey, so treat it as one input. It found 87% are raising their AI budget for FY2027, 45% of those by more than 20%, while 61% already spend more on AI than they can justify with measurable outcomes. Among those who cannot justify current spending, 91% are increasing it anyway. Only 12% can break AI spend down finely enough to act on it within the quarter, and 54% cannot get below a rough category.

Where the numbers agree, and where they do not

The reports measure different things for different audiences, so do not add them up. Menlo sizes a market; West Monroe and RGP survey large buyers; CloudZero surveys finance leaders on its own subject. What they share is direction. Spending is up sharply, the buyers already paying are paying more, and few can show the return yet.

The disagreement is commercial. West Monroe’s sellers are moving toward outcome-linked pricing that buyers did not ask for. That is a lever for buyers, not a threat, as long as you know your own usage.

What it means for CFOs and CISOs

  • Allocation is the gap. If only about one in eight finance teams can attribute AI spend within a quarter, most FY2027 AI lines will be set on totals. Totals only ever go up.
  • Some of the increase is a renewal. Menlo’s 22% from existing software budgets is license conversion. Copilot-style upgrades should go through the same renewal review as any other price increase, not a separate AI budget.
  • The ROI clock is public. RGP’s 24-month figure gives boards a date. Write down what “paid off” means now, in cost per task or hours saved, so the checkpoint is not argued after the fact.
  • Concentration is a supplier risk. With 69% of deployment spend going to three labs, a price change at one of them reaches you through every tool built on it. CISOs should know which vendors route data to which model provider.
  • Smaller firms should be most careful. The 1% figure for companies under $1 billion is a reason to start small and measure, not to stop.

What to do this week

  1. List every AI line in the FY2027 draft: API usage, AI add-ons on existing suites, standalone tools. Note owner, team and contract end date.
  2. Require a unit for each line. Cost per task, per ticket or per team. Our free AI cost-per-task calculator and token cost and margin calculator give a first estimate from vendor prices.
  3. Treat license conversions as renewals. Run each one through the software renewal scorecard and ask for a predictable subscription cap in writing rather than an open usage or outcome term.
  4. Set a dated ROI checkpoint. Pick a date inside 24 months and the metric you will use. Put it in the budget memo.
  5. Ask vendors which model they use and whether a change of model provider changes your price or data terms.

If you want a second pair of eyes on the renewals behind these lines, our Renewal Audit reviews up to 25 software renewals for a fixed $199 and returns a written report in 5 business days. The Renewal & Risk Operator Pack ($29) has the renewal scorecard and tracker as spreadsheets.

What to watch next

  • The full reports. Menlo and West Monroe have published full reports with methodology; check sample definitions before quoting a figure internally.
  • Seller pricing changes at renewal. If a vendor proposes outcome-based or hybrid pricing, ask for the formula, a cap and a fallback to a fixed subscription.
  • Copilot and suite conversions. Our Microsoft 365 renewal briefing covers the July 1 list prices that are reaching customers at renewal now.
  • Your own quarter-end numbers. The best data point for your FY2027 AI line is what you spent this quarter, by team.

Sources

  • Menlo Ventures, “2026 State of Enterprise AI Report,” press release, November 3, 2026, checked November 7, 2026. Full report.
  • West Monroe, “The New Rules of Enterprise Software & AI Spend,” press release, November 5, 2026, checked November 7, 2026
  • CFO.com, “CFOs expect AI to pay off in 2 years: survey,” November 3, 2026
  • CloudZero, “AI budget season: 87% are raising it, 61% can’t justify it,” November 2, 2026 (vendor survey)

Related: Gartner revised the AI bill and all AI cost briefings.

item.title: Zyxel GS1900: the June patch did not stop the exploit
item.description: An exploit used against 996 GS1900 switches still worked on firmware patched in June. The fix is 2.90 Patch 3, released October 22. Reopen the ticket you closed.
item.author: circuits50capital@circuits.fit (Emilio Santos)
item.content:encoded:
If your team closed a ticket for Zyxel GS1900 switches after the June patch, reopen it. Zyxel published an advisory on November 3, 2026 for a second flaw in the same switches, CVE-2026-107441, and researchers at Binarly found that the exploit attackers used against nearly 1,000 of these switches still worked on firmware that carried the June fix. The real fix is the 2.90 Patch 3 firmware, which Zyxel posted on October 22 and October 23.

This is a small-office story. The GS1900 is an inexpensive managed switch that tends to sit in branch closets and under desks, which is exactly where nobody checks firmware twice. It is also a clean example of a lesson that applies to any risk register: a patch installed is not the same as a risk closed.

What happened, in order

  • June 16, 2026. Zyxel released updates for CVE-2026-7273, a pre-authentication stack-based buffer overflow in the GS1900 CGI program. Fixed builds were 2.90 Patch 2, written 2.90(XXXX.2)C0.
  • From about August 17. GreyNoise observed a suspected Chinese-speaking actor it tracks as Kapibala exploiting GS1900 switches. It counted 996 compromised devices in 48 countries. The attackers ran a script that collected device configurations, hashed root credentials and network information. GreyNoise linked the actor to the Red Heron campaign that Acronis had reported earlier.
  • September 21. GreyNoise disclosed the campaign and attributed it to CVE-2026-7273. CISA added CVE-2026-7273 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog the same day, with a federal due date of September 24.
  • September 28. Binarly, investigating Red Heron infrastructure, found an exposed archive holding an obfuscated Python exploit for the switches. It confirmed the exploit still achieved unauthenticated command execution on all ten firmware releases that had been patched for CVE-2026-7273. The exploit checked for those patched versions specifically.
  • September 29 to October 11. Binarly reported the finding to Zyxel, which confirmed a new vulnerability and assigned CVE-2026-107441.
  • October 22. Zyxel released 2.90 Patch 3 firmware, which limits parameter sizes and validates the parameter count before copying data into memory.
  • November 3. Zyxel published its advisory. Canada’s Cyber Centre issued alert AV26-1114 the same day and updated it on November 4 to note open-source reporting that CVE-2026-107441 is exploited in the wild.

It is still unclear whether the exploit was written to bypass the June fix or whether it used a related bug the June fix never covered. For an owner, the answer is the same either way.

Which switches, which firmware

Zyxel describes the flaw as an out-of-bounds write in the CGI program that could let a LAN-based, unauthenticated attacker execute operating system commands with a crafted HTTP request. Its advisory lists ten models:

Swipe the table sideways to see every column.

ModelVulnerableFixed
GS1900-82.90(AAHH.2)C0 and earlier2.90(AAHH.3)C0
GS1900-8HP2.90(AAHI.2)C0 and earlier2.90(AAHI.3)C0
GS1900-10HP2.90(AAZI.2)C0 and earlier2.90(AAZI.3)C0
GS1900-162.90(AAHJ.2)C0 and earlier2.90(AAHJ.3)C0
GS1900-242.90(AAHL.2)C0 and earlier2.90(AAHL.3)C0
GS1900-24E2.90(AAHK.2)C0 and earlier2.90(AAHK.3)C0
GS1900-24EP2.90(ABTO.2)C0 and earlier2.90(ABTO.3)C0
GS1900-24HPv22.90(ABTP.2)C0 and earlier2.90(ABTP.3)C0
GS1900-482.90(AAHN.2)C0 and earlier2.90(AAHN.3)C0
GS1900-48HPv22.90(ABTQ.2)C0 and earlier2.90(ABTQ.3)C0

The pattern is simple: a “.2” build is the June fix and is still vulnerable; you want the “.3” build. Zyxel says on-market products not in the table are unaffected and that it patched models still within their vulnerability support period.

Where the catalog stands

As of CISA’s catalog version 2026.11.06, released November 6, CVE-2026-7273 is listed and CVE-2026-107441 is not. That matters for teams that drive patching from the KEV list. The catalog entry you already handled points at the June fix, and the June fix did not stop the exploit. Do not wait for a second KEV entry to act on this one.

What it means for CFOs and CISOs

  • “Patched” was the wrong closing condition. A ticket that closed when the June firmware was installed recorded the wrong control. The control that matters is “not exploitable by the known exploit,” and the only evidence for that is now the Patch 3 build number.
  • Credentials may already be gone. The attackers took configurations and hashed root credentials. If a switch was exposed during the campaign, assume anything in its config, including SNMP strings, RADIUS or TACACS secrets and reused admin passwords, needs rotating.
  • Cheap devices carry real exposure. A switch that cost a few hundred dollars can hold the same secrets as the firewall next to it. Asset lists that skip unmanaged-looking network gear are where this kind of miss starts.
  • Vendor advisories lag exploitation. Exploitation began around mid-August; the advisory for the real bug arrived November 3. Budget the response time you need on the assumption that the advisory is late, not early.

What to do this week

  1. Find every GS1900. Check your asset list, then the switch list in your network management tool, then branch and home-office closets. Note model and firmware build for each.
  2. Upgrade to the “.3” build for that model from the table above. Confirm the version on the device after reboot, not just in the change ticket.
  3. Take the web interface off untrusted networks. The flaw is in the web management CGI. Limit management access to a dedicated VLAN or admin hosts.
  4. Rotate secrets. Change the admin password and any shared secrets stored in the switch configuration. Store the new ones somewhere shared and audited rather than a spreadsheet.
  5. Look for signs of compromise. Check for unknown accounts, unexpected configuration changes and outbound connections from switch management addresses since mid-August.
  6. Reopen the June ticket and close it again with the Patch 3 build number and the date you verified it.

For step 4, a business password manager with shared vaults and an access log fits the job. We compared four in our password manager guide; one option is NordPass Business. Paid link: we may earn a commission.

If you track exceptions, log any switch you cannot upgrade this week in the free risk exception register with an owner and an expiry date. The Renewal & Risk Operator Pack ($29) includes a spreadsheet version of that register alongside a renewal scorecard.

What to watch next

  • A KEV listing for CVE-2026-107441. If CISA adds it, the due date will be short. We will update this page with the date.
  • Further Binarly or GreyNoise detail. Indicators of compromise for the newer exploit would make step 5 more concrete.
  • Other Zyxel advisories. The Cyber Centre alert also covers a separate buffer overflow in certain Zyxel access points, FWA7 and security routers. If you run those, read Zyxel’s advisory index.
  • The general lesson. Binarly’s researchers said advisories and version numbers “cannot be blindly trusted.” For your own register, close high-risk items on evidence of the fixed state, not on a change ticket.

Sources

  • Zyxel, “Zyxel security advisory for out-of-bounds write vulnerability in GS1900 series switches,” November 3, 2026, checked November 7, 2026
  • Zyxel Community, “Switch GS1900 Series V2.90 Patch 3 Firmware Release,” October 23, 2026, edited November 3
  • Zyxel advisory for CVE-2026-7273, June 16, 2026
  • CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog, version 2026.11.06, checked November 7, 2026
  • Canadian Centre for Cyber Security, AV26-1114, November 3, updated November 4, 2026
  • Help Net Security, “Patched Zyxel GS1900 switches remained open to in-the-wild exploit,” November 5, 2026
  • BleepingComputer, “Zyxel fixes zero-day exploited to hack nearly 1,000 network switches,” November 4, 2026

item.title: Next week’s patch calendar: four KEV deadlines and a Patch Tuesday
item.description: Magento and Brotli are due November 10, VMware ESX November 11 and Ivanti Connect Secure November 13. Microsoft and Fortinet both publish on November 10. One page to plan the week.
item.author: circuits50capital@circuits.fit (Emilio Santos)
item.content:encoded:
Next week stacks up. Four federal patch deadlines from CISA’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog fall between Tuesday, November 10 and Friday, November 13, 2026, and Microsoft and Fortinet both publish on Patch Tuesday, November 10. None of this is new on its own. Together it is a full week of change windows for a small IT team, and it is easier to plan on Wednesday than to discover on Monday.

This is a calendar, not a fresh alert. We covered the Magento and Brotli listings and the Ivanti listing when they were added. What follows puts every date in one place, checked against CISA’s catalog feed version 2026.11.03, released November 3 at 3:00 PM ET.

The calendar

Swipe the table sideways to see every column.

DateWhatWho should care
Tue Nov 10KEV due: Adobe Commerce and Magento, CVE-2026-48356 (added Oct 27)Anyone running a Magento or Adobe Commerce store, or paying an agency to
Tue Nov 10KEV due: Google Brotli, CVE-2026-111497 (added Oct 27)Anyone shipping or hosting software that decompresses Brotli; ask vendors
Tue Nov 10Microsoft November security release (second Tuesday)Every Windows and Microsoft 365 shop
Tue Nov 10Fortinet publishes advisories for its October 22 FortiOS, FortiManager and FortiAnalyzer hardening releaseFortiGate and FortiManager owners
Wed Nov 11KEV due: Broadcom VMware ESX, CVE-2026-41709 (added Oct 28)Anyone running VMware hosts on premises
Fri Nov 13KEV due: Ivanti Connect Secure, CVE-2026-118527 (added Oct 30)Ivanti VPN owners

The catalog marks known ransomware use as Unknown for all five CVEs. Federal due dates bind only federal civilian agencies under BOD 26-04. For a private firm they are a priority signal: CISA lists a flaw only when it has evidence of exploitation.

What each listing is

  • Adobe Commerce and Magento, CVE-2026-48356. CISA describes an unrestricted upload of a file with a dangerous type (CWE-434) that could result in arbitrary code execution. The fix is in Adobe security bulletin APSB26-73.
  • Google Brotli, CVE-2026-111497. An unchecked return value (CWE-252, CWE-787) that lets a remote, unauthenticated attacker corrupt decoder memory with a crafted compressed stream, which can disclose memory, crash the process or potentially run code. Brotli is a library inside many products, so the fix is Brotli 1.2.1 or a vendor update that includes it. CISA’s entry says the flaw “could be used by different products.”
  • Broadcom VMware ESX, CVE-2026-41709. Insufficient logging (CWE-778): an attacker who already has admin access can perform some operations without being logged. It is not an entry point. It is a way to hide. That is why it is on an exploited list.
  • Ivanti Connect Secure, CVE-2026-118527. Generation of predictable identifiers (CWE-340) that lets an authenticated attacker upload attacker-controlled files to a known location. CISA notes it can be chained with CVE-2026-104935 and CVE-2026-111357. The second of those was due November 2.

Patch Tuesday, November 10

November 10 is the second Tuesday of the month, Microsoft’s regular release day. As of this morning, Microsoft’s security update API lists releases through October (published October 13) and no November release yet, which is normal before the day. We will not guess at its contents.

Fortinet is the less routine item. In an October 21 post, Fortinet CISO Carl Windsor said a coordinated hardening release for FortiOS, FortiManager and FortiAnalyzer would ship October 22, with fixes for vulnerabilities found through what Fortinet calls its frontier AI-assisted testing program. The post says the fixes include critical and high-severity issues and that public advisories will be published on November 10. The fixed versions are listed now: for example FortiOS 7.4.13, 7.6.8 and 8.0.2 or above.

That gap matters. Fortinet itself warns that once advisories and patches are public, attackers can diff the fix to find the weakness, and that AI tools can shorten the time from patch to working exploit to “hours or days.” If you have a FortiGate on the internet and it is not on a fixed version, November 10 is the day the details become public, not the day the risk starts.

What it means for CFOs and CISOs

  • Plan the week as one change window, not six. The Microsoft release, the Fortinet upgrade and the VMware and Ivanti fixes touch different systems, but often the same one or two people. Book their time now.
  • Edge devices first. Ivanti Connect Secure and FortiGate sit on the internet by design. They are the systems most often used as an entry point, and both appear on this calendar.
  • Third-party code is the harder question. Brotli is a component, not a product. You will rarely patch it yourself; you will ask your vendors whether their product includes an affected version. An SBOM makes that a lookup instead of an email chain. Our SBOM request pack is built for exactly that ask.
  • Agencies and managed providers count. If an agency hosts your store or an MSP runs your firewall, the deadline is still yours to track. Ask in writing.

What to do this week

  1. Inventory by Friday. Answer four yes-or-no questions: do we run Magento or Adobe Commerce, VMware ESX, Ivanti Connect Secure, or any Fortinet device? Write the owner’s name next to each yes.
  2. Fortinet now. Check the FortiOS, FortiManager and FortiAnalyzer versions against the fixed versions in Fortinet’s post. Upgrade before November 10. If you cannot, Fortinet’s own interim advice is to restrict admin interfaces to trusted IP addresses and keep FortiManager off the internet.
  3. Magento by Tuesday. Apply APSB26-73 or confirm in writing that your agency has. Ask when, and for which store.
  4. Email your key software vendors about Brotli. One line: does your product include Google Brotli, and if so, is it on 1.2.1 or otherwise patched for CVE-2026-111497?
  5. VMware and Ivanti by Wednesday and Friday. Apply Broadcom’s and Ivanti’s fixes from the advisories CISA links. For Ivanti, confirm the earlier chained fixes are also in.
  6. Book Patch Tuesday. Hold a two-hour window on Wednesday, November 11 to read the Microsoft release and push it to a pilot group first.
  7. Check admin logins. These flaws reward stolen admin credentials. Confirm MFA is on for every firewall, VPN, hypervisor and store admin account, and that no admin password is shared in a spreadsheet. Our password manager guide covers how to fix that for a small team.

What to watch next

  • Microsoft’s November release on November 10, and whether any of its fixes are flagged as already exploited. Those tend to reach the KEV catalog within days.
  • Fortinet’s PSIRT advisories on November 10. Watch for CVE numbers, severity scores, and any later note that a flaw is being exploited.
  • New KEV additions. CISA’s feed updates as listings are added, and three-day deadlines, as with WordPress last week, are now common.

We publish a free weekly roundup of newly exploited vulnerabilities: what they are, who is affected and what to patch first. Subscribe free to get it. If you want help deciding what applies to you, our Quick Answer service covers that question.

Sources

  • CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog JSON feed, version 2026.11.03, 1,767 entries, checked November 4, 2026
  • CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog
  • Adobe security bulletin APSB26-73
  • Google Brotli 1.2.1 release
  • Broadcom VMware security advisory
  • Ivanti Connect Secure security advisory
  • Microsoft Security Response Center, security updates API, checked November 4, 2026
  • Fortinet, “Fortinet Releases Security Hardening Release for Multiple Products,” Carl Windsor, October 21, 2026
  • BOD 26-04, Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk

item.title: Your Microsoft 365 renewal price, line by line
item.description: Microsoft’s July 1 list prices reach each customer at its next renewal. Business Basic rises 16%, Business Standard 12%, Premium does not move. The math for 10 and 25 seats.
item.author: circuits50capital@circuits.fit (Emilio Santos)
item.content:encoded:
Microsoft raised list prices on most Microsoft 365 business and enterprise suites on July 1, 2026. Existing customers stay on their current price until renewal, so the increase reaches each firm on its own renewal date. For a business on an annual term, that means renewals landing between now and mid-2027 are when the new price shows up on the invoice.

Here is what changed, line by line, with the math for a 10-person and a 25-person firm, and what to check before you sign.

What Microsoft changed

Microsoft announced the update on December 4, 2025. Its Licensing Resources page, dated February 16, 2026 and re-read on November 4, 2026, sets out the details:

  • Pricing took effect July 1, 2026.
  • Existing customers remain on current pricing until renewal.
  • Prices are list prices in U.S. dollars, per user per month, and “may vary by country and currency.”
  • Standalone Teams and Copilot SKUs are not included.

Business plans (with Teams)

Swipe the table sideways to see every column.

PlanOldNewChange
Microsoft 365 Business Basic$6.00$7.0016%
Microsoft 365 Business Standard$12.50$14.0012%
Microsoft 365 Business Premium$22.00$22.00No change
Microsoft 365 Apps for business$8.25$10.0021%

The no-Teams versions move the same way: Business Basic $4.40 to $5.40, Business Standard $9.29 to $10.79, Business Premium unchanged at $18.79.

Enterprise and add-ons

PlanOldNew
Office 365 E3$23.00$26.00
Office 365 E5$38.00$41.00
Microsoft 365 E3$36.00$39.00
Microsoft 365 E5$57.00$60.00
Microsoft 365 Apps (per user)$12.00$14.00
Entra ID Plan 1$6.00$7.00
Entra ID Plan 2$9.00$10.00
Microsoft 365 F3$8.00$10.00

Microsoft pairs the price change with additions. The Business suites get 50GB more email storage and Copilot Chat enhancements; Business Basic and Standard also get URL time-of-click protection. Microsoft 365 E3 adds Defender for Office 365 Plan 1 and several Intune features. Nonprofit pricing moves with commercial at a fixed 60 to 75% discount, and Business Basic stays free for nonprofits.

The math for a small firm

Examples computed from Microsoft’s list prices, annual totals. Your price may differ if you buy through a reseller, pay monthly, or are outside the U.S.

  • 10 seats of Business Standard: $1,500 a year before, $1,680 after. Up $180.
  • 25 seats of Business Standard: $3,750 before, $4,200 after. Up $450.
  • 25 seats of Business Basic: $1,800 before, $2,100 after. Up $300.
  • 10 seats of Apps for business: $990 before, $1,200 after. Up $210.
  • 25 seats of Business Premium: $6,600 before and after. No change.
  • A mixed 25-person firm, 15 Business Standard and 10 Business Basic, plus Entra ID Plan 1 on 5 admins: $2,250 + $720 + $360 = $3,330 before; $2,520 + $840 + $420 = $3,780 after. Up $450, about 14%.

Those are not large sums. The point is the shape. The gap between Business Standard and Business Premium narrowed from $9.50 to $8.00 per user per month. If you were paying for Standard plus separate security add-ons that Premium already includes, the renewal is the moment to do that comparison again.

What it means for CFOs and CISOs

  • The increase lands on your renewal date, not on July 1. Check the date on your Microsoft 365 admin center billing page or your reseller’s invoice. If it is in the next six months, you have time to act.
  • Unused seats now cost more. A licensed account belonging to someone who left in the spring is a 12 to 16% bigger waste on Basic or Standard after renewal.
  • Premium is relatively cheaper. Business Premium did not move. For firms that need Intune device management or Defender, the case for consolidating onto Premium got slightly better.
  • New features may change your stack. URL time-of-click protection in Basic and Standard may overlap with an email security add-on you already pay for. Overlap is the easiest saving at renewal.

What to do this week

  1. Find the renewal date and term. In the Microsoft 365 admin center, go to Billing, then Your products. Note each subscription’s renewal date, seat count and whether it is annual or monthly.
  2. Export active users. Pull the sign-in report and list licensed accounts with no sign-in in 90 days. Remove or downgrade them before renewal, not after.
  3. Price the renewal yourself. Multiply seats by the new list price for each plan. Compare that to any renewal quote from your reseller.
  4. Run the Premium comparison. List every security or device-management add-on you pay for alongside Business Standard. If the total per user is close to $22, price Premium.
  5. Ask your reseller in writing for the renewal price per SKU, the term, and whether any promotion or multi-year option is available.

If Microsoft 365 is the renewal in front of you, the Microsoft 365 Renewal Check ($79) reviews your license export for unused seats, over-licensed users, add-ons and Copilot seats, and returns a written next-step list in 2 business days.

If you would rather hand this off, our Renewal Audit reviews up to 25 software renewals, Microsoft 365 included, for a fixed $199 and returns a written report in 5 business days. If you want the spreadsheet instead, the Renewal & Risk Operator Pack ($29) includes a renewal scorecard, and the free software renewal scorecard runs in your browser.

What to watch next

  • Message Center notices. Microsoft says tenants get at least 30 days’ notice before packaging changes arrive. Watch for the feature additions that come with your plan.
  • Country and currency pricing. Microsoft’s page says prices may vary outside the U.S. If you pay in another currency, ask your reseller for the local figure.
  • Other vendors. Software renewal increases rarely come alone. Use the same pass on your other large subscriptions this quarter; our guide How to read a SaaS renewal sets out the 90-day timeline.

Backups are not in the renewal

None of the plans above include a separate backup of your mail, OneDrive and SharePoint data. If you are reviewing the renewal anyway, price one in. IDrive Microsoft 365 backup is $20 per seat per year on IDrive’s page, checked November 10, 2026. Paid link: we may earn a commission. Microsoft’s own Microsoft 365 Backup is pay-as-you-go at $0.15 per GiB per month. We compare both in password managers and backup tools for small teams.

Sources

  • Microsoft Licensing Resources, “Microsoft 365 Pricing and Packaging Updates,” February 16, 2026, checked November 4, 2026

Related: How to build a software renewal tracker and Software buying is an operating skill.

item.title: Write the staff AI policy now. The federal-state fight will not write it for you.
item.description: A December 2025 executive order pushes for a federal framework that preempts conflicting state AI laws. A small firm’s real exposure is closer to home: client data, accuracy and payment fraud.
item.author: circuits50capital@circuits.fit (Emilio Santos)
item.content:encoded:
A 20-person firm does not need to predict how the fight between Washington and the states over AI regulation ends. It needs a one- or two-page rule that tells staff what they may put into an AI tool, which tools are approved, and who checks the output before it reaches a client. That rule is useful whichever way federal preemption goes, because almost everything in it is about your own data, contracts and customers.

Here is where the federal and state picture stands as of November 4, 2026, what we could and could not verify today, and what a small firm should write down now.

Where the rules stand

  • December 11, 2025: the White House order. Executive Order 14365, “Ensuring a National Policy Framework for Artificial Intelligence,” sets a policy of “a minimally burdensome national policy framework for AI.” It directed the Attorney General to set up an AI Litigation Task Force within 30 days to challenge state AI laws it considers inconsistent with that policy, and directed the Secretary of Commerce to publish, within 90 days, an evaluation identifying “onerous” state AI laws. It also called for a legislative recommendation for a federal framework that preempts conflicting state laws, while saying that recommendation should not preempt state laws on child safety, AI data center infrastructure, or state government use of AI.
  • The order is not a statute. It directs federal agencies. It does not itself repeal any state law. A state AI law stays in force unless a court strikes it down or Congress preempts it.
  • States keep legislating. Several states have passed laws on AI disclosures and automated decisions in hiring and other areas. We did not cite any specific state law in this piece because we could not re-check the official text today. If you operate in a state with an AI law, read that state’s official text or ask counsel.
  • FTC impersonation rule, comments close November 30. On October 1, 2026, the Federal Trade Commission published a proposed rule in the Federal Register that would address search engines, social media and other digital platforms that further government and business impersonation scams. It is a proposal, not a compliance date. Comments close November 30, 2026. It is relevant here because AI-generated voices and messages are now a common tool in impersonation fraud.

Why a small firm should write a policy anyway

The legal fight is about what AI developers and large deployers must disclose or test. The everyday risk at a small firm is simpler and already covered by rules you live with:

  • Client confidentiality. Pasting a client contract into a consumer AI tool may breach your engagement terms or an NDA, regardless of any AI law.
  • Personal data. Existing privacy and sector rules still apply to employee and customer records you put into a tool.
  • Accuracy. If AI drafts a client deliverable, your firm is responsible for what it says.
  • Impersonation and fraud. A cloned voice asking for a wire transfer is a payment-control problem, not an AI-policy problem. Your policy should still say how payment and password requests are confirmed.
  • Insurers and clients ask. Security questionnaires increasingly ask whether you have an AI use policy and a list of approved tools.

What it means for CFOs and CISOs

  • Do not wait for preemption. Even a broad federal standard would leave your contracts, confidentiality duties and existing privacy obligations in place.
  • The tool list is the control. Most AI risk at a small firm comes from unapproved tools on personal accounts. An approved-tools list, with business accounts and the right data settings, does more than a long policy.
  • Spending follows the list. Once you know which AI tools staff use, you can consolidate subscriptions. Duplicate AI seats are now a common line in software renewals.
  • State exposure is a hiring question first. If you use AI to screen candidates or make employment decisions, that is where state laws most often bite. Ask counsel before you use it there.

What to put in the policy

Keep it to one or two pages. Our one-page AI use rule has a template. At minimum:

  1. Approved tools. Name them, with the account type (business, not personal) and the data setting (for example, model training off).
  2. Data you may not paste. Client confidential material unless the tool is approved for it, personal data about staff or customers, passwords and keys, and anything under NDA.
  3. Human review. Anything that goes to a client, a regulator or the public is read and approved by a named person before it leaves.
  4. No automated decisions about people in hiring, pay or discipline without sign-off from the owner and, where required, counsel.
  5. Payment and password confirmation. A voice, video or message is never approval for a payment, a bank change or a password reset. Confirm on a second channel using the number already on file. Our guide Stop using a voice as approval covers this.
  6. Accounts. AI tools are signed into with business accounts protected by MFA, and those logins are stored in the firm’s password manager, not in a browser or a spreadsheet.
  7. How to ask. One named person approves new tools. Give a turnaround time so staff do not route around the rule.
  8. Review date. Revisit every six months, or when a law that applies to you changes.

What to do this week

  1. Inventory. Send a two-question survey: which AI tools do you use for work, and on which account? Expect more answers than you think.
  2. Pick the approved list. Choose one or two tools, move people onto business accounts, and set data and retention settings.
  3. Write the page using the eight points above and circulate it for sign-off.
  4. Fix the payment rule if it is not already written down. This is the one with direct cash risk.
  5. Note the FTC comment date, November 30, if impersonation scams have touched your business and you want to comment.

If you would rather have it written for you, our AI Use Policy + AI Tool Inventory service delivers a policy and a tool inventory for $149 in 4 business days.

What to watch next

  • Commerce’s evaluation of state AI laws and any lawsuits filed by the Justice Department’s AI Litigation Task Force. Those would be the first concrete signs of which state laws are under challenge.
  • Federal legislation. The order asks for a legislative recommendation. Only Congress can preempt state law broadly.
  • The FTC impersonation proposal after comments close on November 30.
  • Your own state. Check your state legislature’s official site for AI laws with effective dates in 2026 and 2027.

Sources

  • The White House, “Ensuring a National Policy Framework for Artificial Intelligence,” Executive Order 14365, December 11, 2025, checked November 4, 2026
  • Federal Register, Federal Trade Commission, “Rule on Impersonation of Government and Businesses,” proposed rule, October 1, 2026, comments close November 30, 2026
  • NIST AI 600-1, Generative AI Profile of the AI Risk Management Framework

Related: Board questions on generative AI and AI agent inventory.
