item.title: How to Build a Software Renewal Tracker
item.description: Sort by the notice deadline, not the renewal date. Columns, formulas, a four-part score and a worked example.
item.author: circuits50capital@circuits.fit (Emilio Santos)
item.content:encoded:
A software renewal tracker is a list of contracts sorted by the last day you can still say no. Everything else in the sheet exists to help you decide what to say before that day arrives.

Most templates you will find are a vendor list with an expiry date column. That is a start, but it sorts by the wrong date and it does not tell you what to do. This guide walks through a tracker that does both: it calculates the notice deadline for each contract, and it scores each one so the quarterly review starts with a recommendation instead of a blank stare. You can build everything here in Excel, LibreOffice Calc or Google Sheets with ordinary formulas.

What a renewal tracker is for

The tracker has three jobs. First, it stops a contract from renewing without a decision. Many software agreements renew automatically unless you give written notice a set number of days before the term ends. Once that notice window closes, the vendor has no reason to negotiate, because you are already committed to another term. Second, it puts evidence next to each decision: how many people use the tool, what it costs per active user, and what the vendor wants to charge next year. Third, it records who decided what, so the next review does not reopen the same question from scratch.

If your sheet only does the first job, it is a calendar. That is still worth having. But the second and third jobs are where the money is, because they turn "renew" from a default into a choice.

Keep one row per contract, not one row per vendor. A company with two separate order forms from the same vendor, signed a year apart, has two renewal dates and two notice deadlines. Merge them into one row and you will miss one of them.

The input columns

These are the columns a person types into. Keep them on the left of the sheet and visually distinct from the formulas, for example white cells for inputs and grey for calculations, so nobody types over a formula.

ColumnWhat to enterWhere it comes from
Vendor and productThe vendor name and the specific product or order formThe signed order form
CategoryCRM, security, collaboration, finance and so onYour own list; keep it short
Contract ownerOne named person, not a teamWhoever uses the tool and will defend or drop it
Annual costTotal cost per year; multiply monthly plans by 12The last invoice or the order form
Renewal dateThe day the current term endsThe order form, not the billing portal
Notice period (days)Days of notice the contract requires to cancel or change; 0 if noneThe terms, usually in a renewal or termination clause
Auto-renews?Yes or NoThe same clause
Licensed seats and active usersSeats you pay for, and people who actually signed in recentlyThe tool's admin console
Usage % (if not seat-based)Share of a usage commitment actually consumedUsage reports, for metered or platform contracts
Business criticalityLow, Medium, High or CriticalThe owner's honest answer to "what stops if this is down for a day"
Security itemsSSO, MFA, SOC 2 report, SBOM availability, breach historySecurity review, the vendor's trust page, questionnaire answers
Exit difficultyLow, Medium or HighHow hard it would be to export data and move
Price increase at renewal (%)The increase in the renewal quote, or the contractual cap if there is no quote yetThe quote in writing

Use drop-down lists (data validation) for every column with a fixed set of answers. A criticality column that contains "High", "high" and "HIGH - ask Sam" cannot be scored.

Decide in advance what "active" means. A common rule is a sign-in within the last 90 days. Whatever rule you pick, write it on an instructions tab and apply it the same way to every tool, or the usage numbers will not be comparable.

The calculated columns

The notice deadline is the most important formula in the sheet, and it should always be a formula, never a typed date. With the renewal date in column F and the notice period in column G:

Notice deadline:            =IF(AND(ISNUMBER(F5),ISNUMBER(G5)),F5-G5,"")
Days until notice deadline: =IF(U5="","",U5-TODAY())

The ISNUMBER check matters. If the notice period is blank, a plain =F5-G5 treats it as zero and shows the renewal date as the deadline, which looks safe and is not. A blank should produce a blank deadline and a visible prompt to go and read the contract.

If a contract states its notice period in months, use =EDATE(F5,-G5) with months in column G. Calendar months and 30-day blocks do not line up, so match what the contract says.

Then group the days remaining into windows that a meeting can work through: notice passed, next 30 days, 31 to 60 days, 61 to 90 days, later. A nested IF does this, and conditional formatting can colour each band.

Three money columns make the conversation concrete:

  • Effective usage % is active users divided by licensed seats, capped at 100%, or the usage percentage for contracts that are not seat-based.
  • Cost per active user is annual cost divided by active users. This is the number that surprises people, because a tool with a reasonable list price per seat can be expensive per person who uses it.
  • Estimated waste is annual cost multiplied by (1 minus effective usage). It is an estimate, not a refund you are owed, but it is the right starting point for a seat true-down.

Add a next-year cost column, annual cost multiplied by (1 plus the price increase), so the meeting sees the real number being approved.

Scoring a contract

A score does not make the decision. It sorts the list so the meeting spends its time on the contracts that need a conversation. A simple, explainable approach scores four things from 0 to 100 and takes a weighted average.

  • Usage score: effective usage multiplied by 100. A tool used by 65% of its seats scores 65.
  • Criticality score: Low 25, Medium 50, High 75, Critical 100.
  • Security score: the average of points for each security item. For example SSO Yes 100, Partial 50, No 0; MFA Enforced 100, Available 60, No 0; SOC 2 Type II 100, Type I 60, None 0. Treat a blank as Unknown and give it low points (25 is reasonable), so missing answers pull the score down instead of being ignored.
  • Price score: 100 at no increase, falling in a straight line to 0 at an increase you consider unacceptable, such as 20%. The formula is =MAX(0,MIN(100,100*(1-increase/0.2))).

Weights are a policy choice. One reasonable starting set is usage 35, criticality 25, security 25 and price 15. Divide by the total of the weights rather than assuming they add up to 100, so anyone can change them without breaking the formula.

Then turn the score into a recommendation with rules checked in a fixed order:

  1. Cancel if usage is below 25% and criticality is Low or Medium.
  2. Renew if the score is at least 70 and the price increase is 5% or less.
  3. Replace if the score is below 45 and exit difficulty is not High.
  4. Renegotiate for everything else.

The order matters. A barely used, low-importance tool should be flagged for cancellation even if its security posture is excellent. And a poor score on a tool that is very hard to leave becomes Renegotiate, not Replace, because replacement is not a realistic plan this quarter.

Next to the recommendation, add a short "why" column that says which rule fired. People trust a recommendation they can read.

A worked example

Two invented contracts, scored with the weights and rules above, as of November 2, 2026.

Contract 1: a CRM. Annual cost $48,000. Renewal date March 31, 2027. Notice period 60 days, auto-renews. 120 seats licensed, 78 active. Criticality High. SSO Yes, MFA Enforced, SOC 2 Type II, SBOM Unknown, no known breaches. Exit difficulty High. Renewal quote: 8% increase.

  • Notice deadline: March 31, 2027 minus 60 days is January 30, 2027, which is 89 days away. It sits in the 61 to 90 day window, so it belongs on this quarter's agenda.
  • Effective usage: 78 / 120 = 65%. Cost per active user: $48,000 / 78 = about $615. Estimated waste: $48,000 × 35% = $16,800. Next-year cost: $51,840.
  • Scores: usage 65, criticality 75, security (100 + 100 + 100 + 25 + 100) / 5 = 85, price 100 × (1 − 0.08 / 0.20) = 60.
  • Weighted score: (65 × 35 + 75 × 25 + 85 × 25 + 60 × 15) / 100 = 71.75.
  • Recommendation: the score clears 70, but the 8% increase is above the 5% limit, so Renew does not apply. Renegotiate.

The evidence for that negotiation is already in the row: 42 unused seats, about $16,800 of estimated waste, and a quote that adds $3,840. A reasonable ask is a true-down toward the active count and a price cap, agreed before January 30.

Contract 2: a survey tool. Annual cost $6,000. 40 seats, 6 active, so usage is 15%. Criticality Low. The Cancel rule fires first, whatever the other scores say. The meeting's only question is whether the six people who use it have somewhere else to go, and who sends the notice.

Running it every quarter

A tracker that is updated once a year is a historical document. A quarterly rhythm is enough for most companies:

  • A week before, the owner of the sheet refreshes active users from each admin console and asks contract owners for any new quotes.
  • Set a fixed as-of date for the meeting so everyone sees the same day counts, instead of TODAY() shifting while people read.
  • In the meeting, work by deadline first, then by recommendation: anything in the notice-passed or next-30-days window, then Cancel and Replace, then Renegotiate, then a quick confirmation of the Renews.
  • Record the outcome in two input columns, Our decision and Decision owner. Where the decision differs from the recommendation, write one line saying why. That line is what the next review needs.
  • Put a calendar reminder 30 days before every notice deadline in the next 90 days, in the decision owner's calendar, not the spreadsheet owner's.

For the conversation with the vendor itself, the 90-day SaaS renewal checklist covers what to pull at each stage, and the free software renewal scorecard scores a single contract in the browser.

Common mistakes

  • Sorting by renewal date. The renewal date is when the money moves. The notice deadline is when the decision is locked. Sort and filter by the deadline.
  • Typing the deadline by hand. It goes stale the first time someone corrects a renewal date or notice period.
  • Treating a blank notice period as zero. It hides exactly the contracts nobody has read yet.
  • Using the billing portal's date. Portals often show the next invoice date, which is not always the term end in the order form.
  • Counting provisioned accounts as users. An account that has not signed in for a quarter is a cost, not a user.
  • Letting the score decide. The score sorts the agenda. A person still makes the call and writes it down.
  • A team as owner. "IT" never sends the cancellation notice. A named person does.
  • One row per vendor. Separate order forms have separate deadlines.

FAQ

How many contracts does a spreadsheet handle before we need software for this?

A spreadsheet works well into the hundreds of rows if the inputs are disciplined. The limit is usually not size but upkeep: if nobody refreshes usage each quarter, a dedicated tool will not fix that either.

What if a contract has no notice period?

Enter 0, deliberately, so the sheet can tell it apart from a blank. The deadline then equals the renewal date.

Should monthly subscriptions go in the tracker?

Yes, with annualized cost, so they sort by real exposure. They rarely carry notice risk, but they often carry waste.

Who should own the sheet?

Usually finance, because finance sees every invoice. Each row still needs a contract owner outside finance who knows whether the tool is used.

Related

  • How to read a SaaS renewal
  • Software buying as an operating skill
  • Software renewal scorecard (free tool)
  • Software buying is an operating skill

Rather hand it off? The Renewal Audit reviews up to 25 renewals for a fixed $199 and returns a written report in 5 business days.

item.title: How to Build a Risk Exception Register
item.description: Owner, reason, compensating control and an expiry date that enforces itself. Columns, scoring and a review log.
item.author: circuits50capital@circuits.fit (Emilio Santos)
item.content:encoded:
Every company has controls it does not apply everywhere. The difference between a managed exception and a hole is a written row with an owner, a reason, a compensating control and an expiry date.

A risk exception register, sometimes called a policy exception log or risk acceptance register, is where those rows live. This guide covers what to record, how to score it, how to make expiry dates enforce themselves, and the mistakes that turn a register into a list of permanent waivers. It works in any spreadsheet.

What a risk exception is

An exception is an approved, time-limited departure from a specific control or policy. A legacy server that cannot run the endpoint agent. A vendor integration that needs a service account with a password that does not rotate. A lab instrument on an operating system that no longer receives updates. In each case the business has a reason, the control cannot be applied today, and someone senior enough accepts the remaining risk for a defined period.

That definition excludes three things that often end up in the same spreadsheet:

  • Open findings. A vulnerability nobody has looked at yet is not an exception. It becomes one only when someone decides not to fix it on the normal timeline and says why.
  • General risks. "Ransomware" is a risk register entry, not an exception. Keep a separate IT risk register for those.
  • Things that should never be waived. Some controls are close to non-negotiable for most organizations, and many teams mark them as not eligible for exception at all. The site's free risk exception register tool treats known-exploited vulnerabilities, MFA, backups and EDR that way. Decide your own list and write it at the top of the register.

The columns

ColumnWhat to enter
Exception IDA unique reference such as EX-014. Never reuse one.
Risk or control exceptionOne sentence: what is not being done, where.
Control or policy referenceThe clause or control ID being departed from, so reviewers can read the original requirement.
System or assetThe specific host, application or vendor, matching your asset inventory name.
Risk ownerThe named person accountable for the system and the fix.
Business reasonWhy the control cannot be applied now. "Vendor does not support it until version 9" is a reason. "Too hard" is not.
Compensating controlsWhat reduces the risk in the meantime, specifically enough that someone could check it.
Inherent likelihood and impact (1 to 5)The risk with the control missing and nothing else done.
Residual likelihood and impact (1 to 5)The risk with the compensating controls that exist today.
ApprovalRequested, Approved, Rejected, Closed or Withdrawn.
Approved byThe person who accepted the risk. Not the person who asked for it.
Granted date and expiry dateWhen it started and when it stops being valid.
NotesThe fix plan, ticket references, anything a reviewer needs.

Those are the inputs. Everything else in the register should be calculated, so nobody has to remember to update it.

Scoring inherent and residual risk

Score each exception twice on the same likelihood by impact matrix: once as if nothing compensates, and once with the compensating controls in place. The gap between the two is the value of those controls, and it is what the approver is really being asked to rely on.

A 5 by 5 matrix is the usual choice. Multiply likelihood (1 Rare to 5 Almost certain) by impact (1 Minimal to 5 Severe) for a score from 1 to 25. Keep the matrix itself on a settings tab and look scores up from it rather than multiplying in each row, so you can adjust individual cells later without rewriting formulas:

Inherent score: =INDEX(Settings!$C$12:$G$16,H5,I5)
Severity:       =VLOOKUP(Q5,Settings!$B$20:$C$23,2,TRUE)

The severity lookup uses an approximate match against a small table of minimum scores. One workable set of bands:

Minimum scoreSeverityReview every
1Low180 days
5Medium90 days
10High60 days
20Critical30 days

Write one-line definitions for each likelihood and impact level next to the matrix. Without them, two people will score the same exception differently and the register will measure who filled it in rather than the risk. The IT risk register guide goes further into writing those scales.

The rule that matters most: residual risk is scored on controls that exist today. A compensating control that is "planned for next quarter" does not lower the residual score until it is running.

Status, expiry and review dates

Status should be a formula built from the approval column and the expiry date, checked in order:

  1. Rejected if the approval says Rejected.
  2. Closed if it says Closed or Withdrawn.
  3. Pending approval if it is anything other than Approved.
  4. No expiry set if it is approved but the expiry date is blank.
  5. Expired if the expiry date is in the past.
  6. Expiring soon if the expiry is within a set window, such as 30 days.
  7. Active otherwise.

"No expiry set" is its own status on purpose. An approved exception with no end date is the most common way a register fails, and it should be impossible to miss on the dashboard.

Next review due is the last review date plus the review interval for the exception's severity, using residual severity where it exists. A simple overdue flag compares that date with today. With this in place, a Critical exception that has not been looked at in a month shows up without anyone having to remember.

Two integrity checks are worth adding. A duplicate ID check (=IF(COUNTIF($A$5:$A$304,A5)>1,"Duplicate ID","")) catches copied rows. And an expiry check, described below, catches a register that disagrees with its own review history.

The review log

Keep reviews on a separate tab, one row per review: date, exception ID, reviewer, decision (Keep, Extend, Close), new expiry date if extended, and the evidence checked. Do not overwrite the register's history in place. An auditor asking "who extended this, and on what basis" needs the log, not the latest value.

The register can then look up its own last review date from the log with MAXIFS, which returns the newest review date for that ID. It can also compare its expiry date with the new expiry from the latest Extend decision and flag any mismatch. That catches the common case where the meeting agreed an extension and nobody updated the register. Note that MAXIFS needs Excel 2019 or later, Microsoft 365, LibreOffice or Google Sheets.

A worked example

An invented exception, as of November 2, 2026.

  • EX-014. Lab analysis PC runs an operating system that no longer receives security updates. Policy reference: patching standard, section 3.
  • Business reason: the instrument vendor's control software only supports that operating system. A supported version is promised in the vendor's next release.
  • Compensating controls: PC moved to an isolated network segment with no internet access; file transfer only through one monitored share; local admin removed from users.
  • Inherent: likelihood 4, impact 4, score 16, High.
  • Residual: likelihood 2, impact 4, score 8, Medium. Review every 90 days.
  • Approved by: the head of operations, granted October 1, 2026, expiring March 31, 2027.

The register shows it as Active. The next review is due 90 days after the last review date. Suppose the January review finds the vendor release has slipped, and the reviewer extends to June 30, 2027 with a dated plan. The reviewer adds a Review Log row with decision Extend and the new date. Until someone also changes the expiry date on the register, the expiry check flags the row. That flag is the whole point: the register and its history must agree.

Now suppose the network segmentation is undone during an office move. The residual likelihood is no longer 2. The honest response is to rescore residual on the controls that exist today, which here puts it back to the inherent 16, High, and to bring it to the next review early.

Common mistakes

  • No expiry date. An exception without an end date is a policy change nobody approved.
  • Residual scored on intentions. Planned controls do not reduce today's risk.
  • The requester approves their own exception. Approval should come from someone who owns the consequence and is not the person who benefits.
  • Vague compensating controls. "Monitoring" is not checkable. "Alerts on any outbound connection from host X, reviewed daily by the SOC" is.
  • Extending without a plan. Each extension should carry a new date and a reason the fix slipped.
  • Mixing findings and exceptions. The register loses meaning when half the rows are unresolved tickets.
  • Overwriting history. Without a review log, nobody can show how an exception came to be three years old.

FAQ

How long should an exception last?

As long as the fix realistically takes, and no longer than your policy allows. Many teams cap exceptions at a year and require a fresh approval after that.

Who should approve?

Someone with authority over the business area that carries the risk, with security's recommendation recorded. Higher residual severity should need a more senior approver.

How often should we review the whole register?

Monthly or quarterly, working through Expired, Expiring soon, Pending approval, then housekeeping such as missing expiry dates and overdue reviews.

Will an auditor or insurer accept a spreadsheet?

What they usually look for is evidence: owner, approval, compensating controls, expiry and review history. The format matters less than whether those are present and current. Check with your own auditor.

Related

  • Risk exception register (free tool)
  • How to build an IT risk register in Excel
  • What a cyber insurer will still ask
  • The cloud shared-responsibility checklist

item.title: How to Build an IT Risk Register in Excel
item.description: Write the scales first, then look scores up from a 5 by 5 grid. Formulas, severity bands and review dates.
item.author: circuits50capital@circuits.fit (Emilio Santos)
item.content:encoded:
An IT risk register is only as good as the agreement behind its numbers. The spreadsheet part takes an afternoon. Getting two people to give the same risk the same score takes longer, and it is the part that matters.

This guide builds a register in Excel (it works the same way in LibreOffice Calc and Google Sheets) around a 5 by 5 likelihood by impact matrix: the columns, the lookup formulas, severity bands that set how often each risk is reviewed, and a worked example with the arithmetic shown.

What the register is for

A risk register lists the things that could go wrong with your technology, how likely and how damaging each one is, what you are doing about it, and who is accountable. It is a decision tool: it tells leadership where to spend money and attention, and it shows an auditor, insurer or board that risks are known and owned.

Keep it separate from two neighbouring lists. A vulnerability or findings tracker holds individual technical issues with fix dates. A risk exception register holds approved, time-limited departures from a control. A risk register sits above both: "a critical system is compromised through an unpatched internet-facing service" is a risk; a specific missing patch is a finding; an approved decision not to patch one server until March is an exception. The three can reference each other by ID, but merging them makes each harder to read.

The columns

ColumnWhat to enter
Risk IDA unique reference such as R-007
Risk statementCause, event and consequence in one sentence
CategorySecurity, availability, vendor, data, compliance, people
Asset or serviceWhat is affected, using your inventory names
Risk ownerA named person who can approve spending to treat it
Existing controlsWhat is in place today, specifically
Inherent likelihood and impact (1 to 5)The risk before those controls
Residual likelihood and impact (1 to 5)The risk with those controls working
TreatmentReduce, accept, transfer or avoid
Planned actions and due dateWhat will change the residual score, and when
Last reviewedDate of the most recent review

Calculated columns follow: inherent score and severity, residual score and severity, next review due, and an overdue flag.

Write risk statements in the form "because of [cause], [event] could happen, leading to [consequence]". "Phishing" is a topic. "Because staff can approve payment changes by email, an attacker impersonating a supplier could redirect a payment, leading to a direct financial loss" is a risk someone can score and treat.

Write the scales first

Before anyone scores anything, write a one-line definition for each level, and put them on a settings tab next to the matrix. For example:

LevelLikelihoodImpact
1Rare: not expected in the next yearMinimal: little or no effect on operations, data or customers
2Unlikely: could happen, no sign it is being attemptedMinor: short disruption or limited internal data exposure
3Possible: plausible; similar issues seen elsewhereModerate: noticeable disruption, some customer or financial effect
4Likely: expected to be attempted or to occurMajor: significant outage, sensitive data exposure or financial loss
5Almost certain: already happening or easy to exploitSevere: prolonged outage, large breach or regulatory action

Where you can, attach numbers to impact levels that fit your company: a dollar range, hours of downtime, number of customer records. "Major" means something very different to a 30-person firm and a 3,000-person one. If you use a published method such as NIST SP 800-30, follow its structure, but the definitions still have to be written for your organization.

The middle levels are the hardest. If Possible and Likely cannot be told apart in writing, most risks will end up scored 3 by 3, and the register will look tidy while saying very little.

Building the 5 by 5 matrix in Excel

Put the matrix on the settings tab as a grid: likelihood 1 to 5 down the rows, impact 1 to 5 across the columns, and the score in each cell. The default is likelihood multiplied by impact, so the grid runs from 1 in the top left to 25 in the bottom right. Say the grid occupies Settings!C12:G16.

In the register, look the score up from the grid instead of multiplying in each row:

Inherent score: =IF(OR(H5="",I5=""),"",INDEX(Settings!$C$12:$G$16,H5,I5))
Residual score: =IF(OR(J5="",K5=""),"",INDEX(Settings!$C$12:$G$16,J5,K5))

Why bother, when =H5*I5 gives the same answer? Because many organizations eventually want to weight impact more heavily than likelihood, for example so that a rare but severe event scores higher than a frequent trivial one. With a lookup grid, that is a change to a few cells on one tab. With multiplication, it is a rewrite of every row.

Use data validation to limit likelihood and impact cells to whole numbers from 1 to 5. A typed 3.5 or "med" breaks the lookup. If you want the heat map look, apply conditional formatting to the grid itself and to the severity columns so the colour follows the band.

Severity bands and review frequency

Turn the score into a severity with a small table of minimum scores and an approximate-match lookup:

Severity: =IF(Q5="","",VLOOKUP(Q5,Settings!$B$20:$C$23,2,TRUE))
Minimum scoreSeverityReview every
1Low180 days
5Medium90 days
10High60 days
20Critical30 days

VLOOKUP with TRUE returns the band for the largest minimum score that does not exceed the score, so the minimums must stay in ascending order. These bands are an example, not a standard. Set them to match your risk appetite, and write down who approved them.

Add a third column to the band table for review frequency, then calculate next review due from residual severity:

Next review due: =IF(W5="","",W5+VLOOKUP(T5,Settings!$C$20:$D$23,2,FALSE))
Overdue?:        =IF(X5="","",IF(X5<TODAY(),"Overdue","OK"))

This is what keeps the register alive. High and Critical risks come back to the table often; Low ones do not consume meeting time.

A worked example

Two invented risks, scored with the scales and bands above.

R-007: payment redirection. "Because supplier bank details can be changed on the strength of an email, an attacker impersonating a supplier could redirect a payment, leading to a direct financial loss."

  • Inherent: likelihood 4 (these attempts are common), impact 4 (a single payment could be large). Score 16, High.
  • Existing controls: any bank detail change requires a call-back to a number already on file, and a second approver in finance.
  • Residual: likelihood 2, impact 4. Score 8, Medium, reviewed every 90 days.
  • Treatment: reduce. Action: add the call-back step to the payments system workflow so it cannot be skipped, due end of quarter.

R-012: ransomware on file servers. "Because staff can open email attachments on machines with access to shared drives, ransomware could encrypt the file servers, leading to a multi-day outage."

  • Inherent: likelihood 3, impact 5. Score 15, High.
  • Existing controls: EDR on all endpoints, nightly backups with an offline copy, restore tested last quarter.
  • Residual: likelihood 2, impact 5. Score 10, still High, reviewed every 60 days.

R-012 shows something useful. Good controls cut the likelihood, but the impact of a successful attack stays severe, so the residual score lands exactly on the High boundary. That is not a scoring error. It tells the owner that further work should aim at impact, for example faster restore or segmenting the shares, and it tells the board this risk deserves attention even with strong controls in place.

Common mistakes

  • No written scales. Scores then reflect who filled in the row.
  • Everything is a 3 by 3. Usually a sign the middle definitions are too close together.
  • Residual scored on planned controls. Score the controls that are running today. Planned work goes in the actions column.
  • Topics instead of risks. "Cloud" cannot be scored or owned.
  • Typed severities. A severity typed by hand and a severity calculated from the score will disagree eventually. Always calculate.
  • No review date. A register without review dates is a snapshot from the day it was written.
  • Owner is a department. A department cannot approve a budget line. A person can.

FAQ

Should we use a 3 by 3 or a 5 by 5 matrix?

A 3 by 3 is easier to score consistently. A 5 by 5 gives more resolution, but only if the five levels are clearly defined. Start with whichever your team will actually apply the same way.

How many risks should be on the register?

Enough that every significant system and process is covered, few enough that each one gets reviewed. Many small and mid-sized companies keep a few dozen. Combine near-duplicates.

Where do accepted risks go?

An accepted risk stays on the risk register with treatment "accept" and a review date. If acceptance means departing from a specific control, record that departure in the exception register too, with an expiry.

Does Excel 2016 work?

The formulas on this page do. Functions such as MAXIFS, useful for pulling the latest review date from a review log, need Excel 2019 or later.

Related

  • How to build a risk exception register
  • Risk exception register (free tool)
  • What a cyber insurer will still ask
  • Limit what an agent can touch

item.title: PHP2Shell was probed before the patch. Start the log review at October 17.
item.description: PHP fixed two unauthenticated remote code execution bugs on October 21. Amazon saw an exploit attempt on October 17. Most companies run PHP inside software they buy, so the work is a vendor inventory, not only a patch.
item.author: circuits50capital@circuits.fit (Emilio Santos)
item.content:encoded:
On Wednesday, October 21, 2026, the PHP project released PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 and 8.2.35. The releases fix CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, two critical vulnerabilities, both rated 9.2 on CVSS version 4, that the project says “can allow unauthenticated remote code execution.” The pair is now widely called PHP2Shell. The project’s advisory says the people at risk are “all PHP installations serving web requests,” including PHP-FPM, Apache with mod_php, php-cgi, FrankenPHP and LiteSpeed.

Amazon’s threat intelligence team says it saw a PHP2Shell exploit attempt against its honeypots on October 17, four days before the fix was public. Sophos and Amazon have both reported exploitation attempts. Neither has confirmed a successful compromise: Sophos says the attempts it saw failed, and Amazon says PHP2Shell is “now seeing broad exploitation attempts in the wild” but that it is unclear whether any would have succeeded on real-world systems. For most companies, PHP is not something they bought on purpose. It runs under the marketing site, the help desk, the vendor portal and the appliance in the rack. That changes what this week’s work looks like.

What happened

  • October 20: the PHP security team gave advance notice of a critical release for October 21 at 14:00 UTC, addressing two vulnerabilities rated CVSS v4.0 9.2. It said it might release earlier if exploitation appeared.
  • October 17: Amazon Threat Intelligence later reported a PHP2Shell exploit attempt in its MadPot honeypot telemetry dated October 17, from an IP address tied to a commercial anonymization network. Amazon says it is unclear how the actor got exploit information before disclosure.
  • October 21, about 02:00 UTC: Amazon says it found multiple proof-of-concept exploits, the earliest around this time, and further attempts against its sensors through 08:00 UTC from varied infrastructure, which it reads as multiple actors.
  • October 21: PHP published the fixed releases and its advisory. CVE-2026-109618 is code execution through memory corruption when PHP handles an out-of-memory error partway through a request. CVE-2026-109619 is code execution through internal state that survives after its memory is freed and is reused by a later request on the same worker. PHP rates mod_php the highest-risk setup, with “a demonstrated exploit where an unauthenticated request can trigger the attack before any application code runs.”
  • October 21: CISA urged organizations to patch immediately. At publication it said it had not observed exploitation. CERT-EU issued advisory 2026-018 the same day.
  • October 22, 16:18 UTC: Sophos updated its advisory to report multiple exploit attempts and, at the time, one successful exploitation.
  • October 22, 21:21 UTC: Sophos corrected that update. Its customer telemetry shows scanning and a small number of failed exploitation attempts, and there is no evidence of a successful compromise. The payload, likely a Mirai variant Sophos calls Potassium, was not delivered because the attempt was blocked. Sophos adds that building a working exploit is “not straightforward,” and that the vulnerabilities remain serious and patching remains the main recommendation.
  • October 23: PHP published an informational advisory about a further, unlikely remote code execution path (CVE-2026-115560) that needs an unusual combination of configuration and application code. It suggests setting session.upload_progress.enabled=0 until the next regular bugfix release, a mitigation already listed for CVE-2026-109619.

PHP 8.1 and older get no updates from the PHP project. Because of the severity, the security team published minimal source backports for 7.4, 8.0 and 8.1, and some distributions and long-term-support vendors ship their own fixes. PHP 8.2 reaches end of life on December 31, 2026.

As of this writing on October 22, neither CVE is in CISA’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog. We checked the catalog JSON feed, version 2026.10.21 with 1,754 entries, this afternoon. NVD lists both records as “Undergoing Analysis.”

What it means for CISOs

Two working assumptions break here. The first is that the disclosure date is the start of the risk window. Amazon’s advice is direct: “Start investigations from the earliest known exploitation, not from the disclosure date. For PHP2Shell, investigate from at least starting on October 17.” No successful compromise has been confirmed, but a system patched this week was exposed from at least the 17th, and the log review is how you show it was not entered.

The second is the patch service level. Amazon’s CISO writes that for critical bugs in internet-facing systems, teams should “measure patch and mitigation timelines in hours,” because “a 7-day or 30-day SLA assumes a delay that no longer exists.” Whether you adopt that is a policy choice with a staffing cost, and it should be made on purpose rather than discovered during the next incident.

The harder problem is visibility. CISA notes that PHP “is often a component of other software and prevalence may not be directly observable.” CERT-EU makes the same point and points to a list maintained by the Dutch NCSC of third-party products that embed PHP. Your scanner may find the servers you run. It will not tell you which SaaS vendor’s customer portal runs mod_php on 8.1.

What it means for CFOs

This is a supplier question with a paper trail. The useful output this week is a dated list: which vendors run PHP in the service you use, what version, and when they patched. That list is what your auditor, insurer and board will ask for if anything turns up later, and “the vendor said we are fine” is not an answer you can defend without a date and a name.

Budget for the tail. Systems on PHP 8.1 or older either get upgraded, get a paid backport from an LTS vendor, or come offline; CISA and Sophos both recommend taking unpatchable internet-facing systems offline or behind network-layer authentication. If the business refuses, record a dated, owned exception rather than an informal one. The 8.2 end-of-life date on December 31 means a second round of the same decision is ten weeks away. If a compromise is confirmed at a public company, the Form 8-K question follows; the SEC clock starts at the materiality determination, not at the advisory.

What to do this week

  1. Inventory where PHP runs. Start with internet-facing systems you host, then list vendors and products that embed PHP: content sites, help desks, portals, appliances, hosted plugins. Use the NCSC-NL list linked from CERT-EU as a starting point.
  2. Ask suppliers for patch status in writing. One question: do you run PHP in the service we use, on what version, and on what date did you apply the October 21 fixes? Record each answer with the date and the person who gave it. The SBOM request pack and vendor claim checker help with the follow-ups.
  3. Patch. Move to 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 or 8.2.35, or your distribution’s fixed package, internet-facing systems first, and restart every worker. PHP lists configuration mitigations for systems that cannot update at once, but says they “do not make an installation safe.”
  4. Review logs back to October 17. Amazon suggests looking for POST requests carrying the PHP_SESSION_UPLOAD_PROGRESS string in form uploads, and reviewing web server logs. Check vendor-hosted systems by asking the vendor for the same review.
  5. Check for webshells and unexpected processes. CISA says to watch for PHP worker processes launching shells or downloading tools. Amazon adds unexpected process execution or file modification on web servers. Sophos’s post lists indicators from the attempts it saw.
  6. Deal with end-of-life versions. Anything on 8.1 or older goes offline, behind network-layer authentication, or into the risk exception register with an owner and an expiry date.

What to watch next

Watch the KEV catalog. If CISA adds either CVE, the row will carry a federal due date and may mark forensic triage, which would make the October 17 lookback a formal expectation for agencies. Watch Sophos and Amazon for any confirmed successful exploitation; so far both report attempts, and the payload Sophos analyzed, a likely Mirai variant, was blocked before delivery. Watch vendor advisories, which tend to arrive later than the upstream fix. And watch NVD, where analysis of both records is still under way.

Sources

  • PHP news archive, 2026: advance notice of October 20; security advisory and releases 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 and 8.2.35, October 21, 2026 (affected setups, mitigations, backports, 8.2 end of life); informational advisory on session upload progress (CVE-2026-115560), October 23, 2026
  • GitHub security advisories GHSA-w8hw-w9fx-j79w (CVE-2026-109618) and GHSA-6wmf-4rv5-p3rp (CVE-2026-109619)
  • NVD entries CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, both published October 21, 2026, status Undergoing Analysis as of October 22
  • CISA, “Critical Vulnerabilities in PHP Require Immediate Patching,” October 21, 2026
  • CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog and JSON feed, version 2026.10.21, checked October 22, 2026 (neither CVE listed)
  • CERT-EU security advisory 2026-018, “Critical Vulnerabilities in PHP,” October 21, 2026, and the NCSC-NL list of affected third-party software
  • CJ Moses, “Amazon Threat Intelligence identifies PHP2Shell exploitation prior to public disclosure in MadPot,” AWS Security Blog, October 21, 2026
  • Sophos Counter Threat Unit, “Proof-of-concept exploit released for PHP vulnerabilities,” updated October 22, 2026, 16:18 UTC, corrected October 22, 2026, 21:21 UTC

Related: The BeyondTrust bug was used before the patch. Check the logs., the same lookback logic for a remote-support appliance, and CISA listed three bugs attackers are already using.

item.title: The BeyondTrust bug was used before the patch. Check the logs.
item.description: CISA listed BeyondTrust Remote Support CVE-2026-102764 on October 16 with forensic triage required. BeyondTrust says it was exploited as a zero-day on August 29.
item.author: circuits50capital@circuits.fit (Emilio Santos)
item.content:encoded:
On Thursday, October 15, 2026, BeyondTrust published security advisory BT26-05 for its Remote Support product. The flaw is CVE-2026-102764, scored 9.3 on CVSS version 4 and rated Critical. BeyondTrust describes it as improper origin validation in an internal messaging component that could let a remote attacker perform file operations on an affected appliance. Every Remote Support version up to and including 26.2.3 is affected. The next day, October 16, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency added the CVE to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog. The catalog row carries a federal due date of October 19 and marks forensic triage as Yes.

The patch is the easy part. BeyondTrust’s own account says the bug was used as a zero-day in late August, nearly seven weeks before the advisory. If you, or a supplier that reaches into your network, run a self-hosted appliance, the question this week is not only “are we patched?” It is “was the box used before we patched, and could we tell?”

What happened, in order

BeyondTrust’s blog post on BT26-05, last updated October 16 at 12:00 p.m. EDT, gives this timeline:

  • August 29, 2026: an actor exploited the zero-day against one BeyondTrust-hosted Remote Support instance and one self-hosted Remote Support appliance.
  • September 28: BeyondTrust’s threat hunting found indications of the event at the hosted customer. The company says it contained the instance within 27 minutes of first detection.
  • September 30: Mandiant shared findings from the self-hosted customer that matched BeyondTrust’s own.
  • October 8: BeyondTrust released the BT26-05 patch. Hosted instances of Remote Support and Privileged Remote Access were patched automatically. The advisory itself says the patch had been applied to all Remote Support SaaS customers as of October 9.
  • October 15: coordinated public disclosure of the CVE, the advisory, the blog and Mandiant’s analysis.

As of the October 16 update, BeyondTrust says it knows of only those two affected customers and has seen no adversary activity since August. It assesses with moderate to high confidence that the actor is the China-nexus cluster Mandiant and Google Threat Intelligence Group track as UNC5221, which Mandiant now calls ARMORY CASTLE. It also warns that this actor tends to use a zero-day selectively and then, once the flaw is public, move to broad exploitation of every instance still unpatched.

Two details matter for buyers. Privileged Remote Access shares the affected code; BeyondTrust found no way to exploit it there but released the patch for it anyway. And self-hosted Remote Support customers without automatic updates must patch by hand, after first upgrading if they are older than 24.3.1.

Why the catalog row says forensic triage

The catalog entry links to Binding Operational Directive 26-04, which CISA issued on June 10, 2026. It binds only federal civilian agencies, but it is the clearest public statement of how the government ranks urgency. It asks four questions: is the asset publicly exposed, is the CVE in the catalog, can an attacker automate the exploit, and does the attacker gain partial or total control. For the top tier, an agency must remediate within three days and carry out a forensic triage to check whether the system was already compromised.

CISA’s implementation guidance sets recommended, not mandatory, targets: scoping within two hours of the catalog addition, evidence collection and patching within 24 hours, and an escalation decision within 48 to 72 hours. Evidence comes first, because patching can destroy it.

BeyondTrust’s account explains why that order is right here. It says the actor planted a web shell, escalated to full administrative control within minutes, installed persistence designed to survive a reboot, read the appliance’s stored secrets, and then deleted logs and its own tools before leaving. Evidence kept only on the appliance “may not survive,” the company writes, and what is there “cannot be implicitly trusted.” Logs forwarded off the box are what count.

The same week on the catalog

BeyondTrust was one of nine additions to the catalog between October 13 and October 16. CISA added Ivanti Connect Secure CVE-2026-104935 and Windows CVE-2026-96951 on October 13; Palo Alto Networks PAN-OS CVE-2026-0322, Cisco Secure Email Gateway CVE-2026-76519 and two AhsayCBS backup-server flaws, CVE-2026-105133 and CVE-2026-105134, on October 14; an Atlassian Data Center file-access flaw, CVE-2026-21589, on October 15; and Fortinet CVE-2025-61624 alongside BeyondTrust on October 16. Six more, four of them Plex Media Server, followed on October 20. Every one of the nine October 13 to 16 rows, apart from AhsayCBS CVE-2026-105133, is marked for forensic triage.

As in the October 1 catalog briefing and the NetScaler note, most of the list sits at the network edge: VPNs, firewalls, email gateways, remote access and backup servers.

What it means for CISOs

A remote-support appliance is privileged access by design. BeyondTrust says so plainly: the appliance “stores and brokers privileged credentials across an estate,” which makes it both a credential source and a map of who connects to what. Treat a compromise of one as a compromise of every credential it injected.

The second lesson is about your detection stack. BeyondTrust says its sensors fired in real time when the attacker escalated privileges, but the automated triage feature in a third-party detection platform closed those alerts as false positives. The company is now working with that vendor so automated triage cannot close high-severity signals on its own. Ask your managed detection provider, in writing, which high-severity alerts its automation can close without a person.

What it means for CFOs

The exposure is often not your own appliance. Managed service providers, outsourced IT desks and software vendors use remote-support tools to reach their customers. If one of them runs self-hosted Remote Support, your systems sit one hop away from a box that was exploited as a zero-day. That is a third-party risk question with contract consequences: notification clauses, audit rights and who pays for forensic work.

Forensic triage costs money even when it finds nothing; budget for it as part of patching. If you carry cyber insurance, check now whether the notice clause is triggered by a suspected incident or only a confirmed one, and whether the insurer requires its own forensics firm. For a public company, a confirmed compromise also raises the Form 8-K question. The four-business-day clock under Item 1.05 starts at the materiality determination, not at the advisory date; the SEC clock briefing and the 8-K materiality worksheet cover how to record that decision.

What to do this week

  1. Find every instance. List self-hosted BeyondTrust Remote Support and Privileged Remote Access appliances, their versions, and whether automatic updates are on. Anything at 26.2.3 or below without the BT26-05 patch is exposed. Anything below 24.3.1 needs an upgrade first.
  2. Preserve before you patch, where you still can. Image the appliance and export its logs, then apply the patch.
  3. Get logs off the box. Forward appliance syslog and session events to your SIEM, as BeyondTrust recommends. Look back to at least August 29, the first exploitation date it gives.
  4. Hunt for behavior, not indicators. BeyondTrust’s list: privileged sessions from residential broadband or commercial VPN addresses you cannot tie to a known administrator or ticket; unrecognized script files in web directories; web service accounts spawning shells; unexpected permission changes to Jump Items or Teams; and gaps in log forwarding that start and end within a single session.
  5. Rotate if anything looks wrong. Rotate every credential the appliance stored or injected, review new multi-factor registrations on privileged accounts, and watch those accounts for logins outside managed sessions.
  6. Ask your suppliers. Send each MSP and IT vendor with remote access one question: do you use self-hosted BeyondTrust Remote Support or Privileged Remote Access to reach us, and on what date did you apply BT26-05? Record each answer with the date and the name of the person who gave it, so “we’re patched” is a dated fact rather than an assurance.
  7. Do not waive it. If patching slips, record the owner and expiry in the risk exception register, and confirm owners for the week’s other rows you run.

What to watch next

BeyondTrust says it is withholding technical details while self-hosted appliances are still being patched. When those details are published, expect wider exploitation of anything left unpatched, which is the pattern the company itself predicts for this actor. Watch the BT26-05 blog and the catalog row for changes. Under BOD 26-04, federal agencies’ Phase III deadline, 180 days from issuance, falls on December 7, 2026 by our count; agency patch reporting will keep edge-device rows in the news through year-end.

Sources

  • BeyondTrust security advisory BT26-05, issued October 15, 2026 (CVE-2026-102764, CVSSv4 9.3, CWE-290, affected and fixed versions, SaaS patched as of October 9)
  • BeyondTrust, “ARMORY CASTLE and BT26-05: What Security Teams Need to Know”, October 15, 2026, updated October 16 (timeline, attribution, hunting and rotation guidance)
  • CISA alert, two known-exploited vulnerabilities added, October 16, 2026 (BeyondTrust CVE-2026-102764 and Fortinet CVE-2025-61624)
  • CISA catalog entry, CVE-2026-102764, and the catalog JSON feed, version 2026.10.21 (dates added, due dates and forensic triage fields for every row cited)
  • CISA alerts for October 13, October 14 and October 15, 2026
  • BOD 26-04, Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk, June 10, 2026, and its implementation guidance on forensic triage, updated August 25, 2026
  • NVD entry, CVE-2026-102764

Related: PHP2Shell was probed before the patch (October 22), Citrix NetScaler is on the exploited catalog again, CISA listed three bugs attackers are already using, and the guide Limit what an agent can touch, which applies the same least-privilege logic to automated access.
