item.title: Gartner says the AI build-out may not pay back. Check who runs your compute.
item.description: Gartner says $3.5 trillion of AI infrastructure could face impairment by 2030 and that over 80% of neoclouds will cease independent operations. For buyers, that is a supplier-risk question.
item.author: circuits50capital@circuits.fit (Emilio Santos)
item.content:encoded:
On October 14, 2026, Gartner published a forecast that reads less like a market sizing and more like a credit warning. More than $3.5 trillion of AI infrastructure spending could be exposed to impairment by the end of 2030 if AI providers keep spending at the current pace, the firm said. Its arithmetic is simple to state. To cover announced capital spending, financing costs and a 12% return on invested capital, AI data center owners would need to generate a cumulative $8.5 trillion in revenue through 2030. Gartner forecasts that enterprise and consumer AI revenue attributable to those data centers will reach no more than $3.6 trillion over the same period.

One week later, on October 21, Gartner forecast that worldwide IT spending will reach $7.35 trillion in 2027, up 15%, with data center systems the fastest-growing line. Read together, the two releases say the build-out is still accelerating while the revenue to pay for it is not keeping pace. This briefing is not about whether AI stocks are overvalued. It is about what happens to a company that rents its compute from a provider that cannot earn back what it spent.

What Gartner said

The October 14 release, quoting Will Sommer, a senior director analyst at Gartner, sets out these figures:

  • AI providers are expected to spend nearly $1 trillion on AI infrastructure in 2026 and an additional $6 trillion between 2027 and 2030.
  • Covering that capital, its financing and a 12% hurdle return would require $8.5 trillion in cumulative revenue through 2030. Attributable AI revenue is forecast at no more than $3.6 trillion.
  • Because most AI-native providers run asset-light models, Gartner predicts that less than half of AI revenue will be earned by providers that own significant AI infrastructure.
  • On the current trajectory, more than $4 trillion in asset value could be exposed to write-down risk through 2032, and Gartner does not expect the 12% return to be reached until the end of 2032 at the earliest.
  • AI-optimized infrastructure as a service is forecast to grow from $66 billion in 2027 to $174 billion in 2030. Sommer says that growth “will be too low for most AI compute providers to recover their AI investments before the current generation of AI semiconductors is replaced.”
  • By 2030, Gartner predicts that cost pressure and a lack of a differentiating business model will force over 80% of neocloud providers to cease independent operations.

Gartner separates neoclouds from hyperscalers for a reason it states directly: hyperscalers have large, diversified revenue that could sustain AI investment for years, while neoclouds must earn returns on AI-optimized capacity soon to keep operating.

The numbers, read plainly

By our arithmetic from Gartner’s figures, the gap between required and forecast revenue is about $4.9 trillion. Forecast revenue covers roughly 42% of what the spending needs. That is a forecast, with Gartner’s own assumptions behind it, and the full model sits in client research the public cannot read. But the direction matches the rest of the firm’s recent output. On October 21 it put 2027 data center systems spending at $1.366 trillion, up 55.5% after a 73.8% rise in 2026, and said memory prices have more than doubled over the past 12 months. Hardware that costs more and wears out on a short cycle has to earn its money quickly.

The phrase “cease independent operations” matters for buyers. It does not mean four in five neoclouds vanish. It means most are expected to be acquired, merged or folded into someone else. For a customer, that is a change of counterparty. The contract you signed with one company may end up being serviced by another, on that company’s terms.

This site has covered the spending side before. Gartner revised the AI bill looked at the September forecast of $2.7 trillion for 2026 and how little of it lands on a typical company’s purchase orders. AI spend is not the same as AI return looked at whether buyers are getting value. This piece is about the supplier: whether the company selling you compute will still be the company selling you compute in 2028.

What it means for CFOs

Three exposures show up on a buyer’s books. The first is prepayment. Reserved GPU capacity is often sold with large upfront or committed spend. If the provider is acquired or restructured, prepaid capacity may be honored, repriced or stuck in a dispute. The second is price. A provider under pressure to earn a return, or an acquirer that bought it cheaply, has every reason to raise rates at renewal. The third is concentration. If one product line depends on one specialist provider, a forced migration becomes an engineering project with a deadline you did not choose.

None of this argues against using a neocloud. Specialist providers can be cheaper and faster to provision. It argues for pricing counterparty risk the way a treasurer would price a bank deposit above the insured limit: know the exposure, cap it, and have a way out.

What it means for CISOs and founders

For security leaders, a change of control at a compute provider is a data question. Where do model weights, fine-tuning data, logs and customer prompts sit, and who holds the keys after an acquisition? Assignment clauses, data-deletion terms and audit rights decide whether a new owner inherits your data under your terms or theirs. Ask for the subprocessor list now, because it may change.

For founders, the inference line is the risk. If gross margin depends on today’s GPU-hour price from one provider, model a renewal at a higher rate and a migration month at double cost. The token cost to gross margin tool and the AI cost per finished task calculator make that a short exercise.

What to do this week

  1. List every compute and inference contract by provider type: hyperscaler, neocloud or specialist GPU cloud, model API vendor, or reseller. Note who actually owns the hardware.
  2. Total the prepaid and committed amounts by provider, and the months remaining on each commitment.
  3. Read the change-of-control and assignment clauses. Can the provider assign the contract to an acquirer without your consent? Do you get a termination right if it does?
  4. Check data-export and deletion terms. Confirm you can retrieve model artifacts, data and logs in a usable format, within a stated time, at a stated cost.
  5. Run a price-shock case. Model your inference cost at the next renewal with a higher unit price, and a one-month dual-running cost for a migration. Choose the uplift yourself; Gartner did not publish one.
  6. Avoid long prepayments with sub-scale providers until you have answers to items 3 and 4. Shorter terms at a slightly higher rate can be cheaper than a stranded commitment.
  7. Add the provider to your renewal review. The software renewal scorecard already checks price caps, notice periods, data return and export; score compute contracts the same way.

What to watch next

Watch for consolidation among GPU cloud providers: acquisitions, mergers and distressed financings are the early form of “cease independent operations.” Watch hyperscaler capital spending guidance in quarterly earnings, because Gartner’s impairment case rests on spending continuing at the current pace. Watch memory and server pricing, which Gartner expects to stay inflated through 2027. And watch your own provider’s financing: a reserved-capacity contract is only as good as the balance sheet behind it. Gartner analysts are due to present more on AI infrastructure at its IT infrastructure and operations conferences in London (November 16 to 17), Tokyo (December 1 to 3) and Las Vegas (December 8 to 10).

Sources

  • Gartner, “Over $3.5 Trillion of AI Infrastructure Spending Could Be Exposed to Impairment by the End of 2030,” October 14, 2026 (all impairment, revenue, neocloud and AI-optimized IaaS figures)
  • Gartner via Business Wire, “Worldwide IT Spending to Grow 15% in 2027, Totaling $7.35 Trillion,” October 21, 2026 (data center systems and memory pricing)
  • Gartner, worldwide AI spending forecast, September 16, 2026 (context, covered in our earlier briefing)

The gap of about $4.9 trillion and the 42% coverage ratio are Circuit & Capital’s arithmetic from Gartner’s published figures, not Gartner numbers. Related: Gartner revised the AI bill, Private credit is quietly funding the software roll-up, and the guide How to read a SaaS renewal.

Follow Circuit & Capital on Bluesky, Facebook and X (@circuitsfit) for new briefings.

item.title: Citrix NetScaler Is on the Exploited Catalog Again
item.description: CISA added CVE-2026-88779 on October 4. The catalog due date is October 7. The September NetScaler rows are a different pair of bugs.
item.author: circuits50capital@circuits.fit (Emilio Santos)
item.content:encoded:
On Sunday, October 4, 2026, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency published a short alert: one vulnerability had been added to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog, based on evidence of active exploitation. The name on the alert is CVE-2026-88779, Citrix NetScaler, an improper restriction of operations within the bounds of a memory buffer. The alert does not print a due date. The catalog does. The row was added October 4. The due date is October 7. Known ransomware campaign use is Unknown. Forensic triage is marked Yes. The catalog file that carries those fields, version 2026.10.04, was released the same Sunday. On Monday, October 5, CISA Cyber posted the CVE on X: the agency had added Citrix NetScaler vulnerability CVE-2026-88779, that same memory-buffer weakness, to the catalog, and told readers to apply mitigations.

This briefing is dated October 7, 2026, the same calendar day as the due date on the row. For a Federal Civilian Executive Branch agency, that clock is today. It is the date on the entry. It is not a date that has already slipped, and it is not a date that arrives tomorrow. For a company the directive does not name, the row is still the official statement that CISA has evidence the bug is being used.

This is an operator note, not a description of how to use the bug. If you run NetScaler ADC or NetScaler Gateway, including under the older names Citrix ADC and Citrix Gateway, the job is to confirm that, open the vendor page the catalog names, apply the fix that page describes, and write down the date. If you do not run it, write that down too, so the next person does not reopen the thread because a contract still says Citrix.

What the row actually says

CISA’s short description is specific, and it is narrower than the vulnerability name suggests. Citrix NetScaler ADC (formerly Citrix ADC) and Citrix NetScaler Gateway (formerly Citrix Gateway) contain an improper restriction of operations within the bounds of a memory buffer that could allow for a denial of service. The product field is NetScaler. The vendor field is Citrix. The weakness identifier on the row is CWE-119. That is the whole impact line. Denial of service means the box can be taken down. It is not, on this row, a claim of remote code execution, and it is not a claim that an outsider can run commands.

The required action is the catalog instruction on the row. Apply mitigations in accordance with vendor instructions, in line with Binding Operational Directive 26-04 and with CISA’s Forensics Triage Requirements. Follow the directive’s guidance for cloud services, or stop using the product if no mitigation exists. Forensic triage on this row is Yes. That Yes is an agency instruction. It is also the reason a private company should not file the printout under “patch only” without someone asking whether the logs deserve a look.

The notes field is the remediation list. It names two Citrix pages: support article CTX697174, and a Citrix community post titled as an explanation of how to understand and address CVE-2026-88779 in NetScaler ADC and NetScaler Gateway. It then names BOD 26-04, the forensics triage guidance published with that directive, and the National Vulnerability Database entry for the CVE. Those are the pages. This briefing does not reprint build numbers from them. A version string copied into a chat is how a team patches the wrong train and calls the row closed. Open CTX697174, read the affected releases there, and write the build you are on next to the build Citrix says is fixed.

The October 4 alert uses a sentence CISA attaches to this class of bug: this type of vulnerability is a frequent attack vector and poses significant risk to the federal enterprise. That sentence describes the type. It is not a count of how often this CVE has been used, and it is not a finding that this particular bug hands over the whole appliance. Read it as the alert’s boilerplate. Read the catalog description when someone asks what this entry can do.

The alert tells you the name. The catalog tells you the date. The vendor page tells you the fix. Skip one of the three and you are guessing.

Who the date binds

The October 4 alert cites BOD 26-04, Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk, as the directive that sets vulnerability-management requirements for Federal Civilian Executive Branch agencies. The alert says the directive applies only to those agencies, and that CISA encourages every other organization to put catalog vulnerabilities first. BOD 22-01 is the older directive that required those same civilian agencies to remediate a listed vulnerability by the due date on the entry. CISA’s program page still says that older directive does not bind everyone else. This row’s required action and its notes point at BOD 26-04 and at the forensics guidance. That is the document to open if a federal customer asks which rule you followed.

The alert also describes how BOD 26-04 sorts work. Agencies are told to move fastest on catalog entries that, on a publicly exposed asset, grant total control after exploitation, and to defer lower-risk vulnerabilities. That is the directive’s sorting rule. It is not CISA’s description of CVE-2026-88779. The description on this row is denial of service. Do not brief a board that this entry is a total takeover because the alert mentioned total control in that sorting rule. A remote-access gateway that stops answering is still an outage: a failed login for every customer on it, and a long night for whoever still knows the old hostname.

A due date with an agency’s name on it is a federal clock. The same row is still evidence that someone is already using the bug against organizations that have no federal clock at all. Ransomware use is marked Unknown. Unknown is not a clean bill. It means CISA has not published that link. Do not brief a board that “this is not ransomware” off that field.

Forensic triage marked Yes is the catalog’s way of saying agencies under BOD 26-04 have to check whether the system was compromised before the patch, using the forensics guidance linked in the notes. This briefing does not restate that guidance, and it does not list log paths or commands. A private company can still decide, with its own counsel and its own logs, whether a bug CISA has called exploited deserves a look backward as well as a patch forward. That decision is not this article.

This is not the September NetScaler pair

The catalog already had this product family on it. On September 27 CISA added CVE-2026-88771 and CVE-2026-88772, both due September 30. Those federal dates have passed. The write-up of that week is CISA listed three bugs attackers are already using. The September rows are still the rows. This October entry does not replace them, and closing them does not close this one.

The first September bug, CVE-2026-88771, is improper input validation. CISA says it could let an unauthenticated attacker run arbitrary commands on NetScaler ADC and NetScaler Gateway. The second, CVE-2026-88772, carries almost the same vulnerability name as the October row: an improper restriction of operations within the bounds of a memory buffer. The short description is different. CISA says the September memory bug could allow remote code execution or a denial of service. The October memory bug, CVE-2026-88779, is described only as a denial of service. Same product. Similar title. Different CVE, different impact line, different due date, different notes.

The September notes point at a different Citrix bulletin, CTX697096, and at Citrix’s write-up of CVE-2026-88771 through CVE-2026-88778. They also say that running the indicators Citrix provided in the NetScaler console may help identify exploitation, and that customers must do the forensic triage BOD 26-04 directs. That is the September instruction. It is not a procedure this page is going to walk, and it is not the notes field on CVE-2026-88779. The October notes name CTX697174 and the later community post. A build that satisfied the September 30 rows is not, by that fact alone, the build this row requires. If the change window in late September was treated as “NetScaler is done,” reopen it and read the new page.

Names are how this gets missed. CISA’s October description uses both the current names and the former ones, Citrix ADC and Citrix Gateway, in the same sentence. A contract, a diagram, or an invoice may still say Citrix. Ask which box you run, which box a partner runs, and which box a Citrix-operated service already moved. The required action’s cloud line is there because those are often not the same appliance.

What to write down today

Make one line, not a program. Product: NetScaler ADC and NetScaler Gateway, and the former names, because that is how the catalog writes them. Next to it: yes, no, or owned by the host. For every yes, write the build you are on, the build CTX697174 says is fixed, the person who can change it, and the date you will check again. If the answer is owned by the host, write the name of the host and the date you asked. For a federal contractor, also write October 7. A customer may ask why the catalog date was missed even when BOD 22-01 and BOD 26-04 do not name you.

Do not turn the line into a claim that you were or were not compromised. The catalog’s Yes on forensic triage tells agencies to look, under the guidance CISA linked. It does not tell a private company what its logs will show. Unknown on ransomware stays Unknown until CISA changes the field.

If the same week produces a question from a public company, the patch date and the materiality date are different clocks. Item 1.05 of Form 8-K runs from the materiality determination, not from the morning a CVE is added to the catalog. A known-exploited bug is not automatically a material incident. It is a fact your customer’s counsel may ask you to explain quickly: what you run, what you patched, and when you decided the incident was or was not material. The note on that clock is the SEC piece. The checklist beside it is Before the Form 8-K clock.

If the box is in the rack, the page to finish is CTX697174. If the box is not yours, the sentence to send is the one that says so, with the date on it. The monthly window can still exist. This row does not wait for it.

Sources

  • CISA alert, one known-exploited vulnerability added to the catalog, October 4, 2026 (CVE-2026-88779; the alert does not state the due date)
  • CISA Cyber on X, CVE-2026-88779 added to the catalog, October 5, 2026
  • CISA catalog entry, CVE-2026-88779 (added October 4, due October 7, ransomware use Unknown, forensic triage Yes)
  • CISA catalog JSON feed, catalog version 2026.10.04, released October 4, 2026 (the labeled fields quoted above)
  • BOD 26-04, Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk, and the forensics triage guidance linked from the catalog notes
  • CISA, Reducing the Significant Risk of Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (BOD 22-01 binds FCEB agencies; CISA urges every other organization to prioritize the catalog)
  • Citrix support article CTX697174, the vendor page named in the CVE-2026-88779 notes, and Citrix’s community post on the same CVE
  • CVE record linked from the October 4 alert, and the NVD entry named in the catalog notes
  • CISA catalog, CVE-2026-88771 and CVE-2026-88772 (added September 27, due September 30; different notes, including Citrix CTX697096)

Related: CISA listed three bugs attackers are already using and The SEC clock starts when you decide it matters.

Follow Circuit & Capital on Bluesky, Facebook and X (@circuitsfit) for new briefings.

item.title: Free tool: AI model cost per finished task
item.description: Compare list price with the cost of a task that actually finishes, and the daily volume where self-hosting beats the API. Runs in your browser. No sign-in.
item.author: circuits50capital@circuits.fit (Emilio Santos)
item.content:encoded:
Not legal, tax, insurance, or procurement advice. Inputs stay in your browser. Nothing is uploaded.

Attempts per task = 1 + average retries. Token cost uses each attempt. Review cost applies to the share of tasks that fail. Cost per successful task divides that total by the success rate. Listed cost is one attempt, before retries, failures, and review. A month in the break-even chart is 30 days. You type the prices. This page does not call a model.

Showing the example. Replace it with your prices.

Output

The comparison appears here.














How to use this


    

  1. Replace the two example models with the prices and token counts you were quoted. Add a third or fourth if you have them.
    2. 

  2. Use the success rate and retries you actually see. A low list price can lose once failed tasks and review time are in the cost.
    3. 

  3. Fill the self-host lines to see the daily token volume where the server costs less than the API, and whether your throughput reaches it.
    4. 







What this calculator does


AI model prices are quoted per million tokens. That number is easy to compare and often misleading. A cheaper model that fails more often needs retries, and failed tasks need a person to fix them. This page converts list prices into the cost of a task that actually finishes, including retries and human review. It also shows the daily token volume at which running your own server would cost less than paying per token through an API.






The math, in plain English


    

  • Cost of one attempt = input tokens ÷ 1,000,000 × input price + output tokens ÷ 1,000,000 × output price.
    • 

  • Attempts per task = 1 + average retries.
    • 

  • Review cost = share of tasks that fail × review minutes ÷ 60 × hourly rate.
    • 

  • Cost per finished task = (attempt cost × attempts + review cost) ÷ success rate.
    • 

  • Self-host monthly cost = server cost + ops hours × ops hourly rate. Break-even daily tokens = monthly self-host cost ÷ 30 ÷ API price per token.
    • 







Worked example


The page loads with two example models. The prices are example numbers for illustration, not quotes from any provider.


Example: low list price. $0.50 per million input tokens, $2 per million output tokens, 2,000 input and 800 output tokens per attempt. One attempt costs about $0.0026. But it succeeds 60% of the time, averages two retries, and each failure takes 15 minutes of review at $80 an hour. Cost per finished task: about $13.35.


Example: higher list price. $3 input and $15 output per million tokens, 1,500 input and 400 output tokens. One attempt costs about $0.01. It succeeds 95% of the time with no retries, and failures take 10 minutes of review. Cost per finished task: about $0.71.


The model that is roughly four times cheaper per attempt is almost nineteen times more expensive per finished task. Almost all of the difference is human review on failed work, not tokens.


For self-hosting, the example uses a $4,000 monthly server, 10 ops hours at $90, and a blended API price of $8 per million tokens. Monthly self-host cost is $4,900. Break-even is about 20.4 million tokens a day. The example server can carry 50 million a day, so above about 20.4 million daily tokens, self-hosting would cost less in this example.






Where to get your inputs


    

  1. Prices. From your provider’s current pricing page or your contract. Providers such as Anthropic publish per-token prices, and they change. Check the date.
    2. 

  2. Token counts. From your API usage logs, averaged over a real sample of the task, not a demo prompt.
    3. 

  3. Success rate and retries. From a test set of at least a few dozen real tasks, judged by the person who owns the output.
    4. 

  4. Review minutes. Time a reviewer fixing failed outputs. Do not guess.
    5. 







How to read the result


If review cost dominates, improving quality is worth more than finding a cheaper model. If token cost dominates and quality is equal, list price matters. If your daily volume is far below break-even, self-hosting adds risk without saving money. If it is above break-even but beyond the server’s throughput, you need more hardware and the math changes.






Limitations


    

  • The page does not call any model or fetch prices. You type them.
    • 

  • It treats every failure as needing review. Some failures are caught and discarded automatically.
    • 

  • The self-host line ignores hardware depreciation schedules, power, and the cost of staff turnover. Treat it as a first screen. The cloud repatriation note lists the fuller comparison.
    • 

  • Batch discounts, cached-input pricing, and committed-use contracts can change the per-token price. Use the price you actually pay.
    • 







FAQ


Are my numbers saved or sent?


They stay in your browser. Nothing is uploaded.


What success rate should I use?


The rate at which a reviewer would accept the output without edits. Partial credit belongs in review minutes.


How does this connect to gross margin?


Feed the cost per finished task into the token cost to gross margin calculator to see what it does to a product’s margin.






Related


    

  • Token cost to gross margin
    • 

  • Put an AI cost on one workflow
    • 

  • The new unit economics of AI-native startups
    • 

  • The AI productivity paradox at mid-market companies
    • 

  • AI spend is not the same as AI return
    • 

  • Gartner revised the AI bill
    •

item.title: Free tool: AI agent inventory and access map
item.description: List each agent, the identity it uses, and what it can change. Flags stale reviews and shared logins. Runs in your browser. No sign-in.
item.author: circuits50capital@circuits.fit (Emilio Santos)
item.content:encoded:
Not legal, tax, insurance, or procurement advice. Inputs stay in your browser. Nothing is uploaded.

A row is flagged when the agent uses a person's account or a shared account, when it can write and has no owner, or when the last access review is missing or 90 days old or older. The file import is read in this browser. It is not uploaded.

Showing the example. Replace it with your agents.

Output

The flag count appears here.














How to use this


    

  1. Replace the example rows. One agent per row. Use “Its own account” only when the agent does not sign in as a person.
    2. 

  2. Read the flag count. A shared login, write access with no owner, or a review older than 90 days stays on the row until you change it.
    3. 

  3. Export the CSV if you want a copy. Import reads a file on this device and does not send it anywhere.
    4. 







What this inventory does


An AI agent is software that can take actions, not only answer questions. It might reply to a ticket, update a record, send an email, or start a payment. Each of those actions runs under some identity, and that identity decides what the agent can touch. This page is a simple register: one row per agent, the account it uses, what it can read and change, whether it can spend money or send external messages, and when its access was last reviewed.


Gartner’s September 30, 2026 note on CISO priorities reported that 54% of organizations in a second-quarter survey of 297 security leaders had no defined approach to limiting agent access, or relied on access defined for a person. The first step out of that position is a list. You cannot limit what you have not written down.






How the flags work


The page flags three conditions on each row:


    

  • Person’s or shared account. If the agent signs in as an employee or a shared login, its actions are hard to tell apart from a human’s, and it usually has more access than its task needs. The OWASP Top 10 for LLM applications calls this kind of problem excessive agency: excessive functionality, permissions, or autonomy.
    • 

  • Can write, no owner. An agent that can change systems needs a named person who answers for it.
    • 

  • Stale or missing review. No access review date, or a review 90 days old or older. Access drifts. A quarterly review is a practical floor.
    • 







Worked example


The page loads with two example rows. They are illustrations, not real systems.


Example: invoice drafter. Owner A. Patel. It drafts invoice notes, runs in the company tenant under its own account, can read billing, cannot write anywhere, cannot spend or send external messages, and was reviewed 10 days ago. No flags.


Example: support reply. No owner. It replies to tickets in the helpdesk, uses a person’s account, can read tickets and write ticket comments, can send external messages, handles customer data, and was last reviewed 120 days ago. It gets three flags: a person’s account, write access with no owner, and a review older than 90 days.


The fix list for the second row writes itself: give the agent its own service identity with only ticket-comment rights, name an owner, and schedule a review. Because it sends messages to customers, the owner should also decide which replies need a person to approve them.






Filling in a row


    

  1. Name and purpose. Use the name people actually call it, and one line on what it is for.
    2. 

  2. Where it runs. The product or platform: a helpdesk, a CRM, a cloud account, a developer tool.
    3. 

  3. Identity. Check the admin console. If the agent was connected by an employee clicking “authorize,” it probably uses that employee’s access.
    4. 

  4. Can read and can write. List systems, not vague scopes. “Billing” is better than “finance data.”
    5. 

  5. Spend and external messages. Mark Yes if it can make any payment, purchase, or refund, or send anything outside the company.
    6. 

  6. Sensitivity and review date. The most sensitive data it can reach, and the date someone last confirmed its access.
    7. 







Limitations


    

  • The list is only as good as discovery. Agents built into SaaS products you already own may not appear in any IT inventory. Ask each application owner.
    • 

  • The page does not connect to your systems or verify access. It records what you type.
    • 

  • Three flags are a floor, not a full risk assessment. An agent with its own account can still have far too much access.
    • 







FAQ


Does my data leave the browser?


No. The CSV import is read on this device, and nothing is uploaded.


What counts as an agent?


For this list, anything that can take an action in a system without a person clicking each step. A chatbot that only answers questions is lower priority, but list it if it can read sensitive data.


How often should we review?


The page flags reviews at 90 days. Review sooner when the agent gains a new connection or permission.


What comes after the inventory?


Set limits for each agent with the agent access limit sheet, and write a one-page rule for staff with A one-page AI use rule.






Related


    

  • Agent access limit sheet
    • 

  • Limit what an agent can touch
    • 

  • Six questions every board should ask about generative AI
    • 

  • Five moves Gartner wants from a CISO before 2027
    • 

  • Nvidia put the fence outside the agent
    •

item.title: Free tool: SEC 8-K materiality worksheet
item.description: Record who decided an incident was material, and count four business days to the Item 1.05 date. Runs in your browser. No sign-in.
item.author: circuits50capital@circuits.fit (Emilio Santos)
item.content:encoded:
Not legal, tax, insurance, or procurement advice. Inputs stay in your browser. Nothing is uploaded.

Not legal advice. The Item 1.05 clock starts when the company determines the incident is material, not when it is discovered. This page counts four business days after that determination. It skips weekends and US federal holidays in the year of the determination and the following year. A holiday on Saturday is taken on Friday. A holiday on Sunday is taken on Monday. The page does not decide whether the incident is material.

Showing the example. Replace it with your record.

Output

The due date appears here.














How to use this


    

  1. Enter the discovery time and the escalation. Those dates are a record. They do not start the four-day count.
    2. 

  2. Name the person who owns the materiality decision, check the thresholds you actually use, and write the evidence you considered.
    3. 

  3. Enter the determination date. The output is the fourth business day after that date, and a one-page record you can copy or print.
    4. 







Why this worksheet exists


Since the SEC adopted its cybersecurity disclosure rules on July 26, 2023, a public company that determines a cybersecurity incident is material must file a Form 8-K under Item 1.05. The SEC’s release says the filing is generally due four business days after the company determines the incident is material, not four days after it is discovered. The release also allows a delay if the US Attorney General determines that immediate disclosure would pose a substantial risk to national security or public safety and notifies the Commission in writing.


That design puts weight on one moment: the materiality determination. Auditors, regulators and plaintiffs will later ask who made it, when, on what evidence, and against which thresholds. Most companies keep that record in email threads and meeting notes. This page turns it into one dated record you can print, save as PDF and attach to the incident file.






Worked example


The page loads with an example. An incident is discovered on Thursday, October 1, 2026, at 9:30 AM and escalated at 11:00 AM. The CFO owns the decision. The company checks its financial and customer thresholds, notes that a customer list was exposed for two hours, and relies on a counsel memo dated October 6. The materiality determination is recorded at 4:00 PM on Tuesday, October 6.


The count starts the next day. Wednesday, October 7, is day one. Thursday, October 8, is day two. Friday, October 9, is day three. Monday, October 12, is Columbus Day, a US federal holiday, so it is skipped. Tuesday, October 13, 2026, is day four, and that is the date the page prints. The discovery date, five days earlier, does not move it.


Two more dates worth testing: a determination on Wednesday, November 25, 2026, counts past Thanksgiving to Wednesday, December 2. A determination on Wednesday, December 23 counts past Christmas Day to Wednesday, December 30.






Assumptions and limits


    

  • Business days exclude Saturdays, Sundays and US federal holidays for the determination year and the next year. A holiday that falls on a Saturday is treated as observed on Friday, and one that falls on a Sunday is observed on Monday.
    • 

  • The page does not decide materiality. It records that someone did, and when.
    • 

  • It does not model the Attorney General delay, amendments to an earlier 8-K, or foreign private issuer reporting on Form 6-K.
    • 

  • Times are recorded as typed. Use the time zone your disclosure committee uses, and say which one in the evidence note.
    • 

  • Inputs are saved only in this browser’s local storage. Clear removes them.
    • 







Questions readers ask


Does a vulnerability on CISA’s known-exploited list start the clock?


No. A catalog listing is a patching signal. The clock starts only when the company determines an incident is material. If triage finds a compromise, the materiality analysis begins then.


Who should own the decision?


That is a governance choice. Many companies assign it to a disclosure committee that includes the CFO, general counsel and CISO. The worksheet asks for one name so the record is never “the team.”


Can we wait to be sure?


The SEC expects the materiality determination to be made without unreasonable delay after discovery. Record the evidence you were waiting for and why.






Related


    

  • The SEC clock starts when you decide it matters
    • 

  • Before the Form 8-K clock
    • 

  • The BeyondTrust bug was used before the patch, a case where forensic triage can turn into a materiality call
    • 

  • Risk exception register and AI agent inventory
    • 

  • Primary sources: SEC press release 2023-139, July 26, 2023, and the SEC small entity compliance guide (“without unreasonable delay”)
    •

item.title: Free tool: Risk exception register
item.description: Track an exception, its owner, and its expiry. Known-exploited bugs, MFA, backups, and EDR are marked not waivable. Runs in your browser. No sign-in.
item.author: circuits50capital@circuits.fit (Emilio Santos)
item.content:encoded:
Not legal, tax, insurance, or procurement advice. Inputs stay in your browser. Nothing is uploaded.

Exceptions for a CISA Known Exploited Vulnerability, MFA, backups, or EDR are marked Not waivable. A row is also flagged when it has no owner, no expiry, or no funded fix, and when the expiry is past or inside 30 days. The file import is read in this browser. It is not uploaded.

Showing the example. Replace it with your register.

Output

The register summary appears here.














How to use this


    

  1. Replace the example rows. Pick CISA KEV, MFA, Backups, or EDR when the exception is one of those. Those four stay Not waivable.
    2. 

  2. Give every other row an owner, an expiry, and a funded amount above zero. A blank expiry or a no on funding stays flagged.
    3. 

  3. Export the CSV for a copy. Import reads a file on this device and does not send it anywhere.
    4. 







Why a register, and why some rows are not waivable


Every security program carries exceptions: a server that cannot take a patch until a vendor certifies it, a break-glass account without multi-factor sign-in, a laptop group where the endpoint agent conflicts with an old application. Exceptions are normal. Exceptions with no owner, no end date and no money behind the fix are how a temporary gap becomes permanent.


This register treats four controls as not waivable: a vulnerability on CISA’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog, multi-factor authentication, backups and endpoint detection and response. That is an editorial choice, not a legal rule. We chose those four because they are the controls attackers most often find missing, and because cyber insurers routinely ask about them on applications (see What a cyber insurer will still ask). For federal civilian agencies, CISA’s BOD 26-04 already sets a three-day remediation clock, plus forensic triage, for the highest-risk catalog entries on internet-facing systems. A row in one of those four categories can still be recorded. It is labeled Not waivable so nobody mistakes the record for permission.






Worked example


Say that on October 21, 2026, your team records an exception for an internet-facing edge gateway affected by a known-exploited bug. The platform team owns it. The reason is the next change window. The compensating control is a source-address restriction. No fix is funded, the CIO accepted the risk, and the exception expires on October 31.


The register returns: “CISA KEV — Not waivable,” with flags “No funded fix” and “Expires in 10 days.” The summary line counts one not-waivable row and one row with another flag. That is the conversation to have: the change window is not a reason to leave a known-exploited edge device open for ten days, and an exception with no funded fix has no end.


A second example: an “Other” row for a vendor cutover with an owner, a funded amount of 12,000, and an expiry 70 days out returns no flags. That is what a healthy exception looks like.






Assumptions and limits


    

  • A row is flagged when the owner is blank, the expiry is blank or not a date, the fix is not marked funded with an amount above zero, or the expiry is past or within 30 days.
    • 

  • Amounts are in whatever currency you type. The page does not convert or total them.
    • 

  • Dates are compared with this device’s clock.
    • 

  • CSV export and import happen in this browser. The file is not uploaded. The CSV columns are control, system, owner, reason, compensating, funded, amount, expiry and accepted.
    • 

  • This is a working list, not a governance, risk and compliance system. Keep the authoritative record where your auditors expect it.
    • 







Questions readers ask


Who should accept the risk?


Someone who owns the budget that would fix it. If the person accepting the risk cannot fund the fix, the exception is a note, not a decision.


How long should an exception last?


As short as the funded fix allows. Set the expiry to the date the fix ships, and review anything inside 30 days at your weekly security meeting.






Related


    

  • PHP2Shell was probed before the patch (October 22, 2026)
    • 

  • The BeyondTrust bug was used before the patch (October 21, 2026)
    • 

  • CISA listed three bugs attackers are already using
    • 

  • Citrix NetScaler is on the exploited catalog again
    • 

  • What a cyber insurer will still ask
    • 

  • Primary sources: CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog and BOD 26-04
    •

item.title: Free tool: Software renewal scorecard
item.description: Decide keep, renegotiate, or replace before a renewal call. The points stay on the page. Runs in your browser. No sign-in.
item.author: circuits50capital@circuits.fit (Emilio Santos)
item.content:encoded:
Not legal, tax, insurance, or procurement advice. Inputs stay in this browser. Nothing is uploaded.

Each gap has a fixed score. Seat use under 60% of paid seats, no price-up cap or an unknown cap, notice under 30 days, no full export, no SBOM, unknown AI training use, and no exit clause score 2. A named cap, including 0%, scores 0. Unknown export, SBOM, subprocessors or exit clause, and opt-out training, score 1. A data-return window under 30 days scores 1. Unlisted subprocessors score 2. Seats paid, seats active, notice period, data-return window and the cap question are required: if any is blank or invalid, the result is Incomplete, not Keep. 0 points is Keep. 1 to 7 is Renegotiate. 8 or more is Replace. No full export and no exit clause is Replace even when the total is lower.

Output

—

Run the scorecard. Every check stays visible.

What this scorecard does

A software renewal is the one moment each year when the buyer has leverage. Before you sign, the vendor wants the deal. After you sign, the terms are fixed for another term. This scorecard turns the contract and usage facts you already have into a single decision, Keep, Renegotiate, or Replace, and a list of specific requests to send the vendor.

It does not judge whether the product is good. It checks whether the commercial and data terms protect you. A well-loved tool can still score Renegotiate if half the seats sit unused or there is no cap on the next price increase.

How to use it, step by step

  1. Pull usage. From the vendor’s admin console, export the number of seats you pay for and the number of users active in the last 30 days.
  2. Read the order form and master agreement. Find the renewal price cap, the notice period to cancel or change, the data-return window after termination, and whether there is an exit or termination-for-convenience clause.
  3. Check the data terms. Confirm whether you can export all of your data in a usable format, whether subprocessors are listed, and how the vendor uses your data for AI training.
  4. Ask for an SBOM. If you do not know whether the vendor provides one, select Unknown and send the request. The SBOM request pack drafts that email.
  5. Score it. Press Score the renewal. Copy the output into your vendor email or the renewal ticket.

Start at least 90 days before the renewal date. Many contracts require 30 to 90 days’ notice to change terms, and the scorecard flags notice periods under 30 days because they leave no room to negotiate.

Worked example

These are example numbers, not data from a real vendor. A team pays $48,000 a year for an example CRM with 120 paid seats. Only 66 users were active in the last 30 days. There is no price-up cap in the contract. The notice period is 60 days and the data-return window is 14 days. Full export is available, subprocessors are listed, and there is an exit clause. The vendor has not said whether it provides an SBOM, and AI training on customer data is opt-out.

The scorecard returns Renegotiate with 7 points:

  • Seat use is 55%, under the 60% line: 2 points.
  • No price-up cap: 2 points.
  • Data-return window of 14 days, under 30: 1 point.
  • SBOM unknown: 1 point.
  • AI training is opt-out rather than opt-in: 1 point.

The agenda it writes asks the vendor to cut the renewal to active seats, add a price cap, extend the data-return window to at least 30 days, confirm SBOM availability, and move training to opt-in. Cutting to 75 seats at the same per-seat price would bring the example cost from $48,000 to $30,000.

How to read the result

Keep (0 points) means none of the checks found a gap. Renew, and record the date you checked.

Renegotiate (1 to 7 points) is the most common result. Send the agenda. Most items are standard requests that vendors grant regularly, especially seat true-ups and price caps.

Replace (8 or more, or no export and no exit clause) means the terms leave you with little protection. That does not mean cancel tomorrow. It means start evaluating alternatives now, so you have a real option at the next renewal. A product you cannot export from and cannot exit is the one where the vendor sets the price.

Limitations

  • The points are fixed weights chosen by this desk. They are a starting rule, not an industry standard. Adjust your judgment for a tool that is critical to operations.
  • Seat activity in the last 30 days can miss seasonal users, such as staff who only log in at quarter-end. Check a 90-day view before cutting.
  • The scorecard does not read contracts. It relies on what you type. If a required field is blank, it returns Incomplete and names the missing field instead of a decision. If you do not know an answer, choose Unknown rather than guessing.
  • It is not legal or procurement advice. Have counsel review contract changes.

FAQ

Is my data sent anywhere?

No. The scoring runs in your browser. Nothing is uploaded.

Why does opt-out AI training score a point?

Opt-out means your data may be used unless someone remembers to switch it off. Opt-in means it is not used unless you agree. The guide What belongs in a processor clause covers the contract side.

Why ask for an SBOM on a SaaS product?

CISA’s 2026 minimum elements for SBOMs say hosted software is in scope. See Ask a vendor for an SBOM.

What if the vendor refuses every request?

Then you know the price of staying. Record it, and use the next term to build an alternative.

Related

  • Software buying is an operating skill
  • How to read a SaaS renewal

item.title: Free tool: Agent access limit sheet
item.description: Write down what an agent may touch before it is turned on. Runs in your browser. No sign-in.
item.author: circuits50capital@circuits.fit (Emilio Santos)
item.content:encoded:
Not legal, tax, insurance, or procurement advice. Inputs stay in this browser. Nothing is uploaded.

Allow is what you listed. Deny is inherit. If inherit is yes, the gap line stays. Empty read, write, or call lines stay as “not listed.” They are not filled in for you.

Output

Context, Gartner’s figure, not yours. In Gartner’s second-quarter survey of 297 cybersecurity leaders, 54% have no defined limit on agent access, or they let the agent reuse a person’s access.

Why write the limit down first

On September 30, 2026, Gartner reported that 54% of organizations have no defined approach to limiting AI agent access, or rely on predefined human access, based on a second-quarter survey of 297 cybersecurity leaders. Gartner’s advice is to treat frontier AI deployments as insider risks and to govern agents by their action privileges rather than by how capable the model is. An agent that reuses a person’s login can do everything that person can do, at machine speed, and the logs will show the person.

This sheet makes the limit explicit before an agent is switched on: what it may read, what it may write, which tools or APIs it may call, how much it may spend per day, who owns it, and whether a person approves writes and spending.

How to use this

  1. Name the agent and list the systems it may read, the systems it may write and the tools or APIs it may call. Leave a line blank if it gets nothing; the sheet prints “not listed” rather than filling it in.
  2. Set a daily spend cap, name an owner, and choose whether a human approves writes and spending and whether logs are retained.
  3. Answer the key question: can it inherit the user’s access? If yes, the sheet prints a gap line telling you not to turn it on until that is off or the limit is written down.
  4. Copy the sheet into the change ticket or the agent inventory.

Worked example

A finance team wants an invoice-matching agent. It may read the accounts-payable mailbox and the ERP vendor table, write only draft match records, and call the ERP’s matching API. The spend cap is 20 dollars a day in model usage, the AP manager owns it, a human approves every write, and logs are kept. Inherit is set to No. The sheet prints an ALLOW block with those lines, a DENY line for inheriting the user’s access, and “Gap: none on inherit.”

Change inherit to Yes, as happens when an agent is set up under the AP manager’s own account, and the gap line changes: the agent still inherits a person’s access, so do not turn it on. That single line is the conversation most teams skip.

Assumptions and limits

  • The sheet documents intended access. It does not enforce it. Enforcement lives in your identity provider, API gateway or agent platform.
  • “Spend cap” is whatever unit you type: dollars, tokens or calls.
  • Review the sheet when the agent gains a new tool or data source, not only once a year.
  • Nothing you type leaves this browser.

Related

item.title: Free tool: SBOM request pack
item.description: Ask a vendor for an ingredients list, then mark what came back. Runs in your browser. No sign-in.
item.author: circuits50capital@circuits.fit (Emilio Santos)
item.content:encoded:
Not legal, tax, insurance, or procurement advice. Inputs stay in this browser. Nothing is uploaded.

The email asks for the 2026 CISA minimum elements, including for SaaS and AI software, not only code the buyer compiles. The field list below is the ask. Tick Received when a field comes back. Missing rows stay on the page.

Email

What came back

FieldAskedReceivedMissing

Why ask for an SBOM

A software bill of materials is an ingredients list for software: which components a product contains, who supplies them, which versions are inside, and how they depend on each other. When a component turns up on CISA’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog, the buyer with an SBOM can answer “are we affected?” in minutes. The buyer without one sends a questionnaire and waits.

On July 29, 2026, CISA, the NSA, the FBI and international partners published the 2026 Minimum Elements for a Software Bill of Materials. It replaces the minimum elements the National Telecommunications and Information Administration published in 2021. CISA says the minimum elements apply to all software, and that some types, including AI and software as a service, may need additional elements. That matters for buyers: “we are SaaS, so an SBOM does not apply” is no longer the answer the guidance supports.

How to use this

  1. Enter the vendor, the product and your name, and say whether you are buying SaaS, installed software or an AI feature.
  2. Select Write the request. The page writes a plain email that asks for each field on the list below. Copy it into your own email or procurement portal.
  3. When the vendor replies, tick Received for each field that actually came back. Anything left unticked stays marked Missing. Put the missing rows on the renewal agenda.

Worked example

A finance team is renewing an expense-management SaaS product. The buyer enters the vendor and product, chooses SaaS, and sends the request. Two weeks later the vendor returns a spreadsheet with component names, versions and licenses, plus a note that it “monitors vulnerabilities continuously.” The buyer ticks Component name, Version and License. Supplier name, Unique identifier, Dependency relationship, Author of SBOM data, Timestamp and Known vulnerabilities stay Missing.

That result is useful on its own. Without unique identifiers, the list cannot be matched reliably against vulnerability databases. Without a timestamp, nobody knows whether it describes the product running today. Without dependency relationships, an exploited library buried two levels down will not show up. The six missing fields become six lines in the renewal call, and the software renewal scorecard scores the SBOM answer alongside price caps and data export.

Assumptions and limits

  • The field list is our working list drawn from the minimum-elements guidance. Check the CISA document for the exact element names and definitions before you put them in a contract.
  • The page does not read or validate an SBOM file. It tracks whether each field came back.
  • A received field is only as good as the data in it. A stale SBOM can be worse than none if it gives false comfort, so ask how often it is regenerated.
  • Nothing you type leaves this browser.

Questions readers ask

Will a small vendor be able to answer?

Many build tools can generate an SBOM automatically. A vendor that cannot produce one at all is telling you something about how it tracks its own components.

What about AI features?

Ask the AI-specific questions in the guide Extra questions for an AI bill of materials, which covers the May 12, 2026 G7 and CISA note.

item.title: Free tool: Vendor claim checker
item.description: Separate a speed or savings claim from the bill. Runs in your browser. No sign-in.
item.author: circuits50capital@circuits.fit (Emilio Santos)
item.content:encoded:
Not legal, tax, insurance, or procurement advice. Inputs stay in this browser. Nothing is uploaded.

The pasted claim stays a claim. A vendor comparison is not the fact. If you enter volume and unit price, your cost is your arithmetic. It is printed next to the claim. It does not confirm the claim. If the figure belongs to NVIDIA, Gartner, CISA, or the vendor, the “whose number” line says so.

Output

Why check a vendor claim

“Up to 8x faster.” “Cuts costs by 40%.” A vendor benchmark is a useful signal, but it is the vendor’s measurement, on the vendor’s workload, against a baseline the vendor chose. It is not a measurement of your bill. This tool turns a claim into a short note for the buying file: whose number it is, what it did not measure, what the bill is at your volume, and three questions for the next call.

How to use this

  1. Paste the claim exactly as the vendor wrote it, and name the vendor and product.
  2. Say who measured it (vendor, analyst, another customer or unknown) and what the metric is.
  3. Say whether the claim names a baseline (faster than what?) and a price source (which meter, at what price?).
  4. Optionally enter your own volume and unit price. The page multiplies them so your bill sits next to the claim.
  5. Select the button, copy the note, and paste it into the evaluation or renewal record.

Worked example

A vendor announces a fast mode with “up to 8x faster token generation than our standard mode.” This is the kind of claim covered in Astra Ultrafast is a speed claim. You enter: measured by the vendor; metric, tokens per second; baseline named, yes (the standard mode); price source named, no. You expect 30 million tokens a month at a unit price of 12 dollars per million.

The note says the number is the vendor’s comparison, not the fact. Under “what was not measured” it lists two gaps: no price source is named, and the comparison was not run on your volume. It prints your arithmetic, 30 × 12 = 360, in the units you typed, and says that does not confirm the claim. The three questions are: walk the baseline (what was held constant?), show where the price is and which meter it covers, and say what the claim does at your volume of 30. That is a better agenda than “is it really 8x?”

Assumptions and limits

  • The page does not test the product or look anything up. It structures what you entered.
  • The bill line is volume times unit price in whatever units you type. Keep them consistent.
  • A named baseline and price source do not make a claim true. They make it checkable.
  • Nothing you type leaves this browser.

Questions readers ask

What if an analyst published the number?

Choose Analyst. The note says it is the analyst’s number, not a measurement on your workload. Read the analyst’s release for the sample and the date before you rely on it.

Can I use this for security claims?

It is built for performance and cost claims. For a supplier’s security assurances, ask for dated evidence instead: the patch date, the version, and who confirmed it. The SBOM request pack covers component lists.

Related

  • PHP2Shell was probed before the patch, test vendor “not affected” replies against a dated patch record
  • Astra Ultrafast is a speed claim. The bill is still yours.
  • Gartner says the AI build-out may not pay back (October 21, 2026)

item.title: Free tool: Token cost to gross margin
item.description: See if an AI-native task still contributes after tokens and human review. Runs in your browser. No sign-in.
item.author: circuits50capital@circuits.fit (Emilio Santos)
item.content:encoded:
Not legal, tax, insurance, or procurement advice. Inputs stay in this browser. Nothing is uploaded.

Token cost = (input tokens / 1,000,000) × price per 1M input tokens + (output tokens / 1,000,000) × price per 1M output tokens. Review cost = (minutes / 60) × loaded cost per hour. Contribution = price charged − token cost − review cost. Margin = contribution / price charged. You type the prices. This page does not call a model.

Output

The worked line appears here after you run it.

Why tokens are rarely the whole cost

AI-native products are often priced as if the model call were the main cost. In practice, many tasks also need a person to check, correct or approve the output before a customer sees it. That review time is usually priced in dollars per hour, not fractions of a cent per thousand tokens, and it can dominate the unit economics. This tool puts both costs on one line so you can see which one drives the margin.

How to use this

  1. Enter the price you charge per task and the average input and output tokens one task uses. Your model provider’s usage logs give the token counts.
  2. Enter the provider’s price per million input tokens and per million output tokens from its current price list.
  3. Enter the average human-review minutes per task and the loaded hourly cost of the reviewer, including benefits and overhead.
  4. Optionally, add tasks per month to see the monthly contribution. Select Work the margin.

Worked example

These prices are illustrative, not any vendor’s list price. A company charges $2.00 per task. One task uses 6,000 input tokens and 1,500 output tokens. The model costs $3 per million input tokens and $15 per million output tokens. A reviewer spends three minutes per task at a loaded cost of $60 an hour, and the company runs 20,000 tasks a month.

Token cost is (6,000 ÷ 1,000,000) × $3 plus (1,500 ÷ 1,000,000) × $15, which is about $0.04. Review cost is (3 ÷ 60) × $60, or $3.00. Contribution is $2.00 − $0.04 − $3.00, a loss of about $1.04 per task, a margin of −52%, and about −$20,810 a month. Cut review to one minute and the same task contributes about $0.96, a 48% margin, or about $19,190 a month. The model price barely moved the answer. The review minutes decided it, which is why the tool prints “Human review costs more than the tokens” when that is true.

Assumptions and limits

  • Contribution here is price minus token cost minus review cost. It leaves out hosting, payment fees, support, retries, failed tasks and sales cost. Use the AI cost per finished task tool to account for retries and failures.
  • The page does not call a model or look up prices. You type every number, in one currency.
  • Averages hide spread. If a tenth of tasks need twenty minutes of review, run that case separately.

Questions readers ask

What if my provider raises prices?

Rerun with the new price. Gartner warned on October 14, 2026 that most neocloud providers may not stay independent through 2030; our briefing explains why that is a pricing risk for buyers. Test a higher token price before you sign a long commitment.

Should review time ever be zero?

Only where a wrong answer is cheap and reversible. For anything a customer relies on, budget some review and measure it.

Related

  • The new unit economics of AI-native startups
  • Gartner says the AI build-out may not pay back (October 21, 2026)
  • Put an AI cost on one workflow

item.title: Ask a Vendor for an SBOM
item.description: CISA’s 2026 minimum elements apply to SaaS and AI software. Ask for the fields, the format, and the date. A slide is not a bill of materials.
item.author: circuits50capital@circuits.fit (Emilio Santos)
item.content:encoded:
CISA’s July 29, 2026 minimum elements apply to all software, including open source, AI software, and SaaS. They update the 2021 NTIA baseline. Use them as a procurement list, not as a claim that every vendor is legally required to send you one tomorrow.

The fields

CISA’s release names four additions on top of the older baseline: component hash algorithm, component license, the name of the tool that generated the SBOM, and the context in which it was generated. Ask for those by name. Also ask for the component names and versions the document is built to carry. If a field is missing, the reply is incomplete against the 2026 list, even if the PDF looks thick.

The ask

  • Machine-readable, not only a PDF. Say CycloneDX or SPDX if you already consume one of those. If you do not, still refuse a screenshot.
  • The generation date, and how often a new file is produced. A file from the year the product launched is a souvenir.
  • Whether hosted software is in scope. CISA says SaaS is in scope for the minimum elements. “We are a cloud app” is not an answer.
  • Who will send an updated file after a critical component changes, and on what clock.

What fails

ReplyTreat it as
“We are SOC 2”A different document
A logo slide of “trusted components”Not an SBOM
A list with no license and no hash algorithmShort of the 2026 elements
“Legal will not share our ingredients”A commercial position you can price

Why it is worth asking

An SBOM is a list of the components inside a piece of software. When a serious vulnerability is announced in a common library, the companies that can answer “do we use this, and where?” in an hour are the ones with SBOMs from their vendors. The rest send emails and wait. The NTIA’s 2021 minimum elements set the original baseline: supplier name, component name, version, other unique identifiers, dependency relationships, the author of the SBOM data, and a timestamp. CISA’s 2026 update builds on that list with the four additions above.

The SBOM is also a signal. CISA’s Secure by Demand guide, published with the FBI in August 2024, lists the SBOM among the artifacts a customer can collect to judge whether a vendor builds security into its products. A vendor that can produce one quickly usually has its build process under control.

How to make the request, step by step

  1. Pick the products. Start with software that is internet-facing, handles sensitive data, or runs with high privilege. You do not need SBOMs for everything on day one.
  2. Write the ask in the contract or renewal. Name the 2026 minimum elements, the format (CycloneDX or SPDX), the update frequency, and the time to deliver a new file after a critical component change.
  3. Decide who receives it. A named security contact, not a shared inbox nobody reads.
  4. Check the first file. Open it with a tool or at least a text editor. Confirm it has versions, licenses, a hash algorithm, the generating tool, and a date.
  5. Use it once. The next time a major library vulnerability is announced, search your SBOMs for it. That test tells you whether the files are worth keeping current.

A worked example

Illustrative case. Your company renews a document management product. The order form now says: “Supplier will provide a machine-readable SBOM in CycloneDX or SPDX format meeting CISA’s 2026 minimum elements within 30 days of signature, an updated SBOM with each major release, and an updated SBOM within 10 business days of remediating a critical vulnerability in a third-party component.” The vendor agrees to the first two and pushes back on the third. You settle on 15 business days. That is a real improvement over no clause at all, and it is in the contract rather than in a sales email.

The SBOM request pack builds this request, and the software renewal scorecard counts a missing SBOM against the renewal.

Limits to keep in mind

An SBOM shows what is inside, not whether each component is exploitable in that product. Pair it with the vendor’s vulnerability disclosure policy and, where available, statements on whether a given vulnerability affects the product. It also does not replace patching. It tells you where to look faster.

Before you sign off

  • The products in scope are listed, starting with internet-facing and high-privilege software.
  • The contract names the 2026 minimum elements, a format, an update frequency, and a delivery clock after a critical fix.
  • A named person receives the files and checks the first one.
  • You have searched the files at least once for a real vulnerability.
  • Refusals are recorded and priced into the renewal.

If the product includes a model or agent, add the questions in Extra SBOM questions for AI products.

FAQ

Does CISA require my vendor to send this?

The July 2026 document is guidance on minimum elements. Your leverage is the contract. If the order does not ask for the file, you will not get the file.

Is an SBOM a vulnerability report?

No. It is an ingredient list. You still need a way to compare those ingredients to the vulnerabilities you care about.

What about AI features?

Ask for this general SBOM and for the May 12, 2026 AI supplement. They are not substitutes.

Sources

  • CISA, 2026 Minimum Elements for an SBOM
  • CISA news release, July 29, 2026
  • CISA SBOM overview
  • NTIA, The Minimum Elements for a Software Bill of Materials, July 2021
  • CISA and FBI, Secure by Demand Guide, August 2024
  • CycloneDX project
  • SPDX specifications

Related

  • The software ingredients list now covers the suite
  • Extra questions for an AI bill of materials
  • Software buying is an operating skill

item.title: Extra Questions for an AI Bill of Materials
item.description: The May 12, 2026 G7 and CISA note is an add-on, not a replacement. A model name with no components is not an ingredients list.
item.author: circuits50capital@circuits.fit (Emilio Santos)
item.content:encoded:
On May 12, 2026, CISA and G7 partners published minimum elements for a software bill of materials for AI. CISA says AI systems are software systems, so the AI list sits on top of the general SBOM elements. The guide is not exhaustive and not, by itself, a mandate. It is still the public list to point at.

What the AI note adds

Use it when the product is a model, a copilot, or an agent, not only when the vendor’s engineers compiled a binary. Ask which pieces are the model, which are data or adapters, and which are ordinary application code. If the vendor cannot separate those, you cannot tell whether a later incident is in the model, the data, or the wrapper.

Questions

  • Will you provide the general 2026 SBOM and the AI supplement, as two labeled files or one file that clearly includes both?
  • What is the model’s name and version, and who provides it if it is not yours?
  • Which components can change without a new SBOM, and which cannot?
  • Does the file include enough license information to show a component you are not allowed to ship to a customer?
  • If you only embed a third-party model, whose SBOM covers the model, and whose covers your application?

Why an AI product needs more than a normal SBOM

A traditional SBOM answers a narrow question: which software components, at which versions, are inside this product. That is enough to answer “are we exposed to this new vulnerability in a library?” An AI product adds parts that a component list does not describe well. The model may come from a third party. It may be fine-tuned with adapters. It may depend on datasets, prompt templates, and retrieval indexes that change without a new software release. If a problem shows up, you need to know which of those parts changed and who supplied it.

Two open formats already carry this kind of information. CycloneDX has a machine-learning bill of materials (ML-BOM) capability for describing models and datasets. SPDX 3.0 includes AI and dataset profiles. Asking for one of these formats gives the vendor a concrete target and gives you something your tools can read.

How to run the request, step by step

  1. Identify the AI features in scope. List every product feature that uses a model: assistants, summarizers, classifiers, agents. Include features switched on inside software you already pay for.
  2. Send the questions above in writing. Ask for the general SBOM and the AI supplement together, so you can see how they line up.
  3. Ask for the format. CycloneDX or SPDX, machine-readable. A PDF can be read by a person but not checked by a tool.
  4. Check the change rules. Ask how you will be told when the model version, provider, or training data changes. A model swap can change behavior more than a code release.
  5. File the answers with the contract. Note what the vendor declined to share and why. That record matters at the next renewal and after an incident.

A worked example

This is an illustrative case, not a real vendor. A support platform adds an AI reply feature. The vendor sends its standard SBOM, which lists the web application’s open-source libraries. It does not mention the model. On follow-up, the vendor says the feature calls a third-party hosted model and uses a retrieval index built from your help-center articles.

What you now know: the vendor’s SBOM covers its application, the model provider’s documentation covers the model, and the retrieval index contains your own content. What you still need: the model name and version, the provider, how you will be notified of a model change, and whether your articles or tickets are used for anything other than retrieval. Those questions go into the renewal agenda. The SBOM request pack drafts the email.

What this does not solve

An AI SBOM lists parts. It does not tell you whether the model is accurate, fair, or safe for your use. For those questions, use a risk framework such as NIST’s AI Risk Management Framework and its Generative AI Profile, NIST AI 600-1. Treat the SBOM as the inventory and the risk review as the judgment. You need both.

Before you sign off

  • Every AI feature in the product is listed, including ones switched on by default.
  • You have the model name, version, and provider, or a written reason why not.
  • You know how you will hear about a model or provider change.
  • The general SBOM and the AI supplement arrived in a machine-readable format.
  • Anything the vendor declined to share is recorded with the contract, so the next renewal starts from the same list.

For the general SBOM request, see Ask a vendor for an SBOM. For what the agent inside the product can do, see Limit what an agent can touch.

FAQ

Is a model card the same as an AI SBOM?

No. A model card describes behavior and limits. An SBOM lists components. Ask for the document CISA describes, and keep the model card if you want it for a different question.

What if the vendor says the model is a trade secret?

Trade secret is a reason to negotiate scope. It is not a reason to accept a blank page. Ask what can be shared: name, version, supplier, license, hash algorithm, generation date.

Sources

  • CISA, Software Bill of Materials for AI — Minimum Elements, May 12, 2026
  • CISA, 2026 general SBOM minimum elements
  • CycloneDX, Machine Learning Bill of Materials (ML-BOM)
  • SPDX specifications, including SPDX 3.0 AI and dataset profiles
  • NIST AI 600-1, Generative Artificial Intelligence Profile, July 2024
  • CISA, Software Bill of Materials

Related

  • The software ingredients list now covers the suite
  • Ask a vendor for an SBOM

item.title: Limit What an Agent Can Touch
item.description: In Gartner’s second-quarter survey of 297 security leaders, 54% have no defined limit on agent access, or they reuse a person’s access.
item.author: circuits50capital@circuits.fit (Emilio Santos)
item.content:encoded:
Gartner’s September 30, 2026 note says an AI system does not need general intelligence to create cyber risk. It needs a way to affect operations. In a second-quarter 2026 survey of 297 cybersecurity leaders, 54% of organizations had no defined approach to limit AI-agent access, or relied on access already defined for a person.

The fact

Treat that 54% as a description of a default, not as a score you must beat for its own sake. The default is: the integration user, the service account, or the employee who clicked connect. Gartner’s recommended shift is to govern by action privileges, and to constrain how far a workflow can go.

The list

Write this downA bad answer
Whose identity the agent uses“The admin who set it up”
Which systems it can read“Whatever the connector allows”
Which systems it can change“Same as the user”
What it cannot do without a person“It will ask if it is unsure”
Who can turn it off tonight“The vendor”

If the agent can send mail, move money, open a ticket, or change a record, those are separate lines. “It only helps” is not a line.

Why “same as the user” fails

The OWASP Top 10 for large language model applications lists excessive agency as a top risk. OWASP says the root cause is typically one or more of three things: excessive functionality, excessive permissions, or excessive autonomy. An agent connected with an employee’s account usually has all three. It can reach everything the employee can, it can use tools the task does not need, and it can act without anyone checking.

The risk is not only a model making a mistake. OWASP notes that an agent can be steered by prompt injection, including instructions hidden in a document, an email, or a web page it reads. An agent that can read untrusted content and also send email or change records is the combination to limit first.

How to set limits, step by step

  1. Inventory first. List every agent, its owner, and the identity it uses. The agent inventory does this and flags shared or personal accounts.
  2. Give each agent its own identity. A dedicated service account or app registration, so its actions can be logged and its access removed without touching a person.
  3. Grant only the actions the task needs. If it drafts replies, it does not need to close tickets. If it reads invoices, it does not need to pay them.
  4. Require a person for high-impact actions. Payments, external messages to customers, deletions, and permission changes should need approval.
  5. Log and review. Keep a log of what the agent did. Review its access at least every 90 days, and whenever it gains a new connection.
  6. Name the off switch. Write down who can disable the agent tonight, and how.

A worked example

Illustrative case. A finance team connects an AI assistant to email and the accounting system using the controller’s account. It summarizes invoices. Under the list above, the assistant gets its own account with read access to the accounts payable inbox and the invoice module. It cannot send email, approve payments, or change vendor records. When it finds an invoice that needs action, it creates a draft for a person. If a malicious invoice contains hidden instructions to change bank details, the assistant has no permission to do it. The agent access limit sheet records these choices.

Where this fits in a wider program

NIST’s AI Risk Management Framework organizes AI risk work into four functions: Govern, Map, Measure, and Manage. Agent access limits sit mostly in Manage, but they depend on Map: you cannot limit what you have not listed. NIST AI 600-1, the Generative AI Profile, adds risks specific to generative systems. Use those documents to explain the program to auditors. Use this page to start.

Before you sign off

  • Every agent is listed with an owner and its own identity.
  • Read and write rights are listed by system, and match the task.
  • Payments, external messages, deletions, and permission changes need a person.
  • Agents that read untrusted content cannot also take high-impact actions on their own.
  • There is an access review date and a named person who can switch each agent off.

The five-line version for a staff meeting is the table at the top of this page.

If you only have time for one change this quarter, move every agent off a person’s account and onto its own identity. That single step makes its actions visible in logs, lets you cut its access without locking out an employee, and turns the rest of this list into configuration rather than a project. Record the change in the agent inventory so the next review starts from facts.

FAQ

Is inheriting a human’s access ever acceptable?

Only if you would give that same person a second unattended session with the same rights, overnight, with no manager in the room. Most “same as the user” designs fail that test.

Do we need a new product to start?

No. Start with the identity the workflow already uses. A tool can come later. A nameless service account is the current risk.

Sources

  • Gartner, five actions for CISOs, September 30, 2026
  • OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025, LLM06: Excessive Agency
  • NIST, AI Risk Management Framework
  • NIST AI 600-1, Generative Artificial Intelligence Profile
