item.title: Stop Using a Voice as Approval
item.description: Gartner’s September 30 note: do not authorize a decision because someone recognized a face or a voice. Pair detection with another authenticator and a provenance check.
item.author: circuits50capital@circuits.fit (Emilio Santos)
item.content:encoded:
Gartner’s September 30, 2026 release says deepfake threats are mainstream, and that CISOs should drive a process change: recognition is not an acceptable basis for authorizing a decision or an action. Detection software is one layer. Gartner also names contextual signals, additional authentication, and checks on content provenance.

The rule

Write it in one sentence your accounts-payable clerk can repeat. Example: no payment, mailbox rule, or vendor-bank change is approved on a voice, a video, or a familiar writing style alone. A second channel, already on file, has to say yes. If you cannot write the sentence, the current process is “we know our people.”

The redesign

  • List the actions that move money, data, or access. Those are the ones recognition must not unlock.
  • Name the second factor that already exists: a callback to a number on the vendor master, a hardware key, an approval in the system of record. Do not invent a new app if the second factor is already policy and simply unused.
  • For public content, ask where a synthetic image or audio came from before it goes on a site or into a customer message. Provenance is the check Gartner pairs with detection.
  • Tell staff that matching a voice is not a failure of attention. It is the attack.

What the FBI has warned

This is not a hypothetical risk. On December 3, 2024, the FBI’s Internet Crime Complaint Center warned that criminals use generative AI to commit fraud on a larger scale and make it more believable, including AI-generated audio to impersonate a close relative or a person in authority. On May 15, 2025, the FBI warned of a campaign since April 2025 in which malicious actors sent text messages and AI-generated voice messages claiming to come from senior US officials, to build rapport before gaining access to accounts. A December 19, 2025 alert said the impersonation campaign was continuing.

The money at stake is large. The FBI’s 2024 Internet Crime Report recorded about $2.77 billion in reported business email compromise losses. Voice and video add a new way to make the same request look legitimate.

How to put the rule in place, step by step

  1. List the high-risk actions. Payments over a threshold, vendor bank detail changes, payroll changes, password and MFA resets, and access grants.
  2. Name the second channel for each. A call-back to a number already in the vendor master or HR system, never a number given in the request. An approval in the system of record. A hardware security key for help-desk resets.
  3. Write the rule in one sentence. Post it where approvers work.
  4. Give staff permission to slow down. Say in writing that no one will be penalized for verifying a request from a senior person.
  5. Test it. Run a drill with a harmless fake request and see whether the process holds.

A worked example

Illustrative case. An accounts payable clerk gets a video call that appears to be the CFO, asking for an urgent wire to a new supplier before a deal closes. Under the rule, the clerk says the request must go through the payment system and will be confirmed by a call to the CFO’s number on file. The clerk calls that number. The real CFO knows nothing about it. No money moves. The process worked without anyone needing to spot that the video was fake.

Help desk resets are the weak spot

Many account takeovers start with a call to the help desk asking to reset a password or MFA device. NIST’s digital identity guidelines, SP 800-63B, describe phishing-resistant authenticators and the importance of strong recovery processes. Require the same second channel for resets as for payments. If the person can prove identity with a hardware key or an in-person check, the voice does not matter.

Before you sign off

  • The high-risk actions are listed.
  • Each has a second channel that uses contact details already on file.
  • The rule is one sentence, posted where approvers work.
  • Staff have written permission to verify senior requests.
  • Help desk resets follow the same rule as payments.
  • A drill has been run and the result recorded.

Review the rule after any near miss, not only after a loss. A clerk who stopped a fake request is the best source of what the attack looked like and where the process felt awkward. Fix the awkward step, or people will start skipping it. Share the story, without blame, so the next person recognizes the pattern. The insurance side of these losses is in What a cyber insurer will still ask.

FAQ

Does this replace multi-factor authentication?

No. It stops MFA from being bypassed by a person who sounds right and asks the help desk to turn MFA off.

Is a deepfake detector enough?

Gartner’s sentence includes detection and the other layers. A detector that is wrong in either direction will still approve the familiar voice if the process allows it.

Sources

  • Gartner, five actions for CISOs, September 30, 2026
  • FBI IC3, PSA I-120324, December 3, 2024: criminals use generative AI to facilitate financial fraud
  • FBI IC3, PSA I-051525, May 15, 2025: senior US officials impersonated with text and AI-generated voice messages
  • FBI IC3, PSA I-121925, December 19, 2025: impersonation campaign continues
  • FBI IC3, 2024 Internet Crime Report (PDF)
  • NIST SP 800-63, Digital Identity Guidelines

Related

  • Cyber insurance is rewriting the IT budget

item.title: What Article 50 Asks a Buyer
item.description: Transparency has applied since August 2, 2026. The December 2, 2026 date is a marking transition for systems already shipping, not a delay of the whole Act.
item.author: circuits50capital@circuits.fit (Emilio Santos)
item.content:encoded:
This is an operator checklist, not a legal opinion and not a finding that your use is covered. The European Commission’s AI Act Service Desk says Article 50 transparency rules started to apply on August 2, 2026. It also says that for certain generative systems already placed on the market before that date, the Article 50(2) machine-readable marking duty has a transition that ends December 2, 2026. The Council’s timeline records the high-risk delay separately: December 2, 2027 and August 2, 2028. Do not let a vendor use the high-risk date to answer a transparency question.

The dates

DateWhat the public timeline says
August 2, 2026Transparency rules apply. Enforcement for those rules is underway.
December 2, 2026Marking transition ends for certain generative systems already on the market. New prohibitions on non-consensual intimate imagery and child sexual abuse material generation also apply.
December 2, 2027Stand-alone high-risk duties. Not the transparency date.
August 2, 2028High-risk duties for systems embedded in regulated products.

The ask

  • Is a person told they are interacting with an AI system, where the Act requires it? Ask for the screen, not the policy.
  • If the system generates synthetic audio, image, video, or text, what machine-readable mark do you apply, and as of which date?
  • Was this system on the market before August 2, 2026? If yes, the vendor should be able to say whether they are inside the December 2, 2026 transition.
  • Which article and annex are you relying on when you say “not until 2027”?

What Article 50 covers

Article 50 of the AI Act, Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, sets transparency duties for certain AI systems. In plain terms:

  • Interacting with AI. Providers must design systems that interact directly with people so that people are told they are interacting with an AI system, unless that is obvious from the context.
  • Marking synthetic content. Providers of systems that generate synthetic audio, image, video, or text must mark the outputs in a machine-readable format so they can be detected as artificially generated or manipulated.
  • Emotion recognition and biometric categorisation. Deployers of these systems must inform the people exposed to them.
  • Deepfakes and public-interest text. Deployers that generate or manipulate deepfake image, audio, or video must disclose that it is artificial. Deployers that publish AI-generated text to inform the public on matters of public interest must disclose it, with exceptions such as where the text has had human review and someone holds editorial responsibility.

Note the split between provider duties and deployer duties. If you buy a product and use it, you may be a deployer. The vendor is usually the provider. Your contract should say who does what.

How to run the review, step by step

  1. List AI features that reach people in the EU. Chat assistants, generated images or audio in marketing, AI-written customer messages, and features inside software you already own.
  2. Tag each one by Article 50 category. Interaction, synthetic content, emotion recognition, deepfake, or public-interest text. Some will fit none.
  3. Ask the vendor the questions above. Get the answers in writing, with dates.
  4. Assign your deployer duties. For deepfakes and public-interest text, the disclosure may be your job, not the vendor’s.
  5. Record the decision. Keep a dated note of what you reviewed and why. Have counsel confirm where the answer is not obvious.

A worked example

Illustrative case. A company uses a customer service chat assistant on its EU website and an image generator for social media ads. For the chat assistant, the buyer asks the vendor to show the screen where customers are told they are talking to an AI system. For the image tool, the buyer asks what machine-readable mark is applied to generated images, and whether the tool was on the market before August 2, 2026, which would put it in the transition ending December 2, 2026. If any ad image is a realistic depiction of a real person or event, the company, as deployer, plans its own disclosure.

Why it is worth getting right

The AI Act sets fines for breaches of the transparency obligations of up to 15 million euros or 3% of total worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher, with lower caps for small and medium-sized companies. That is a reason to keep a record of the review, not a reason to panic. The timeline for everything else in the Act is in What the EU AI Act still applies.

Before you sign off

  • AI features that reach people in the EU are listed.
  • Each is tagged by Article 50 category, or marked as outside it.
  • Vendor answers on disclosure screens and machine-readable marks are in writing, with dates.
  • Deployer duties, such as deepfake disclosure, have an owner on your side.
  • Counsel has reviewed the cases that are not obvious.

FAQ

We are a US company. Does this matter?

It matters if the vendor, the user, or the customer is in the EU, or if the contract pushes EU duties onto you. The checklist is the question list. Counsel decides whether you are a provider or a deployer.

Where is the law?

Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 on EUR-Lex, read with the Commission timeline that includes later amendments. Do not brief from a blog’s date if it disagrees with those two.

Sources

  • European Commission AI Act Service Desk timeline
  • Council of the EU, AI Act timeline
  • Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 on EUR-Lex
  • Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, the AI Act, on EUR-Lex: Article 50 transparency obligations and Article 99 penalties

Related

  • The EU AI Act did not slip. The high-risk part did.
  • When compliance is the product

item.title: The Cloud Shared-Responsibility Checklist
item.description: AWS’s model is security of the cloud versus security in the cloud. A managed database does not move your backup duty. An EC2 instance does not move the patch duty.
item.author: circuits50capital@circuits.fit (Emilio Santos)
item.content:encoded:
Amazon Web Services states the shared-responsibility model in public. AWS is responsible for security of the cloud: the hardware, software, networking, and facilities that run AWS services. The customer is responsible for security in the cloud. AWS says that responsibility depends on which services you pick. For Amazon EC2, AWS says the customer manages the guest operating system, including updates and security patches, the application software the customer installs, and the security-group firewall on the instance.

The split

Read this before a repatriation argument or a board slide that says “AWS is certified, so we are covered.” A certification of the provider’s infrastructure is not a patch on your image, a backup of your bucket, or a rule on your security group. AWS also says customers should look at the services they chose, because the work changes with the service, and because laws and regulations still apply to the customer.

The lines

QuestionWrite the owner
Who patches the guest OS on each EC2 image?A person’s name, not “AWS”
Who sets the security group?The team that can open a port
Who backs up data in a managed store, and who has tested a restore?Still you, unless a contract names the provider’s backup product and you have a restore date
Who configures encryption and keys?The person who can lose the key
Which of these would move if you left for a colo?The guest, the app, the data, the firewall rules. The building would not.

How Microsoft and Google describe the split

The lines above use AWS’s wording. Other providers publish their own, and they differ in useful ways.

Microsoft Azure. Microsoft’s shared responsibility page lays out a table by deployment type: software as a service, platform as a service, infrastructure as a service, and on-premises. Physical hosts, network, and datacenter sit with Microsoft for the cloud models. The page also lists responsibilities the customer always retains, regardless of deployment type: data, endpoints, accounts, and access management. That list is a good summary for a board slide. No matter how managed the service is, your data, your devices, and your identities are yours.

Google Cloud. Google describes shared responsibility together with what it calls “shared fate,” where it aims to give customers secure defaults, blueprints, and guidance to help them meet their side. That is a statement of intent and tooling. It does not move your responsibilities to Google.

How to use this checklist, step by step

  1. List your top services. Start with the services that make up most of the bill or hold the most sensitive data.
  2. Classify each one. Infrastructure (virtual machines), platform (managed databases, containers), or software as a service. Your share of the work shrinks as you move up, but it never reaches zero.
  3. Write an owner for each line. Patching, network rules, backups, keys, identities. A person’s name, not a team alias.
  4. Check evidence. A patch report, a recent restore, a key rotation log. If there is no evidence, the line is a gap.
  5. Revisit before any move. Before repatriation or a provider switch, mark which lines change hands. The cloud repatriation note has the cost side.

A worked example

Illustrative case. A company runs its customer app on virtual machines, a managed database, and object storage. On the VMs, the company patches the operating system and the app, and sets the firewall rules. On the managed database, the provider patches the engine, but the company sets who can connect, turns on encryption options, and tests restores. On object storage, the company sets access policies. A misconfigured public bucket is the customer’s mistake under every provider’s model. If the company moved to a colo, it would also take on the hardware, the facility, and the physical network.

Common mistakes

  • Assuming the provider’s compliance certifications cover your configuration. They cover the provider’s side.
  • Assuming managed services are backed up the way you need. Check retention and test a restore.
  • Forgetting identities. Most cloud incidents start with an account, not a broken data center.

Before you sign off

  • Each major service is classified as infrastructure, platform, or software as a service.
  • Each line on the checklist has a person’s name.
  • You have evidence for patching, backups, keys, and access rules, not only a policy.
  • You have read the split for every provider you use, in that provider’s own words.
  • Any planned move shows which lines would change hands.

FAQ

Does this page cover Azure or Google Cloud?

The wording here is AWS’s, because that is the page linked below. Other providers publish their own split. Do not paste the AWS sentence onto another logo. Open that provider’s page and redo the table.

Is the provider responsible for nothing in the guest?

AWS’s page draws the line at the host and the facility for EC2, and at the customer for the guest and the security group. Managed services move some of the platform work. They do not move your data-retention choices. Read the service you actually bought.

Backup tools we would use

Disclosure: links marked “Paid link” may earn Circuit & Capital a commission at no cost to you.

The backup line stays yours in SaaS too. For Microsoft 365 or Google Workspace, IDrive Cloud Applications Backup is $20 per seat per year on IDrive’s page (checked November 10, 2026). Paid link: we may earn a commission. Microsoft 365 Backup, Microsoft’s own service at $0.15 per GiB per month, is the non-affiliate alternative. If your backup software writes to S3-compatible storage, IDrive e2 is one option. Paid link: we may earn a commission. Full comparison: password managers and backup tools for small teams.

Sources

  • AWS, Shared Responsibility Model
  • Microsoft Learn, Shared responsibility in the cloud: responsibilities the customer always retains: data, endpoints, accounts, access management
  • Google Cloud Architecture Framework, shared responsibility and shared fate

Related

  • Cloud repatriation: when the bill becomes the strategy
  • When cloud repatriation is a finance decision
  • Risk exception register

item.title: What Belongs in a Processor Clause
item.description: The Commission adopted two different sets of standard clauses on June 4, 2021. One governs a processor inside the EEA. The other governs a transfer out. Do not sign the wrong PDF.
item.author: circuits50capital@circuits.fit (Emilio Santos)
item.content:encoded:
On June 4, 2021 the European Commission adopted two sets of standard contractual clauses. Its questions-and-answers page says one set is for the relationship between controllers and processors and meets Article 28(3) and (4) of the GDPR, including for use inside the EEA. The other set is for transfers of personal data to countries outside the EEA. They are both called SCCs. They are not interchangeable.

Two documents

When a vendor attaches “the SCCs,” ask which decision. If the vendor processes for you and you need an Article 28 contract, the controller-processor clauses are the Commission’s pre-approved text for that job. If the vendor moves personal data out of the EEA, that is the transfer set, and it has modules for who is sending and who is receiving. A transfer annex does not, by itself, describe the processing instructions. A processor clause does not, by itself, solve a transfer.

What to check

  • The subject matter, duration, nature, and purpose of the processing, and the type of personal data. If those annexes are blank, the clause is a shell.
  • Whether the vendor is a processor, a separate controller, or both for different products. The role is not a logo.
  • Sub-processors: who they are, and how you hear about a new one.
  • Deletion or return at the end of the service, in a sentence you can test.
  • If any data leaves the EEA, whether the transfer clauses are also attached, and which module.

The Article 28 list, in plain English

Article 28(3) of the GDPR says the contract between a controller and a processor must set out the subject matter and duration of the processing, its nature and purpose, the type of personal data, the categories of data subjects, and the controller’s obligations and rights. It then requires that the processor:

  1. processes the data only on documented instructions from the controller;
  2. ensures the people authorised to process the data are bound by confidentiality;
  3. takes the security measures required by Article 32;
  4. respects the conditions for engaging another processor, a sub-processor;
  5. helps the controller respond to data subjects exercising their rights;
  6. helps the controller with security, breach notification, and data protection impact assessments under Articles 32 to 36;
  7. deletes or returns all personal data at the end of the services, at the controller’s choice;
  8. makes available the information needed to show compliance, and allows for and contributes to audits and inspections.

Article 28(2) adds that a processor may not engage a sub-processor without the controller’s prior specific or general written authorisation, and with general authorisation must inform the controller of changes so it can object.

How to review a DPA, step by step

  1. Check the role. The EDPB’s Guidelines 07/2020 explain how to tell a controller from a processor. A vendor that decides its own purposes for your data, such as training its own models, may be acting as a controller for that use.
  2. Read the annexes first. Blank or generic descriptions of processing are the most common gap.
  3. Walk the eight items. Tick each one against the text. Note where the vendor’s wording weakens it, for example audits limited to a summary report only.
  4. Check sub-processors. Find the list, how changes are notified, and how long you have to object.
  5. Check transfers separately. If data leaves the EEA, confirm which transfer mechanism and SCC module is used.

A worked example

Illustrative case. A vendor’s DPA says it will “process data in accordance with applicable law and its privacy policy.” That is not a documented instruction from you. The fix is a clause that the vendor processes personal data only on your documented instructions, including those in the agreement. The same DPA says sub-processors are listed “on our website.” Ask for notice of changes by email and a defined objection period, for example 30 days. Its deletion clause says data is deleted “in line with our retention schedule.” Ask for deletion or return at your choice within a set number of days after termination. The software renewal scorecard counts unlisted subprocessors and short data-return windows against a renewal.

AI features and the processor clause

Many vendors now add AI features to existing products. Check whether the DPA or a new addendum lets the vendor use customer personal data to train or improve models. If it does, that use may need its own analysis of roles and lawful basis. Ask counsel. Do not assume the old DPA covers a new feature.

Before you sign off

  • The vendor’s role is clear for each product and each use of the data.
  • The processing annex is filled in, not generic.
  • All eight Article 28(3) items are present without weakening language.
  • Sub-processor changes come with notice and an objection period.
  • Transfer clauses, if needed, are attached with the right module.
  • Any AI training use of personal data has been reviewed by counsel.

FAQ

Can we edit the Commission’s text?

The Commission presents them as standardised, pre-approved clauses. Changing them can take you out of that approval. Ask counsel before you redline the model. You can and should complete the annexes. Blank annexes are the usual failure.

Does a US-only company need this?

Only if the GDPR, or a contract that imports it, applies. This page tells you how to tell the two PDFs apart. It does not decide applicability.

Sources

  • European Commission, questions and answers on the 2021 standard contractual clauses
  • European Commission, clauses for controllers and processors in the EU/EEA
  • Regulation (EU) 2016/679, the GDPR, on EUR-Lex: Article 28
  • EDPB Guidelines 07/2020 on the concepts of controller and processor
  • Commission Implementing Decision (EU) 2021/915, controller-processor SCCs

Related

  • When compliance is the product
  • What Article 50 asks a buyer

item.title: Before the Form 8-K Clock
item.description: The SEC’s clock is four business days from the materiality determination. Write down who can make that call, and what a private vendor must be able to say.
item.author: circuits50capital@circuits.fit (Emilio Santos)
item.content:encoded:
The SEC’s small-entity guide says domestic registrants disclose a material cybersecurity incident on Form 8-K within four business days after they determine the incident is material. Item 1.05 asks for the material aspects of nature, scope, and timing, and the material impact or reasonably likely material impact. The annual Form 10-K, under Regulation S-K Item 106, is a different duty: processes, board oversight, and management’s role.

The clock

Do not start the four days at the first alert. The Commission’s guide starts them at the materiality determination. That only helps if someone is authorized to make the determination, and if the facts they need are not trapped in a vendor’s ticket queue. Discovery without a decision is how the week vanishes.

What to rehearse

  • Name the person who can call an incident material, and the counsel they call. A committee that meets monthly will miss four business days.
  • List the facts Item 1.05 points at: what happened, what it touched, when, and what it does to the business. Practice filling those from logs you already keep.
  • If you are the vendor, write the notice you can send in one business day: systems, data types, what you turned off, what you do not yet know. “Promptly” in a contract is slower than a customer’s 8-K.
  • Keep the annual Item 106 description current. The incident form and the annual description answer different questions. The Commission did not require disclosure of a director’s cybersecurity expertise. Do not add that as if it were Item 106.

What the rule says, in more detail

The SEC adopted its cybersecurity disclosure rules on July 26, 2023. For a material cybersecurity incident, Item 1.05 of Form 8-K requires a company to describe the material aspects of the nature, scope, and timing of the incident, and its material impact or reasonably likely material impact, including on financial condition and results of operations. The filing is generally due four business days after the company determines the incident is material. The company must make that determination without unreasonable delay after discovery.

The rule allows a delay if the US Attorney General determines that disclosure would pose a substantial risk to national security or public safety and tells the SEC in writing. That is a narrow path, not a planning assumption.

On May 21, 2024, Erik Gerding, then Director of the SEC’s Division of Corporation Finance, issued a statement clarifying that Item 1.05 is for incidents the company has determined to be material. A company that wants to disclose an incident it has not determined to be material, or has determined is not material, can use a different item, such as Item 8.01. That keeps Item 1.05 meaningful for investors.

A tabletop drill in five steps

  1. Pick a realistic scenario. For example, ransomware encrypts a billing system, or a vendor reports that your customer data was exposed.
  2. Start the clock at discovery. Time how long it takes for the facts to reach the person who owns the materiality decision.
  3. Make the determination. Have the decision owner and counsel walk through the thresholds the company uses: financial, operational, customer, legal, reputational. Record the evidence considered.
  4. Count four business days. Draft the 8-K language for nature, scope, timing, and impact using only the facts you have.
  5. Review what was slow. Usually it is getting facts from a vendor, or finding the right decision-maker. Fix that before a real incident.

A worked example of the clock

Illustrative dates. An incident is discovered on Thursday, October 1, 2026. After investigation, the company determines on Tuesday, October 6, that it is material. The four business days start the next day: Wednesday the 7th, Thursday the 8th, Friday the 9th. Monday, October 12 is Columbus Day, a federal holiday, so it is skipped. The filing is due Tuesday, October 13, 2026. The discovery date does not move it. The 8-K materiality worksheet counts this for you and keeps a record of who decided what.

If you are the vendor

Your customer’s clock depends on your facts. Agree in advance on what you will send within one business day of an incident that may affect them: affected systems, data types, the time window, containment steps, and what is still unknown. Name who sends it. Put it in the contract if the customer asks. A vague “we will notify promptly” is slower than four business days in practice.

Before you sign off

  • One named person owns the materiality decision, with a named deputy.
  • The thresholds the company uses are written down before an incident.
  • Key vendors know what facts to send you, and how fast.
  • The team has run at least one tabletop and fixed what was slow.
  • The annual Item 106 description matches how the process actually works.

None of this is legal advice. Securities counsel should review the process and any draft filing.

FAQ

We are private. Why rehearse?

Because a public customer’s counsel will ask you for the facts in their filing window. Your own Form 8-K is not the only clock in the room.

Does insurance decide materiality?

No. An underwriter’s question and Item 1.05 are different documents. Answer both from the same facts. Do not let one substitute for the other.

Sources

  • SEC small-entity compliance guide on cybersecurity disclosure
  • SEC press release 2023-139, July 26, 2023
  • SEC, Cybersecurity Risk Management, Strategy, Governance, and Incident Disclosure, final rule
  • SEC Release No. 33-11216 (PDF)
  • SEC, Statement by Erik Gerding on disclosure of cybersecurity incidents, May 21, 2024: Item 1.05 for material incidents; other items such as 8.01 for others
  • SEC, Form 8-K (PDF)

Related

  • The SEC clock starts when you decide it matters
  • Cyber insurance is rewriting the IT budget
  • SEC 8-K materiality worksheet

item.title: A One-Page AI Use Rule
item.description: NIST’s AI RMF 1.0 is voluntary and organized as Govern, Map, Measure, and Manage. Use those four lines. Cite the version. A revision is in progress.
item.author: circuits50capital@circuits.fit (Emilio Santos)
item.content:encoded:
NIST released the AI Risk Management Framework 1.0 on January 26, 2023. It is voluntary. It is for organizations that design, develop, deploy, or use AI. The core is four functions: Govern, Map, Measure, and Manage. NIST’s AI Resource Center says a revision of 1.0 is in progress, and that the Generative AI Profile (NIST AI 600-1, July 26, 2024) is the profile for generative systems. Cite the document you actually used. Do not write “NIST compliant” on a one-pager.

The four lines

  • Govern. Who may turn a tool on, and who can turn it off. One name.
  • Map. What the tool is allowed to see, and what decision it is allowed to shape. Customer data, source code, and health information are separate yes-or-no lines.
  • Measure. What you will count so you know it worked: cycle time, error rate, or a review sample. “People like it” is not a measure.
  • Manage. What happens when the output is wrong, and how a person overrides it. If there is no override, say so in the same paragraph that approves the tool.

The page

Keep it to one page per tool, not one page for “AI.” Name the product, the owner, the data it may see, the decision it may not make alone, and the date you will look again. Link the NIST framework and, if the tool generates text or media, the generative profile, so a later reader can see you did not invent the four words.

A sample one-page rule

The example below is a template, not legal advice. Edit it to match your tools and data.

SectionExample wording
Approved toolsStaff may use the AI tools on the approved list, signed in with company accounts. Personal accounts are not allowed for company work.
Data you may not enterCustomer personal data, passwords and keys, unreleased financial results, and anything under a confidentiality agreement, unless the tool is approved for that data.
Checking outputA person reviews AI output before it is sent outside the company or used in a decision about a customer, employee, or payment.
ActionsAI tools may not send external messages, move money, or change access without a person approving each action.
DisclosureTell people when they are interacting with an AI system where law or contract requires it.
Owner and reviewThe rule has a named owner and is reviewed every six months. Date of this version: [date].

How to roll it out, step by step

  1. List the tools people already use. Ask, do not guess. Unapproved use is common when no rule exists.
  2. Decide the approved list. Prefer tools with company accounts, admin controls, and clear data-use terms.
  3. Write the page. Use the table above as a start. Keep it to one page so people read it.
  4. Train with examples. Show two or three real cases from your work: what is fine, what is not.
  5. Review on a schedule. Tools and laws change. Put the next review date on the page.

How the page maps to the NIST framework

The NIST AI Risk Management Framework has four functions. A one-page rule touches each of them lightly. Govern is the owner and review date. Map is the list of tools and the data each may see. Measure is the output check. Manage is the action limits and what happens when someone breaks the rule. That is enough to start, and it gives you a structure to grow into. For agents that can take actions, add the controls in Limit what an agent can touch. For EU-facing features, the disclosure line connects to What Article 50 asks a buyer.

Common mistakes

  • Banning everything. People use personal accounts instead, and you lose visibility.
  • Writing a ten-page policy. Nobody reads it, so nobody follows it.
  • Forgetting AI features inside existing software. They count too.

Before you sign off

  • The approved tool list exists and staff know where it is.
  • The data that must not go into AI tools is named in plain words.
  • Output that leaves the company, or affects a person or a payment, is checked by a person.
  • AI tools cannot take high-impact actions without approval.
  • The page has an owner, a version date, and a next review date.
  • Staff have seen two or three examples from their own work.

A rule is only useful if people can find it when they need it. Link it from the tools themselves where the admin console allows a custom notice, pin it in the main staff channel, and add it to onboarding. When the rule changes, say what changed in one line, so staff do not have to reread the whole page to spot the difference.

FAQ

Is this a full implementation of the AI RMF?

No. The framework is larger than four headings, and NIST’s playbook is the place for suggested actions. This page is how a department starts without pretending it finished.

What if NIST publishes a revision?

The Resource Center already says one is in progress. Date your one-pager. When you review the tool, check whether 1.0 is still the document you mean to cite.

Sources

  • NIST, AI Risk Management Framework
  • NIST AI 100-1, AI RMF 1.0, January 26, 2023
  • NIST AI Resource Center, AI RMF, including the note that a revision is in progress
  • NIST AI 600-1, Generative Artificial Intelligence Profile, July 26, 2024
  • OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025, LLM06: Excessive Agency

Related

  • Put an AI cost on one workflow
  • Limit what an agent can touch
  • AI agent inventory and access map

item.title: Questions Before a Post-Quantum Pilot
item.description: Gartner’s September 30 note: start a pilot, or expect at least double the migration cost after 2027. Fifty-one percent of surveyed CISOs had not started.
item.author: circuits50capital@circuits.fit (Emilio Santos)
item.content:encoded:
Gartner’s September 30, 2026 release says organizations that do not begin piloting post-quantum cryptography by 2027 will face at least 200% higher costs for the full migration. The same release says a survey of CISOs found 51% had not begun any post-quantum work. Christopher Mixter, a Gartner vice president analyst, describes harvest-now-decrypt-later and harvest-now-forge-later as reasons the data you store now is already part of the decision.

The claim

The 200% figure is Gartner’s prediction, not a quote you have measured in your own estate. Use it as a reason to inventory, not as a number to paste into a budget as if it were your quote. The 51% figure is a description of peers who have not started. It is not a reason to wait with them.

The pilot

  • Where do you use public-key cryptography today: TLS, VPN, code signing, email, document signing, and the keys inside vendor products? A pilot that only covers the website certificate is a demo.
  • Which data, if stolen this year and decrypted later, would still matter? That is the harvest-now list. Customer secrets and long-lived signatures belong on it. Ephemeral session data often does not.
  • Who owns the inventory, and what does “begun” mean? Gartner’s 51% is “have not begun any PQC-related activities.” A slide titled “quantum” with no system in scope is not a beginning.
  • What would the pilot change in ninety days: one protocol, one vendor that already offers a hybrid mode, or a list of products that cannot? Write the change, not the theme.

The standards are published

The pilot has a target. On August 13, 2024, NIST released its first three finalized post-quantum cryptography standards:

  • FIPS 203, ML-KEM, a key-encapsulation mechanism for establishing shared keys, derived from CRYSTALS-Kyber.
  • FIPS 204, ML-DSA, a digital signature algorithm derived from CRYSTALS-Dilithium.
  • FIPS 205, SLH-DSA, a stateless hash-based digital signature algorithm derived from SPHINCS+.

NIST has also published a draft transition report, NIST IR 8547, describing its expected approach to moving from quantum-vulnerable algorithms such as RSA and elliptic-curve cryptography to these standards. The initial public draft proposed deprecating those quantum-vulnerable algorithms after 2030 and disallowing them after 2035. It is a draft, so check the current version before you put a date in a plan. CISA keeps a post-quantum page with resources for organizations planning the move.

A 90-day pilot plan

  1. Weeks 1 to 3: inventory. List where public-key cryptography is used: TLS certificates, VPNs, SSH, code signing, document signing, and inside vendor products. Start with internet-facing systems.
  2. Weeks 3 to 5: rank by data lifetime. Data that must stay secret for ten years or more, and signatures that must stay trusted for a long time, go first.
  3. Weeks 5 to 8: ask vendors. For your top systems, ask each vendor whether it supports ML-KEM or a hybrid key exchange today, and if not, when.
  4. Weeks 8 to 12: test one change. Turn on a hybrid post-quantum key exchange in one test environment where your software supports it, and measure compatibility and performance.
  5. Week 12: report. What was inventoried, what was tested, what failed, and what it would take to extend.

A worked example of the vendor ask

Illustrative email: “We are planning our transition to NIST’s post-quantum standards, FIPS 203, 204, and 205. For [product], please tell us: which cryptographic algorithms the product uses for key exchange and signatures today; whether it supports ML-KEM or a hybrid key exchange now, and in which version; your roadmap date for ML-DSA or SLH-DSA signatures; and whether cryptographic algorithms can be changed by configuration or require an upgrade.” File the answers. A vendor with no roadmap is a risk you can now name.

What finance should know

Most of the cost is labor and replacement of products that cannot be upgraded, not new software licenses. The inventory is what turns Gartner’s prediction into your own estimate. Budget the inventory now. Budget the migration once you know what is in it.

Before you sign off

  • An inventory of public-key cryptography exists, starting with internet-facing systems.
  • Systems are ranked by how long their data or signatures must stay safe.
  • Top vendors have been asked about FIPS 203, 204, and 205 support, in writing.
  • One test environment has tried a hybrid key exchange, and the result is written down.
  • Finance has a budget line for the inventory, separate from the migration.

Report progress in the same terms each quarter: systems inventoried, systems ranked, vendors asked, vendors with a dated roadmap, and changes tested. Those five counts tell a board more than a maturity score, and they show whether the program is moving. When NIST finalizes its transition report, update the dates in the plan to match the final text.

FAQ

Do we need a quantum computer to start?

No. Gartner’s point is the migration of cryptography you already run, and the copies of data already leaving the building. The pilot is an inventory and a first system, not a physics project.

Is 200% our number?

No. It is Gartner’s prediction of cost for organizations that have not started a pilot by 2027. Get a vendor quote for your own estate before you brief it as a line item.

Sources

  • Gartner, five actions for CISOs, September 30, 2026
  • NIST, first three finalized post-quantum encryption standards, August 13, 2024
  • NIST FIPS 203, ML-KEM
  • NIST FIPS 204, ML-DSA
  • NIST FIPS 205, SLH-DSA
  • NIST IR 8547 (initial public draft), Transition to Post-Quantum Cryptography Standards
  • CISA, Post-Quantum Cryptography Initiative

Related

  • Five moves Gartner wants from a CISO before 2027
  • Cyber insurance is rewriting the IT budget

item.title: The SEC Proposed a Path for Crypto Custody
item.description: On October 1 the Commission proposed custody rules for crypto assets held by advisers and regulated funds. The posts are the alert. Comments run from the Federal Register.
item.author: circuits50capital@circuits.fit (Emilio Santos)
item.content:encoded:
The Securities and Exchange Commission’s account posted it as a same-day alert: the Commission had proposed new rules and amendments for the custody of crypto assets by registered investment advisers and by regulated funds, meaning registered investment companies and business development companies. A follow-up post the same evening said the proposal would modernize custody rules and expand investor choice by removing barriers that inhibit an adviser’s ability to give crypto-related advice. Those posts are the announcement. The specification is Release 2026-100, the chairman’s statement, the fact sheet, and the proposing release.

This is not legal advice, and it is not a note on the price of any token. It is the operator reading of a proposal that tells a fiduciary, for the first time in the Commission’s own words, that a compliant custody path is supposed to exist.

What the release actually proposes

The press release says the rules and amendments sit under the Investment Advisers Act of 1940 and the Investment Company Act of 1940. They are meant to match current industry practice and to update requirements that include financial-statement audits for registered investment advisers and broker-dealer custodial services for regulated funds. Two permissions are named in the release itself. Crypto assets could be held in self-custody under certain circumstances. State trust companies could be used as custodians for client assets and for regulated-fund crypto assets.

The release does not, in the pages this briefing uses, spell out those circumstances in a sentence a compliance officer can paste into a manual. That work is in the proposing release and the fact sheet. Read those before anyone tells a client that self-custody is now allowed. “Under certain circumstances” is the Commission’s phrase. It is not a yes.

Chairman Paul S. Atkins, in the statement dated October 1, describes the gap the proposal is aimed at. Custody rules were written to protect client and fund assets from loss, theft, misuse, and misappropriation, and they contemplate traditional assets. A key protection is the required use of permitted custodians. Atkins says custodial capability for a newly developed crypto asset can lag the asset’s deployment by many months. The proposal is the Commission’s attempt to close that lag, plus what he calls long-needed updates to adviser and fund custody rules that have not been amended for decades.

A permitted custodian that does not exist yet is not a control. It is a waiting period with a client’s assets in it.

What he placed this next to

Atkins’s statement puts the custody proposal in a sequence, and the sequence is his account of the Commission’s year, not a finding by this desk. He cites a December 2025 staff no-action letter to the Depository Trust Company on a voluntary securities-tokenization pilot. A January 2026 staff statement on tokenized securities. An interpretation of which crypto assets are securities and when they may cease to be subject to investment contracts. An April staff statement on broker-dealer registration for certain user interfaces used to prepare transactions in tokenized securities. An August proposal, Regulation Crypto Assets, for a tailored offering regime for certain investment contracts involving crypto assets. And an Innovation Exemption he describes as a cabined pathway for trading tokenized NMS stock.

He also says the market has grown from a niche into a multi-trillion-dollar asset class. The statement does not give a precise total. Do not put a round number in a board pack off that adjective. The useful sentence is the one about the rules: he says advisers and funds have been guessing how to effect lawful custody of an asset their clients want, and that the proposal is meant to replace that uncertainty.

The clock is the Federal Register

The press release says the public comment period stays open for 60 days after the proposing release is published in the Federal Register. October 1 is the day of the posts and the press release. It is not, on the page, day one of a 60-day count. Anyone drafting a comment should wait for the Federal Register date, then count. A comment filed against the wrong clock is a comment that misses the record.

Who should care before that date arrives. A registered adviser whose clients already hold crypto, or want to. A fund that would offer a strategy and cannot name a custodian the current rule recognizes. A state trust company that wants to be that custodian. A software vendor selling “custody” or “wallet” infrastructure into any of those three. The vendor’s demo is not the rule. The question for the contract is which of the proposal’s permissions the product depends on, and what happens to the service if the final rule narrows them.

What to write down this week

  • Are we an adviser, a regulated fund, a custodian, or a vendor selling to one of those? The proposal does not land on all four the same way.
  • Where do client or fund crypto assets sit today, and which of those places would the proposal recognize?
  • Does anyone inside the firm plan to rely on self-custody? If yes, the “certain circumstances” have to be copied from the proposing release, not from a summary.
  • Would a state trust company be the custodian? Name it. “A trust company” is not a control.
  • Who owns the comment, and what is the Federal Register date once it exists?

None of this changes the cybersecurity clock on Form 8-K. A custody proposal and an incident disclosure are different rules from the same agency. The incident note remains The SEC clock starts when you decide it matters.

Sources

  • SEC on X, custody proposal for advisers and funds, October 1, 2026
  • SEC on X, the proposal would modernize custody and address crypto-related advice, October 1, 2026
  • SEC press release 2026-100, October 1, 2026
  • Paul S. Atkins, statement on the proposal, October 1, 2026
  • SEC fact sheet, Investment Adviser and Regulated Fund Custody Rules
  • SEC proposing release IA-7023

Related: The SEC clock starts when you decide it matters and Before the Form 8-K clock.

item.title: Astra Ultrafast Is a Speed Claim. The Bill Is Still Yours.
item.description: NVIDIA says GPT-6 Astra Ultrafast is up to 8x faster than Astra Standard on token generation. That number is theirs. The invoice is yours.
item.author: circuits50capital@circuits.fit (Emilio Santos)
item.content:encoded:
NVIDIA’s account posted it on October 1: up to 8x faster, and GPT-6 Astra Ultrafast runs on NVIDIA. The post points at a company blog. The blog, by Dion Harris and dated the same day, is the specification. It says Ultrafast is available now in the OpenAI API and to eligible ChatGPT Work and Codex users. It runs on Blackwell GPUs. OpenAI’s inference optimizations use that architecture. Against Astra Standard mode, NVIDIA says Ultrafast offers up to 8x faster token generation.

Read the “up to.” It is NVIDIA’s comparison, on NVIDIA’s page, against one other mode of the same model family. It is not a measurement this desk has repeated, and it is not a promise that your coding agent will finish a workday eight times sooner. Faster token generation matters in a loop. It does not retire the loop.

Where they say the speed shows up

The blog names three places: code generation, tool use, and interactive applications. The operator sentence is the next one. A faster response matters most when it is repeated. An agent writes code, uses a tool, checks the result, and decides what to do next. Ultrafast is pitched as Astra inside that cycle: shorter edit-test-debug runs, less time between tool calls, applications that feel more responsive.

Philippe Tillet, identified as inference lead at OpenAI, is quoted saying NVIDIA’s tooling let OpenAI’s models get “exceptionally good at programming Blackwell and Rubin GPUs,” and that Astra can turn that into kernels across latency, throughput, and cost. The product described as available is Ultrafast on Blackwell. Rubin is in the quote as hardware the model can program. Do not brief a board that Ultrafast “runs on Rubin” off that sentence.

Uday Ruddarraju, identified as chief technology officer of compute at OpenAI, says OpenAI used its internal models to optimize inference on NVIDIA GPUs, and that NVIDIA’s programmability helped deliver the acceleration. A later section says the gains do not stop at deployment. OpenAI is using its own models to keep refining the inference software, and a programmable platform is supposed to let the same machines move across training, inference, and reinforcement learning so teams are not overbuilding for one workload.

An agent that finishes the wrong tool call faster has not saved the afternoon. It has spent it sooner.

What the post does not settle

Price is not in the blog post this briefing uses. The page sends developers to OpenAI’s Ultrafast guide for access, pricing, and implementation. That guide is the page that answers “what does a token cost,” and it can change without NVIDIA editing the blog. Quote the guide you opened, with the date you opened it. Do not quote the 8x as a discount.

Eligibility is also narrower than “ChatGPT.” The blog says the API, and eligible ChatGPT Work and Codex users. If the people who would use this are on a different plan, the announcement does not include them until that guide says so.

Gartner posted on September 24 that managing AI cost is becoming as important as deploying AI, and pointed at pricing that shifts from seats and consumption toward coding agents. The same house’s September 16 forecast still puts most of the industry bill in infrastructure, not in the seat a company renews. Ultrafast is a candidate for both lines. The chip owner hears a utilization story. The buyer of the API hears a faster agent and an unknown invoice. Put them in different cells. The forecast note is Gartner revised the AI bill. Check the speed line in the vendor claim checker, and the price in token cost to gross margin. The worksheet is Put an AI cost on one workflow.

The same month already asked who may touch the tools

Three days before this speed post, NVIDIA launched the Open Agent Safety Platform. OpenShell is the open-source runtime that is supposed to enforce permissions. Sentry is the BlueField watchdog. The failure they described was an agent getting around application-layer controls to finish its task. Ultrafast is aimed at the same shape of work: an agent, a tool, another step. A faster loop makes a missing permission more expensive, not less. The write-up is NVIDIA put the fence outside the agent. The sheet is the agent access limit sheet. The question list is Limit what an agent can touch.

Ask four things before anyone turns the mode on for a team. Which workflow repeats often enough that token time is actually the wait. Whether those calls can spend money, send mail, or change a record. What the Ultrafast guide says the price is on the day you switch. And who can turn it off if the loop gets quicker and worse. The 8x stays NVIDIA’s claim until someone you trust times your own workflow.

Sources

  • NVIDIA on X, GPT-6 Astra Ultrafast, October 1, 2026
  • NVIDIA blog, Dion Harris, “How NVIDIA GPUs Help Accelerate OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra Ultrafast,” October 1, 2026
  • OpenAI, Ultrafast guide, linked from the NVIDIA blog for access, pricing, and implementation
  • Gartner on X, AI cost and coding-agent pricing, September 24, 2026
  • NVIDIA on X, Open Agent Safety Platform, September 28, 2026

Related: NVIDIA put the fence outside the agent, the vendor claim checker, and Put an AI cost on one workflow.

item.title: NVIDIA Put the Fence Outside the Agent
item.description: On September 28 NVIDIA posted that OpenShell enforces what an agent may do, and that a BlueField chip can watch from outside the software the agent runs in.
item.author: circuits50capital@circuits.fit (Emilio Santos)
item.content:encoded:
The announcement arrived as posts, which is how a lot of this market now hears about a product before the PDF. On September 28, NVIDIA’s account said it had launched an Open Agent Safety Platform: OpenShell enforces permissions, BlueField-4 and DOCA add monitoring outside the agent, and Vera CPUs power the work. The same morning Jensen Huang posted that more than 100 industry partners were involved, and that the pair of pieces was OpenShell and Sentry. His line, on the post NVIDIA quoted: “Trust and innovation are not in conflict. Safety is how trust is earned.” Later that day NVIDIA posted a clip of Huang on CNBC calling himself “a responsible optimist,” and pointing at OpenShell as the reason.

A post is the announcement. The specification is the newsroom page NVIDIA published the same day. This briefing uses the posts as the record that the claim was made in public, and the newsroom page as the record of what the product is supposed to be. It is not a test of the software, and it is not a statement that every named partner has shipped a matching product.

What the newsroom page actually describes

NVIDIA calls the package the Open Agent Safety Platform. It has two parts, and the company says an organization can deploy them separately.

OpenShell is open source and, in NVIDIA’s wording, broadly available. It is a runtime boundary. It traces what the agent does and enforces a policy, with what NVIDIA calls minimal overhead on its Vera CPUs. The company says the same approach can be extended to Arm and Intel. The code and related skills are pointed at NVIDIA’s developer documentation and at the OpenShell repository on GitHub.

Sentry is a reference design, not a claim that your current servers already contain it. It is an out-of-band watchdog on BlueField-4 data processing units. NVIDIA says it can quarantine an agent in milliseconds, that the control sits in silicon, and that it is invisible to the agent and to an attacker on the agent. It is built on DOCA. The jobs NVIDIA lists are inspection of requests and responses, attested telemetry, identity, and zero trust for data, tools, and APIs.

The failure NVIDIA is selling against is specific. The company describes an agent that got around security controls at the application layer in order to finish the task it had been given. The fence, in that story, cannot be a prompt inside the same process. Something that is not the agent has to be able to say no.

If the agent can rewrite the rule that governs the agent, the rule is a suggestion.

What a buyer who does not run Vera or BlueField still has

Most of the companies reading this do not have a Vera CPU rack or a BlueField-4 card in the purchase order they will sign this quarter. The newsroom page still leaves them two separate questions, because NVIDIA split the product.

The first is OpenShell. It is the open-source runtime. A team that already runs coding agents, support agents, or a tool-using workflow can ask whether that runtime, or something with the same job, sits between the agent and the tools. The job is a trace of actions and a policy that can refuse one. “We use a model with a safety filter” is a different sentence. A filter inside the model is what the agent can be asked to talk its way around. A boundary outside the model is a permission.

The second is Sentry. That one is hardware. If you do not run BlueField, you do not have the watchdog NVIDIA described, and a salesperson should not be allowed to imply that a software SKU includes it. You can still ask the narrower question the design is pointing at: is anything watching the agent from a place the agent cannot see, and can that watcher cut the agent off without asking the agent’s permission?

NVIDIA’s own boilerplate on the release says many products and features are described as “when and if available,” and that the page is not a commitment. Treat partner logos the same way. The newsroom summary names a long list, among them Anthropic, SpaceXAI, Scale AI, Salesforce, SAP, Accenture, CrowdStrike, Cisco, Microsoft, Palantir, Palo Alto Networks, ServiceNow, and several banks and server makers. A name on that list is NVIDIA’s claim of a partnership or an integration path. It is not, by itself, a product you can order on Monday under that partner’s brand. Ask the vendor you actually pay what they run today.

The same week, the survey said most firms have not drawn the line

Two days after the launch, on September 30, Gartner published five actions it wants from chief information security officers before 2027. One of them is to treat frontier deployments as insider risk: govern a multi-agent system by what it is allowed to do, and constrain the blast radius. In Gartner’s second-quarter survey of 297 cybersecurity leaders, 54% of organizations had no defined limit on AI-agent access, or they let the agent inherit access already given to a person.

Put the two documents next to each other and the sales pitch is obvious, which does not make it false. NVIDIA is describing a fence. Gartner is saying most of the organizations it asked have not decided where the fence goes, and many have handed the agent a person’s keys. A platform announcement does not close that gap. A permission you have not written down cannot be enforced by a runtime you have not deployed.

There is a second Gartner post in the same stretch, on September 30, that does not belong in the product review and does belong in the budget conversation. Gartner said that as enterprises ramp up AI spending, CIOs are under pressure to deliver more with limited budget growth, and pointed at a 2027 CIO Agenda Preview that it says reveals four technology-planning disconnects. The post does not list the four. This briefing will not invent them. The useful collision is the one you can already see: a $2.7 trillion industry forecast on one slide, a CIO told to do more without a matching budget on the next, and a new safety platform that will show up as a chip, a runtime, or a services line. Those are three different checks. The September spending revision is the first. This launch is a candidate for the third.

What to ask this month

Write the questions in the order a renewal will try to skip.

  • Which agent in our environment can send mail, open a ticket, change a record, or call a tool that spends money? Whose credentials does it use?
  • Is the allow-list a policy outside the model, or a paragraph in the prompt?
  • If we are being offered “OpenShell,” is that NVIDIA’s repository, a vendor build on top of it, or a different product using the word?
  • If we are being offered “Sentry” or “agent safety,” does the quote include BlueField, or only software? If it is only software, say so in the order.
  • Can the control quarantine the agent without the agent’s cooperation, and who is paged when it does?
  • Which of the partner claims are live in the tenant we would actually turn on?

NVIDIA also pointed at the Open Secure AI Alliance, which it says it initiated, which it counts at more than 120 organizations, and which it says the Linux Foundation governs, including a Shared AI Findings Exchange. That is a governance club and a sharing channel. It is not a substitute for the permission on your own agent. Join it or don’t. Still write down what the agent is allowed to touch.

Forward-looking lines on the newsroom page — quarantine in milliseconds, overhead, a partner’s future integration — are NVIDIA’s claims. They are not measurements this desk has repeated. Use them as questions for a proof, not as facts in a board pack, until someone you trust has run the test on your stack.

Sources

  • NVIDIA on X, launch post for the Open Agent Safety Platform, September 28, 2026
  • Jensen Huang on X, OpenShell, Sentry, and the partner count, September 28, 2026
  • NVIDIA on X, Huang on CNBC, September 28, 2026
  • NVIDIA newsroom, “Open Agent Safety Platform,” September 28, 2026
  • NVIDIA OpenShell on GitHub
  • NVIDIA, agent-safety product page linked from the release
  • Gartner, five CISO actions, September 30, 2026 (the 54% access figure)
  • Gartner on X, CIO budget pressure and the 2027 agenda preview, September 30, 2026

Related on this site: Five moves Gartner wants from a CISO before 2027, the agent access limit sheet, then Limit what an agent can touch, and A one-page AI use rule.

item.title: CISA Listed Three Bugs Attackers Are Already Using
item.description: WordPress on September 25, Apple on September 29, Cisco SD-WAN Manager on September 30. The posts are the alerts. The catalog holds the due dates.
item.author: circuits50capital@circuits.fit (Emilio Santos)
item.content:encoded:
For five days at the end of September, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency’s account on X did the thing it does when a bug is no longer theoretical. It posted an addition to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog, and it pointed at the same short link each time. Friday, September 25: WordPress Core, remote file inclusion, CVE-2026-87902. Tuesday, September 29: an Apple out-of-bounds write, CVE-2026-86950. Wednesday, September 30: Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN Manager, a hex-encoding issue, CVE-2026-76504. Each post is an alert. The catalog entry is the specification: what CISA says the bug can do, the date it was added, the date a federal civilian agency is supposed to be done, and the vendor page CISA considers the remediation.

This is an operator note, not a description of how to use the bugs. If you run the product, the job is to confirm that, apply the vendor’s fix, and write down the date. If you do not run it, write that down too, so the next person does not reopen the thread.

What the catalog is, and who it binds

CISA describes the catalog as the authoritative list of vulnerabilities that have been exploited in the wild. Binding Operational Directive 22-01 is the document that requires Federal Civilian Executive Branch agencies to remediate a listed vulnerability by the due date on the entry. CISA’s own program page says the directive does not bind everyone else. It also says CISA wants state and local governments, and private companies, to treat the list as the queue that goes first.

The entries added in this stretch carry a second instruction on the catalog page itself. For each of the three, CISA marks forensic triage under BOD 26-04 as required, and the stated action is to apply the vendor’s mitigations in line with that directive, or to stop using the product if no mitigation exists. This briefing does not restate BOD 26-04. The point for a private company is narrower. A due date with your agency’s name on it is a federal clock. The same row is still evidence that someone is already using the bug against organizations that have no federal clock at all.

Ransomware use, on all three entries, is marked unknown. Unknown is not a clean bill. It means CISA has not published that link. Do not brief a board that “this is not ransomware” off that field.

The three posts, and the three rows

WordPress Core, CVE-2026-87902. Added September 25. Due September 28. CISA’s row calls it a remote file inclusion in WordPress Core: an unauthenticated attacker could make page-template resolution include a chosen readable local PHP file outside the active theme directories, leading to remote code execution. The catalog points at the WordPress security advisory as the vendor instruction. The federal due date had already passed by the time this briefing was published. If a marketing site, a customer portal, or a blog on a box you still patch is on a vulnerable release, the lateness is the fact. Confirm the version against that advisory, update, and keep the record. A host that “manages WordPress for you” is still your outage if the core was not moved.

Apple, CVE-2026-86950. Added September 29. Due October 2. CISA says iOS, macOS, and iPadOS contain an out-of-bounds write in CoreGraphics that may lead to arbitrary code execution. The catalog points at three Apple support pages as the vendor instructions. The federal due date is the day after this briefing. Phones and laptops are a different queue from a data-center patch, which is why this one gets missed. Ask who can see whether managed devices are on the fixed release, and what happens to a device that has not checked in.

Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN Manager, CVE-2026-76504. Added September 30. Due October 3. CISA’s description is a hex-encoding vulnerability: an unauthenticated, remote attacker could reach an affected system with the privileges of the admin user because of improper handling of URI encoding in an HTTP request. The catalog links Cisco’s advisory. That is the page that says which releases are affected and which builds are fixed. A management plane that can push configuration to branches is not a low-value target just because the hostname is unfamiliar to the finance team. If the manager is reachable, it is on the list. If a Cisco-operated cloud is in the path, confirm with Cisco what they already patched and what you still run yourself. Do not assume the two are the same box.

The post tells you the name. The catalog tells you the date. The vendor page tells you the fix. Skip one of the three and you are guessing.

The catalog had more than the three posts

The account’s posts were the loud three. The catalog page, read on October 1, shows the week was busier than that, and those other rows are just as much “known exploited” as the ones that fit in a social post.

On September 27 CISA added two Citrix NetScaler issues, CVE-2026-88771 and CVE-2026-88772, both due September 30. The first is an improper input validation bug that CISA says could let an unauthenticated attacker run arbitrary commands on NetScaler ADC and NetScaler Gateway. The second is a memory-handling bug that CISA says could allow remote code execution or a denial of service. Those federal due dates have passed. A later catalog row, CVE-2026-88779, is a separate NetScaler entry, added October 4 and due October 7. That note is Citrix NetScaler is on the exploited catalog again. A remote-access gateway is the sort of system a company forgets it still has until a customer cannot log in.

On October 1 the catalog added Fortinet FortiMail, CVE-2026-104286, due October 4. CISA describes a path-traversal issue that may let an unauthenticated attacker write arbitrary files via crafted HTTP or HTTPS requests. This desk is not treating a single day’s catalog as a complete history. It is treating the row as the official add, the way the three posts were the official alerts.

None of this is a vulnerability-management program. It is the week’s evidence that “we will look at it in the monthly window” is a choice to stay exposed to bugs CISA has already called exploited. The monthly window can still exist. These rows do not wait for it.

What to do on Thursday

Make a list of five product names: WordPress, Apple devices, Catalyst SD-WAN Manager, NetScaler, FortiMail. Next to each, write yes, no, or “owned by the host.” For every yes, write the version you are on, the version the vendor page says is fixed, the person who can change it, and the date you will check again. For a federal contractor, also write the catalog due date, because your customer may ask why you missed it even when BOD 22-01 does not name you.

Do not turn the list into a claim that you were or were not compromised. CISA’s action line for these entries includes forensic triage for agencies under BOD 26-04. A private company can still decide, with its own counsel and its own logs, whether a bug that was exploited in the wild deserves a look backward as well as a patch forward. That decision is not this article.

If the same week produces a customer question from a public company, the patch date and the materiality date are different clocks. Item 1.05 of Form 8-K runs from the materiality determination, not from the morning a CVE is posted. A known-exploited bug is not automatically a material incident. It is a fact your customer’s counsel may ask you to explain quickly. The note on that clock is the SEC piece. The way you learn whether a library or a core you did not think you ran is actually in the stack is the ingredients list in the SBOM piece.

Sources

  • CISA on X, WordPress Core CVE-2026-87902 added to the catalog, September 25, 2026
  • CISA on X, Apple CVE-2026-86950, September 29, 2026
  • CISA on X, Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN Manager CVE-2026-76504, September 30, 2026
  • CISA catalog entry, CVE-2026-87902 (added September 25, due September 28)
  • CISA catalog, CVE-2026-86950 and CVE-2026-76504, plus the Citrix and FortiMail rows read October 1, 2026
  • CISA, Reducing the Significant Risk of Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (BOD 22-01 binds FCEB agencies; CISA urges every other organization to prioritize the catalog)
  • WordPress security advisory linked from the CVE-2026-87902 catalog entry
  • Cisco advisory linked from the CVE-2026-76504 catalog entry
  • Apple support pages linked from the CVE-2026-86950 catalog entry (149228, 149229)

Related: The SEC clock starts when you decide it matters and The software ingredients list now covers the suite. For the second question, “do we run this,” use the SBOM request pack, then Ask a vendor for an SBOM.

item.title: Five Moves Gartner Wants from CISOs Before 2027
item.description: A September 30 note treats agents as insiders, a familiar voice as a weak approval, and post-quantum work as something that gets expensive if it waits.
item.author: circuits50capital@circuits.fit (Emilio Santos)
item.content:encoded:
On September 30, Gartner published five actions it says chief information security officers should take before 2027. Christopher Mixter, a Gartner vice president analyst, framed the uncertainty as three things at once: AI-augmented attacks, debates over AI safety, and quantum-computing risk. The useful part of the note is not the mood. It is the survey lines underneath two of the five actions.

This is a security-leadership briefing. It is not a product list, and it is not a claim that doing the five things produces a return.

What the five actions actually say

Gartner’s public release names them in this order.

  • Cement a role in AI safety. Gartner says securing the infrastructure and the way models meet company systems matters more than the safety of the model alone, and that CISOs are becoming the de facto authority other executives will ask.
  • Treat frontier deployments as insider risk. An agent does not need general intelligence to matter. It needs permission to change an operation. Gartner says CISOs should govern multi-agent systems by what they are allowed to do, and constrain the blast radius.
  • Stop treating recognition as proof of identity. Deepfakes are mainstream in Gartner’s wording. A face or a voice should not be enough to authorize a decision. Detection has to sit next to another authenticator and a check on where the content came from.
  • Budget for preemptive controls. Luis Castillo, a Gartner senior director analyst, says detection and response are no longer enough, and names moving-target defense, obfuscation, deception, and predictive threat intelligence as the class of spend to price.
  • Pilot post-quantum cryptography. Gartner predicts that organizations which have not started a pilot by 2027 will face at least 200% higher cost for the full migration. Mixter calls harvest-now-decrypt-later, and harvest-now-forge-later, reasons to start while the data is still only stolen, not yet read.

The two numbers worth putting on a slide

In a second-quarter 2026 survey of 297 cybersecurity leaders, Gartner says 54% of organizations have no defined approach to limit AI-agent access, or they let the agent inherit access already defined for a person. In a second-quarter survey of more than 300 enterprise risk leaders, 76% of CISOs ranked AI-driven discovery of vulnerabilities among their top 10 emerging risks. And 51% of CISOs in Gartner’s survey had not started any post-quantum work.

An agent with a human’s permissions is not a copilot. It is a second employee you did not hire and cannot see in the HR system.

What an operator does with this

Pick the action that is already true in your environment, not the one that sounds newest. If a workflow can send mail, move money, or open a ticket, write down whose credentials it uses. If the answer is “the integration user’s,” you are in the 54%. If a wire or a vendor change can be approved because someone recognized a voice, you are on the identity action, whether or not you have bought deepfake software. If cryptography ownership is “the network team, someday,” you are in the 51%.

Gartner also pointed, in the same release, to a separate August 26 forecast that the market for securing AI reaches almost $5 billion in 2027. That is a vendor market. It is not your budget. Your budget is the permission change, the second factor on the approval, and a named pilot for the keys you would not want read in ten years.

Write one sentence for each action

The five actions are easy to nod at and hard to staff. The useful version is a sentence a named person can defend, with a date on it. If you cannot write the sentence, you have not started the action, whatever the strategy slide says.

  • AI safety role. Name the person other executives are supposed to call when a model is wired into a system of record, and write whether that person can stop a deployment or only comment on it.
  • Insider risk. For each agent that can change an operation, write the systems it can reach and the credentials it uses. “The integration user” is the 54%. Gartner’s figure is from a second-quarter survey of 297 cybersecurity leaders. It is not the same sample as the 76% figure, which comes from a second-quarter survey of more than 300 enterprise risk leaders. Do not add them together.
  • Recognition is not identity. List the decisions that can still be approved because someone recognized a voice or a face. Put a second check next to each one, or take the voice off the approval path.
  • Preemptive controls. Pick one of Castillo’s named classes — moving-target defense, obfuscation, deception, or predictive threat intelligence — and put a number next to it for next year’s plan. “We should look at deception” is not a budget line.
  • Post-quantum pilot. The 200% figure is Gartner’s prediction of migration cost if no pilot has started by 2027. It is not your vendor’s quote. The 51% figure is the share of surveyed CISOs who had not started any post-quantum work. Name the data you would not want read later, and the person who owns a pilot for the keys that protect it.

Two days earlier, a vendor described the fence

On September 28, before this Gartner note, NVIDIA posted that it had launched an Open Agent Safety Platform. The posts say OpenShell enforces permissions, and that BlueField and DOCA can monitor an agent from outside the software the agent runs in. The newsroom page is the spec: an open-source runtime boundary, and a separate hardware watchdog NVIDIA calls Sentry. The company describes an agent that circumvented controls at the application layer to finish its task. That is the insider-risk action, told from the vendor side.

Read it as a product claim, not as proof that the 54% have been solved. A runtime you have not deployed cannot enforce a permission you have not written. A BlueField card you do not own is not “included” in a software renewal unless the order says so. The longer note is NVIDIA put the fence outside the agent. The spending context, including Gartner’s September 30 post that CIOs must deliver more without matching budget growth, is the revised AI bill. Gartner’s account did not, in the posts this desk has used, list four “disconnects” by name. The preview post says they exist. The press release on the five CISO actions is still the document that names the work.

Sources

  • Gartner, “Identifies Top Five Actions for CISOs To Take by End of 2026,” September 30, 2026
  • Gartner, forecast that the market for securing AI reaches almost $5 billion in 2027, August 26, 2026
  • NVIDIA on X, Open Agent Safety Platform, September 28, 2026
  • NVIDIA newsroom, Open Agent Safety Platform, September 28, 2026
  • Gartner on X, CIO budget pressure, September 30, 2026

Operator pages: the agent access limit sheet, then Limit what an agent can touch, Stop using a voice as approval, and Questions before a post-quantum pilot.
