item.title: The EU AI Act Did Not Slip. The High-Risk Part Did.
item.description: Article 50 transparency has been in force since August 2. Stand-alone high-risk duties move to December 2, 2027. A US buyer still has to ask which date the vendor is selling.
item.author: circuits50capital@circuits.fit (Emilio Santos)
item.content:encoded:
The Council of the European Union’s timeline for the Artificial Intelligence Act, updated after its June 29, 2026 sign-off, splits the law into dates a buyer can actually use. Most of the Act’s rules reached their general application on August 2, 2026. The high-risk regime did not. The Council records a fixed delay: December 2, 2027 for stand-alone high-risk systems, and August 2, 2028 for high-risk systems embedded in products. The European Commission’s AI Act Service Desk, which says its timeline includes the Digital Omnibus amendments, lists the same two high-risk dates, and a nearer one: December 2, 2026.

This briefing is for a company that buys software, including a company outside the EU whose vendor, customer, or data sits inside it. It is not a determination that your system is high-risk. That is a legal question. The operator question is whether the contract names a date.

What is already on

The Service Desk says transparency rules in Article 50 started to apply on August 2, 2026, along with enforcement for those rules, for prohibitions already in force, for general-purpose AI, and for AI literacy. On December 2, 2026 two further things arrive. New prohibitions cover AI systems that generate non-consensual sexual deepfakes and child sexual abuse material. And providers of certain generative systems that were already on the market before August 2, 2026 hit the end of the transition for the Article 50(2) machine-readable marking duty.

So “the AI Act was delayed” is the wrong sentence in a renewal. The delay the Council adopted is the high-risk application date. Transparency, and the December marking deadline for systems already shipping, were not given that same extra year.

What a vendor will try to collapse

A pitch that says “high-risk is 2027, so we are fine” may be describing Annex III stand-alone systems, the employment, education, credit, and essential-service uses the delay covers. It may also be describing a chatbot, a synthetic image, or a feature inside a suite you already license. Those are not the same article of the regulation. Ask the vendor to name the article, the annex, and the date, in the order form or in a schedule. If they cannot, you do not have a compliance claim. You have a slogan.

A delay of the high-risk chapter is not a delay of the duty to say that a person is talking to a machine.

What to write down this month

List every AI feature you have turned on, or that a vendor turned on inside a product, that a customer or employee in the EU can reach. Next to each one, write whether the output is synthetic, whether a person is told, and whether the vendor’s marking deadline is December 2, 2026 or a later high-risk date. Keep the Council timeline and the Service Desk timeline in the packet. When they disagree with a salesperson, the public timeline wins until counsel says otherwise.

Four dates, in the order a contract will scramble them

Put the dates on one page and refuse a vendor slide that uses only the furthest one.

  • February 2, 2025. The AI literacy duty in Article 4 and the first prohibitions applied. Providers and deployers have had to take AI literacy measures since this date.
  • August 2, 2026. Article 50 transparency is already in application. The same date starts enforcement, at national and EU level, of rules that already applied: the prohibitions, general-purpose AI, and AI literacy. For literacy, August 2 is when enforcement began, not when the duty began. This date was not the one the Council moved.
  • December 2, 2026. New Article 5 prohibitions on non-consensual intimate imagery and on generation of child sexual abuse material. The same day ends the machine-readable marking transition for certain generative systems that were already on the market before August 2, 2026.
  • December 2, 2027. Stand-alone Annex III high-risk systems. This is the delay people mean when they say the Act slipped. It is not a delay of the two dates above.
  • August 2, 2028. High-risk systems embedded in products under Annex I. Later still, and still not a excuse for a chatbot that never tells a person it is a machine.

Where the Council’s public timeline and the Service Desk disagree, including on sandboxes, prefer the Service Desk wording if it is the one that says it includes the Digital Omnibus. Then ask counsel. Do not let a salesperson pick the source that flatters the demo.

What Gartner posted, and what it does not add

On September 19, Gartner’s account posted that AI literacy requirements under the EU AI Act were “now in effect,” and used the post to point at a webinar. Treat that as Gartner’s claim, made in public, on top of a timeline the Commission had already published. The AI literacy duty in Article 4 has applied since February 2, 2025. What the Service Desk places in the August 2, 2026 package is enforcement of that duty, not the duty itself. The post does not create a new legal instrument, and it does not spell out a checklist. This briefing will not invent literacy mechanics the post does not contain. Read the Service Desk timeline for what the Commission has actually dated.

For a buyer, literacy is the awkward middle item. It is not the high-risk chapter that moved to 2027. It is also not a marking pixel on a generated image. It is the question of whether the people who turn the feature on, and the people who are subject to it, have been told enough to use it without pretending the law is still pending. Ask the vendor what they provide — training, a notice, a configuration — and ask your own team who attended. A webinar invitation from an analyst firm is not your record.

A company outside the EU still writes the dates down when a vendor, a customer, or the data sits inside the Union. The contract should name the article, the annex if there is one, and the date. “We will comply with the AI Act” names none of the three.

Updated October 26, 2026: clarified that the AI literacy duty has applied since February 2, 2025, and that August 2, 2026 is when enforcement of it began. Listed in the corrections log.

Sources

  • Council of the European Union, Artificial Intelligence Act timeline (high-risk dates recorded after the June 29, 2026 Council decision)
  • European Commission, AI Act Service Desk, implementation timeline (includes the Omnibus amendments)
  • AI Act Service Desk, Article 113, entry into force and application (Chapters I and II, including Article 4 on AI literacy, apply from February 2, 2025)
  • Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, the Artificial Intelligence Act, EUR-Lex
  • Gartner on X, AI literacy requirements “now in effect,” September 19, 2026

Operator pages: What Article 50 asks a buyer and A one-page AI use rule. Earlier briefing: When compliance is the product.

item.title: The Software Ingredients List Now Covers the Suite
item.description: CISA’s July 29 revision of the SBOM minimum elements applies to SaaS and AI software, not only to code you compile. The new fields are the ones to ask for.
item.author: circuits50capital@circuits.fit (Emilio Santos)
item.content:encoded:
On July 29, 2026, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, with the National Security Agency, the FBI, and international partners, published the 2026 Minimum Elements for a Software Bill of Materials. CISA says the revision updates and replaces the minimum elements the National Telecommunications and Information Administration published in 2021. The line that changes a renewal: the minimum elements apply to all software, including open source, AI software, and software-as-a-service.

An SBOM is the ingredients list. CISA’s own description is that it lets a buyer see components and make a risk decision. It is not a vulnerability scan, and it is not a promise that the vendor is safe. It is the document you can ask for before you sign.

What was added

CISA’s release names new minimum elements that were not in the 2021 baseline: component hash algorithm, component license, the name of the tool that produced the SBOM, and SBOM generation context. The agency also says some software types, including AI and SaaS, may need elements beyond that baseline. A separate May 12, 2026 guide, written with G7 partners, is the supplemental list for AI systems. CISA is explicit that the AI list is in addition to the general minimum elements, and that it is guidance, not a statute that by itself obliges every vendor.

That distinction matters in a negotiation. You can require the document in a contract even where no regulator has yet required your vendor to hand it over. If you do not write it into the order, “we follow CISA” is a sentence, not a file.

A SaaS bill of materials that arrives as a PDF of marketing claims is not an SBOM. The 2026 elements are fields, not a brochure.

What to ask before the quarter closes

For each product you will renew, ask for an SBOM that includes the new fields, in a machine-readable format, and ask how often it is regenerated. For anything the vendor calls AI, ask for the general SBOM and the AI supplement, and ask which components are the model, the data, and the application around them. If the vendor sells only a hosted service, do not accept “SaaS does not have an SBOM.” CISA’s July revision says the minimum elements apply to SaaS.

Keep the ask tied to a decision. You want the list so you can see a license you cannot accept, a component you already banned, or a generation date older than the last incident. A list nobody reads is a folder.

What each new field is for

CISA named four additions. A renewal that “includes an SBOM” can still omit every one of them. Ask for the field, then ask what decision it supports.

  • Component hash algorithm. A hash without the algorithm that produced it is a string you cannot recompute. Ask which algorithm, and ask for the hash, not a screenshot of a hash.
  • Component license. This is the field that catches the component your counsel already banned. A product description that says “open source” is not a license name.
  • SBOM tool name. You want to know what generated the file, because two tools can describe the same product differently, and a hand-built spreadsheet will not tell you that it was hand-built unless you ask.
  • Generation context. Ask what context the file claims, and when it was produced. A generation date older than the release you are about to install is a stale list. CISA does not, on the pages this briefing uses, give you a single required sentence for the field. Do not accept a vendor’s invention of one and call it the minimum element.

AI and SaaS may need more than that baseline. That is CISA’s line, not a hint that SaaS is exempt. The May 12 AI supplement, written with G7 partners, sits on top of the general elements. Ask for both when the product is a model, a dataset, and an application wrapped together and sold as one login.

Why the list showed up in the same season as the exploit catalog

Between September 25 and September 30, CISA’s account posted three additions to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog: WordPress Core, an Apple bug, and Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN Manager. The catalog, read the next morning, also showed Citrix rows from September 27 and a Fortinet FortiMail row added October 1. The posts are the alerts. The catalog rows are the spec. The write-up is CISA listed three bugs attackers are already using.

An ingredients list is how you answer the first question those alerts create, which is not “how does the bug work.” It is “do we run this.” WordPress core, a mail gateway, a remote-access appliance, and an SD-WAN manager do not always appear in the application inventory the security team keeps. They appear, when you are lucky, in a bill of materials, a hosting contract, or a network diagram somebody last updated at renewal. Ask for the SBOM before you need it to identify a component CISA has already said is being used against somebody. Guidance is still not a statute. The contract is what makes the file show up.

Sources

  • CISA on X, 2026 Minimum Elements for an SBOM, July 29, 2026
  • CISA, release on the 2026 Minimum Elements for an SBOM, July 29, 2026
  • CISA, 2026 Minimum Elements for a Software Bill of Materials
  • CISA, Software Bill of Materials for AI — Minimum Elements, May 12, 2026
  • CISA on X, WordPress, Apple, and Cisco catalog posts, September 25–30, 2026 (Apple, Cisco)
  • CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog, rows read October 1, 2026

Operator pages: the SBOM request pack, then Ask a vendor for an SBOM and Extra questions for an AI bill of materials.

item.title: The SEC Clock Starts When You Decide It Matters
item.description: Public companies disclose a material cyber incident on Form 8-K within four business days of the materiality call. The annual report still has to describe who watches the risk.
item.author: circuits50capital@circuits.fit (Emilio Santos)
item.content:encoded:
The Securities and Exchange Commission’s cybersecurity disclosure rules, adopted July 26, 2023, are still the clock public companies live on. The Commission’s small-entity guide states the split cleanly. A domestic registrant discloses a material cybersecurity incident on Form 8-K, under Item 1.05, within four business days of determining that the incident is material. Separately, the annual report on Form 10-K describes the company’s processes for cybersecurity risk, and the board’s and management’s roles. The four days run from the materiality determination, not from the moment someone notices a strange login.

This is not legal advice, and it is not a statement that every incident is material. It is the operator reading of a rule that vendors, private companies, and acquirers keep bumping into, because a public customer will ask you for facts on their clock.

What the form actually wants

The Commission’s July 26, 2023 release says Item 1.05 asks for the material aspects of the incident’s nature, scope, and timing, and for the material impact or the reasonably likely material impact. The small-entity guide says the same, and adds that foreign private issuers use Form 6-K when the incident is disclosed or required to be disclosed in another channel. Annual disclosure lives in Regulation S-K Item 106: processes for assessing and managing material cyber risk, the board’s oversight, and management’s role. The Commission did not adopt a requirement to disclose whether a particular director is a cybersecurity expert. Do not let a questionnaire invent that line and call it the rule.

Compliance dates are long past for calendar-year filers. Annual disclosures began with fiscal years ending on or after December 15, 2023. Non-smaller registrants began the 8-K duty on December 18, 2023. Smaller reporting companies had until June 15, 2024. If a playbook still says “the SEC rule is coming,” the playbook is late.

Discovery starts the investigation. Materiality starts the filing clock. Confusing the two is how a week disappears.

What a private company should still write down

You may not file an 8-K. Your customer might. Name, before an incident, who can decide that a customer-facing outage or a data theft is something a public customer must hear, and how fast you can say what systems, what data, and what you have turned off. The SEC’s rule does not draft your contract. It explains why the contract’s notice window of “promptly” will feel slow to a registrant whose counsel is counting business days from a materiality call.

Pair the clock with the insurance questionnaire you already answer. A control that satisfies an underwriter does not decide materiality. A materiality call that nobody has rehearsed will be made by whoever is awake.

A catalog post is not a materiality call

The last week of September gave the calendar a concrete test. CISA’s account posted three known-exploited vulnerabilities: WordPress Core on September 25 (CVE-2026-87902), an Apple bug on September 29 (CVE-2026-86950), and Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN Manager on September 30 (CVE-2026-76504). The catalog, not the post, holds the federal due dates: September 28, October 2, and October 3. Citrix NetScaler rows added September 27 were already due September 30. Fortinet FortiMail was added October 1, due October 4. The piece that walks those rows is CISA listed three bugs attackers are already using.

None of those facts is an Item 1.05 filing. The Commission’s clock starts when the company determines the incident is material, and Item 1.05 asks for the material aspects of nature, scope, and timing, plus the material impact or the reasonably likely material impact. A CVE number trending on a given morning does not, by itself, answer any of those. It can be the moment someone should ask the question. It can also be a bug in a product you do not run.

Write the two dates on separate lines when a public customer calls. One line is the day you patched, or the day you confirmed you do not run the product. The other line is the day, if it ever comes, that someone with authority decided the incident was material to the registrant. Confusing “CISA posted it” with “we have determined materiality” is how a private vendor blows a customer’s four business days, or invents a disclosure the customer did not need.

Rehearse the call with the people who would actually be on it. Who can say which systems were touched. Who can say whether data left. Who is allowed to tell a public customer, and who is allowed only to tell counsel. The annual Item 106 disclosure still has to describe processes, board oversight, and management’s role. It still does not require you to name a director as a cybersecurity expert. A questionnaire that demands that title is asking for something the Commission declined to require.

Foreign private issuers remain on Form 6-K when the incident is disclosed, or required to be disclosed, in another channel. A playbook written only for domestic 8-K filers will miss the parent company that asks for the same facts on a different form. This is still not legal advice. It is the reading that keeps the patching queue and the disclosure queue from sharing a single panicked email.

Sources

  • SEC, “SEC Adopts Rules on Cybersecurity Risk Management, Strategy, Governance, and Incident Disclosure,” July 26, 2023
  • SEC small-entity compliance guide, Cybersecurity Risk Management, Strategy, Governance, and Incident Disclosure
  • SEC final rule page, Release 33-11216
  • CISA on X, the September 25–30 catalog posts (Apple, Cisco)
  • CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog, rows read October 1, 2026

Operator page: Before the Form 8-K clock. Related: Cyber insurance is rewriting the IT budget.
