item.title: Gartner Revised the AI Bill. Most of It Is Not Your Budget.
item.description: The September forecast is $2.7 trillion, up 49.5%. About 56% of the table is infrastructure. The check a company signs is the feature inside software it already owns.
item.author: circuits50capital@circuits.fit (Emilio Santos)
item.content:encoded:
On September 16, Gartner revised its 2026 AI spending forecast to $2.7 trillion, a 49.5% increase from 2025. In May the same house had said $2.59 trillion and 47%. The headline moved. The buyer did not. John-David Lovelock, a distinguished vice president analyst at Gartner, said demand for AI infrastructure is still strong and inelastic to higher memory prices, and that hyperscalers and service providers buying AI-optimized servers remain the largest single area of spending.

Read the table under the headline before you take the round number into a board pack. Gartner’s line items for 2026 sum to $2.67 trillion. AI infrastructure is $1.48 trillion of that. AI services are $576 billion. AI software is $462 billion. AI cybersecurity is $51 billion, almost double the 2025 line. Agents and assistants are $29 billion. Generative AI models are $28 billion. Infrastructure is about 56% of the table. The software a mid-market company can actually put on a purchase order is a minority of the story Gartner is telling.

What changed since May

Gartner raised two near-term growth rates in this quarter’s forecast. Spending on AI application-development platforms is now expected to grow 39% in 2026, up from 28% in the prior forecast, because enterprises, software vendors, and services firms want custom applications. Growth in generative AI models moved from 110% to 117%. Gartner called that a small but growing opening for domain-specific models that cost less and fit a job, not a general demo.

It also split cross-functional agents and assistants out of the AI software line, and added consumer agents, so the new table is not a clean restatement of the May pile. Do not subtract $2.59 trillion from $2.7 trillion and call the difference new enterprise demand. Part of the revision is a bigger infrastructure build. Part of it is a new way of counting agents.

If more than half the forecast is servers, chips, networks, and AI cloud, matching “the industry” is not a budget. It is a category error.

Where the company’s check actually lands

Gartner says generative AI is in the trough of disillusionment in 2026, and that enterprises are using simpler AI features embedded in software they already have: faster workflows, customer responses, decisions. Lovelock’s other point is the one a CFO can use. Buyers are going to service firms less often for a transformation program and more often for smaller projects that turn on the AI already inside an incumbent system. Gartner still sees those two kinds of work combining into a $1.2 trillion AI-services opportunity by 2030. That is a vendor forecast. It is also a description of the renewal you will see this quarter: the suite you own, plus an agent SKU, plus a services line to switch it on.

That is a different problem from the $2.7 trillion. You do not buy the hyperscaler’s data center. You do buy the seat, the consumption overage, and the implementation that “just enables” the feature the vendor shipped to stay relevant. Gartner said vendors are embedding agentic AI in existing products to defend against new cross-functional agents. The defense shows up on your invoice.

What to take to the next renewal

Separate three numbers and refuse to let them share a slide. One: industry infrastructure spend, which you do not control. Two: the AI line inside a product you already license. Three: a workflow with a definition of done, and whether that workflow moved.

Ask the vendor which of Gartner’s buckets the quote sits in. An embedded feature in a suite you renew is software. A usage meter on a model is not a seat. A partner “to turn it on” is services. If the quote will not say which, you are being sold the headline.

The May piece on this site still stands on the part that was never about the size of the forecast. A larger industry bill does not create a return on your line. Gartner revised the bill upward in four months. The question for an operator is unchanged: which check on this forecast is yours, and what does it retire?

The post, then the table

Gartner’s own account posted the revision on September 16 and linked the newsroom page: AI spending up 49.5% in 2026. That post is the announcement. It is not the table. The table is on the newsroom page, and it is less round than the post. The line items sum to about $2.67 trillion, not a clean $2.7 trillion. Infrastructure is $1,484,397 million. Services are $576,481 million. Software is $461,637 million. Cybersecurity is $51,347 million, against $25,920 million in 2025. Agents are $29,219 million. Models are $28,266 million. The 2025 total on the same table is $1,786,671 million. Gartner’s 2027 total is $3,637,292 million, which is about 36% above 2026. Use the post to know the day the claim went public. Use the table when someone tries to put “$2.7 trillion” in a cell that is supposed to be your budget.

Two weeks later, on September 30, Gartner posted a different pressure. As enterprises ramp AI spending, the account said, CIOs face growing pressure to deliver more with limited budget growth. The post points at a 2027 CIO Agenda Preview and says the preview reveals four technology-planning disconnects. It does not name the four. This piece will not name them either. What an operator can use without the preview is the collision. The September 16 forecast says the industry bill is still rising, and that more than half of it is infrastructure a mid-market company does not buy. The September 30 post says the CIO is being asked to produce more without a budget that rises in step. Those two sentences are how a renewal gets approved on a headline and paid for out of a flat operating plan. Separate them in the pack: industry spend, the line you will sign, and the workflow that has to move.

The same week’s other major product event sits in a third bucket. On September 28 NVIDIA announced a fence around agents, OpenShell in software and a BlueField watchdog it calls Sentry. That is not a line in Gartner’s infrastructure total unless you are the one buying the chip. It is a candidate for the services-and-software check this forecast keeps hiding under the round number. The write-up is NVIDIA put the fence outside the agent.

Sources

  • Gartner on X, AI spending up 49.5% in 2026, September 16, 2026
  • Gartner, “Forecasts Worldwide AI Spending to Grow 49.5% in 2026,” September 16, 2026
  • Gartner, “Forecasts Worldwide AI Spending to Grow 47% in 2026,” May 19, 2026
  • Gartner on X, CIO budget pressure and the 2027 agenda preview, September 30, 2026
  • Gartner on X, managing AI cost is becoming as important as deploying it, September 24, 2026

Earlier briefing: AI spend is not the same as AI return. Operator guides: How to tell AI spend from AI return. For one workflow, use token cost to gross margin, then Put an AI cost on one workflow.

Follow Circuit & Capital on Bluesky, Facebook and X (@circuitsfit) for new briefings.

item.title: Cyber insurance renewal prep for mid-market IT budgets (2026)
item.description: Preparing a 2026 cyber insurance renewal application: who owns the broker versus IT, the questionnaire items that stall a binder, and how to budget each control as a line item. Collecting evidence for each control is a separate guide.
item.author: circuits50capital@circuits.fit (Emilio Santos)
item.content:encoded:
Swiss Re’s 2026 cyber view, as covered September 2, still has global premium on track for $16.4 billion, growing about 5% a year since 2022, even as rates fell for a fourth year. The cut shrank: roughly −13% globally in 2025 versus about −5% in 2026, with the U.S. stabilizing faster than Europe. Marsh’s Global Insurance Market Index put the U.S. cyber rate change at −2% in the second quarter of 2026 — the twelfth consecutive quarterly decline globally (−4%). Cheap paper is not a thin application.

Mid-market is the layer insurers still want. Swiss Re’s segment split, in that same coverage, put mid-market at 40–50% penetration and about $4.1 billion of premium. You are not too small to be asked the same five things a large corporate is asked. You are large enough for the no to hurt.

The questionnaire is a budget

Map each yes/no on the form to a named owner, a vendor, and a line on the IT plan. If MFA is “rolling out,” that is a no. If EDR is installed and nobody is on call, that is a no. If backups exist and restores have not been tested, that is a no. Underwriters do not fund a roadmap. They price a current state.

AM Best, via Insurance Journal in July, still had U.S. prices cutting in the first quarter and a 2025 loss ratio around 53. A soft market is not a reason to skip hygiene. It is a reason to lock the control list while the rate is still walking down.

Use the form as a floor, not a strategy. Controls that please an underwriter can still fail a determined attacker. They will, however, decide whether you have a policy or a brochure.

Who owns broker versus IT

If the broker sits only with finance, IT will be surprised by a control they cannot implement in 30 days. If IT owns the packet alone, finance will be surprised by the premium, the retention, and the sublimit on social engineering. Put both in the room in month nine, not month twelve.

Name three seats: the person who signs, the person who can change identity and endpoint settings, and the person who will call counsel at 2 a.m. If one chair is empty, you will renew by default or you will scramble in a denial.

The broker’s job is the market: markets, wordings, retentions, additional insureds, and whether “computer system” still means what you think it means when a model leaks into an unlisted vendor. IT’s job is evidence: MFA coverage reports, EDR on-call, restore test dates, privilege logs. Do not let either side fill in the other’s blanks.

Controls that stall a binder

Control What “yes” means What fails
MFA Enforced on email, VPN, RDP, cloud admin, and other accounts that touch business data “Rolling out.” SMS-only on privileged accounts. Shared logins
EDR Deployed and watched. A named on-call for the 2 a.m. alert Agents installed, nobody paged. A dashboard nobody opens
Immutable or offline backups A restore has been tested on a date you can show A screenshot of a backup job. Tapes nobody has mounted
Privilege Who can disable EDR and identity tools, and is that logged Shared admin. Domain admin on every laptop
IR retainer Named counsel and forensics you can call without a procurement cycle A vendor list with no contract. “We’ll figure it out”

Shared logins are the easiest line to fix. A team password manager gives each person their own vault entry and lets you revoke access when someone leaves. 1Password, Bitwarden and NordPass all offer business plans. Paid link: we may earn a commission.

What operators actually get asked

The packet varies by carrier. The repeats do not. Operators in U.S. mid-market shops keep seeing some version of these:

  • Is MFA enforced (not offered) on email, remote access, and cloud consoles? Can you export the coverage report?
  • Is EDR or MDR on every endpoint that matters, and who is on call after hours?
  • Are backups immutable or offline, and when was the last restore test?
  • Who can disable those tools? Is privileged access logged and reviewed?
  • Do you have a named incident retainer — counsel and forensics — already on paper?
  • How do you handle third-party software and vendor access after the last supply-chain headline?
  • What AI tools sit in production, and are they in the system inventory the policy already assumes?

Marsh’s U.S. Q2 2026 note said some insurers included clarifying AI language, with most asking questions on AI exposure, use, and controls. Swiss Re argues many AI incidents may already sit inside existing “computer system” wordings, with claims of that flavor still limited. Read the form. Do not assume a model leak into an unlisted vendor is covered because the rate is down 2%.

A cheaper policy written on controls you do not run is a denial at claim time.

Shop limits if a payments or cloud outage would take a quarter. Do not skip the line items the questionnaire already priced in to “save” a premium that assumed you had them.

Backup tools we would use

Disclosure: links marked “Paid link” may earn Circuit & Capital a commission at no cost to you.

  • Microsoft 365 or Google Workspace: IDrive Cloud Applications Backup, $20 per seat per year on IDrive’s page (checked November 10, 2026), with a 7-day trial. Paid link: we may earn a commission. Microsoft’s own Microsoft 365 Backup, at $0.15 per GiB per month, is the non-affiliate alternative.
  • Laptops and desktops: IDrive Team, from $9.99 a month for 5 computers on a yearly plan. Paid link: we may earn a commission. Backblaze Business Backup, $99 per computer per year, is a good non-affiliate option.
  • Shared team files with version history: pCloud Business. Paid link: we may earn a commission. Synced storage is not a backup by itself, so pair it with one of the above.

Prices and the full comparison: password managers and backup tools for small teams.

Sources

  • Risk & Insurance / Swiss Re, Sept. 2, 2026
  • Marsh, Global Insurance Market Index, Q2 2026 (U.S. detail: U.S. insurance rates)
  • Insurance Journal / AM Best, July 27, 2026

FAQ

Does a cheaper premium mean we can skip a control?

No. Marsh had U.S. cyber rates down 2% in Q2 2026. The questionnaire still wants MFA, watched EDR, and a restore test. The rate cut is not a waiver.

Who should own the broker?

Finance signs. IT supplies evidence. Both sit in month nine. The broker does not fill in MFA coverage from memory.

Is an IR retainer required if we have an internal team?

You still want counsel and forensics on paper. Internal teams do not replace a call you can make at 2 a.m. without procurement.

Will a soft market last?

Nobody who is honest will guarantee it. Swiss Re already flagged loss ratios walking up while prices walked down. Take the rate. Keep the controls.

Related briefing

  • Cyber insurance is rewriting the IT budget
  • Cyber insurance got cheaper. The questionnaire did not.

item.title: When Cloud Repatriation Is a Finance Decision, Not an Engineering Slogan
item.description: Cost drivers, FinOps questions, and stay-versus-leave — with a labeled list-price egress example, not a fake calculator.
item.author: circuits50capital@circuits.fit (Emilio Santos)
item.content:encoded:
The cloud argument of the 2010s was elasticity. The cloud argument of the mid-2020s is the invoice. Workloads that run every hour of the quarter do not need a burst story. They need a unit cost. When that unit cost is higher than a colo row plus a small platform team, finance starts using the word “repatriation.” That is a matching problem, not a morality play.

Some products still belong on the public cloud: spiky demand, a global edge, a managed store you do not want to staff. Others were lifted and shifted in a hurry and never earned their keep. This page is how a mid-market shop decides which is which without inventing a calculator that pretends to know your discount.

Cost drivers that actually move the bill

Compute and storage are the lines everyone can see. The damage usually sits next to them.

  • Egress and data gravity. Getting data in is cheap. Getting it out is a toll. AWS’s published on-demand transfer table still prices the first 10 TB per month of internet egress from EC2 at $0.09 per GB after a small free tier, then steps down. That is list, not your EDP.
  • Cross-AZ and cross-region chatter. A chatty database that copies itself for “high availability” can look cheap until you price the copies as a product.
  • Managed-service multipliers. RDS, warehouse, and similar services buy you staffing you do not have. They also hide a premium you only see when you compare to a box you would have to run.
  • Commitments you cannot unwind. Reserved instances and savings plans that outrun actual use are a tax you already signed. Moving a workload does not erase the commit.
  • People. A company that outsourced operations cannot “bring it home” without hiring. Hiring is slower than a board slide.

If you cannot attach the top twenty lines to a service, a team, and a product, you are not ready to move anything. You are ready to argue.

FinOps questions before anyone buys a rack

FinOps that only produces dashboards is theater. FinOps that can attach a cost to a SKU can choose.

  1. Which workloads run above a high, steady utilization most hours of the quarter — and which only look expensive because they are on-demand by habit?
  2. What share of the bill is untagged, and who is allowed to launch an untagged resource?
  3. What is the fully loaded twelve-month cloud number: list minus real discounts, plus support, plus the commit you will still pay if you leave?
  4. What is the fully loaded “home” number: colo or owned row, hardware, power, software, and the platform people you do not have yet?
  5. What feature disappears if you leave — global backbone, managed failover, a region you cannot staff — and is that a product risk or a rounding error?
  6. If two people resign in the first year, does the savings still exist?
Repatriation without an ownership model is just a more expensive outage.

When staying versus leaving makes sense

Signal Lean stay Lean leave (or hybrid)
Demand Spiky, global, unknown Steady, local, known for four quarters
Data Small, or already at the edge Heavy gravity, clumsy egress, batch that never bursts
Staff No platform team, and no plan to hire one Named owners who have run a row before
Commit Leaving would strand a savings plan you still owe The commit is already a bad fit and the workload is separable
Product risk You need a region or failover you will not build The missing managed feature is a nice-to-have

The usual candidates to come home are batch analytics, predictable inference, and stateful systems that were never elastic. Customer-facing apps with a global edge usually stay. Hybrid is the real destination for most mid-market shops: reserved cloud for the bursty surface, owned or colo capacity for the furnace.

Staff the platform team first. Migrate a boring workload second. Only then hold a quote. If the savings only appear if nobody leaves the company, the savings are fictional.

Labeled list-price example

This is not your bill. It is a published list-price illustration so egress is not a vibe.

AWS’s public on-demand table (U.S. regions, internet egress from EC2, after the small monthly free tier) still lists $0.09 per GB for the first 10 TB in a month. Ten terabytes is 10,240 GB. 10,240 × $0.09 is $921.60 at list, before NAT gateways, cross-AZ traffic, CloudFront, or any discount you actually have.

Use that only as a scale check: if your architecture ships terabytes out every month, the toll is a product decision. Pull your own invoice lines. Do not run a spreadsheet that pretends a blog’s $900 is your number.

Sources

  • AWS EC2 on-demand pricing, data transfer (list prices; not a quote)

FAQ

Should we leave the cloud?

Not as a slogan. Leave the workload whose fully loaded twelve-month cost, after people and egress, is higher than a row you can actually staff — and whose missing managed features you can live with.

Can we use a public calculator as the decision?

No. List prices are a scale check. Your discounts, commits, NAT, and cross-AZ lines are the decision. This page does not invent a bill for you.

What if we have no platform team?

Then “home” is a hiring plan, not a migration. Hire first or stay.

Is hybrid a cop-out?

It is the usual honest answer. Burst at the edge. Own the furnace. Pretending every workload wants the same home is how you get a second invoice.

Related briefing

  • Cloud repatriation: when the bill becomes the strategy

item.title: AI budget review: how to tell AI spend from AI return
item.description: For the CFO reviewing the whole AI budget: sort every AI line into seat or usage and pilot or production, then ask the board questions that separate spend from return. Costing one workflow is a separate guide.
item.author: circuits50capital@circuits.fit (Emilio Santos)
item.content:encoded:
Gartner’s May 2026 forecast put worldwide AI spending at $2.59 trillion this year, up 47%, with infrastructure more than 45% of the pile. John-David Lovelock’s line is the one that belongs in a mid-market packet: so far the spend is driven by vendors and hyperscalers. Enterprises “have yet to really flex their spending potential,” and CIOs still struggle to show a business outcome.

McKinsey’s 2026 State of AI survey still had only 37% of respondents attributing any EBIT to AI — roughly unchanged — and about 6% as high performers (significant impact and at least 5% of EBIT). Eighty percent said AI improved their own productivity. Those two facts can both be true. A faster draft is not a cheaper close. This page is how you stop mixing them. It is not a promise that a tool will pay for itself.

Seat cost versus token cost

Two invoices get lumped as “AI.” They do not behave the same way.

Seat / copilot license Tokens / usage
What you buy A named human, a month at a time Work the model actually did
How it hides Shelfware. A seat that never opens Retries, long context, agents looping
What to count Active seats versus paid seats, on one workflow Spend on that workflow only — not the company pile
What not to count “Everyone should have one” The hyperscaler capex story on a keynote slide

McKinsey found about 20% of respondents already saying AI operating costs, including tokens, constrained use — while most still planned to spend more. If the only metric is seats, the organization will buy seats. If the only metric is tokens, it will run them without a finish line.

Add a third cost that never appears on the vendor invoice: human review after the draft, and rework when the draft invents a date, a customer, or a covenant. Time saved at the desk does not show up as margin if the review step and the headcount plan do not change.

Pilot versus production

A pilot has a demo. Production has a definition of done, an owner, and a number that can move. Gartner said in September that only 22% of organizations had successfully scaled AI across multiple business units. You do not need to be in the 22%. You need one artifact you can date.

Good production tests: monthly close commentary, support macros, bid/no-bid memos, invoice exceptions. Bad: “make the company more AI-native.” If you cannot name the artifact that is done, you are still in the pilot, whatever the slide says.

Write the current path: who starts it, how long it takes, where it fails, what “done” looks like. That is the baseline. No baseline, no after. Ninety days, one owner whose bonus includes cycle time or error rate. If nothing moved, cut the overlapping copilots and keep the model on the one path that has an owner.

A budget that grows 47% while the EBIT share stays flat is not a strategy. It is a bet that the spreadsheet will catch up.

Questions a board can ask

Directors do not need a model architecture briefing. They need a control framework that survives the next vendor cycle.

  1. Which single workflow is in production, and what is the definition of done?
  2. What did that workflow cost last quarter in seats, tokens, and review time — separately?
  3. What number moved: cycle time, error rate, or headcount plan? “People feel faster” is not a number.
  4. Who can turn the spend off, and who owns the data the model can see?
  5. What happens if the vendor changes the price or the model next quarter — is there an exit, or only a renewal?
  6. Are we in the 37% who can attribute any EBIT, or are we buying seats because the industry forecast is $2.59 trillion?

None of those questions imply a guaranteed return. They imply a company that can tell spend from a result. If the packet cannot answer them, the next copilot is a catalog item, not an operating change.

Sources

  • Gartner AI spending forecast, May 19, 2026
  • Gartner scaling survey, Sept. 1, 2026
  • McKinsey, The State of AI: Global Survey 2026

FAQ

Will this pay for itself?

This page does not say that. Most surveyed firms still cannot put EBIT on the slide. Measure one workflow. If the number does not move, stop buying seats for that path.

Is a copilot seat “AI return”?

Only if a named process got cheaper or faster with the review step counted. A license that is not opened is spend.

Do we need to match Gartner’s $2.59 trillion?

No. That pile is mostly infrastructure and hyperscalers. Your job is one definition of done.

What if tokens are already constraining use?

Then you are not under-adopting. You are over-running a process with no finish line. Cap the workflow, not the slogan.

Related

  • AI spend is not the same as AI return
  • The AI productivity paradox at mid-market companies
  • AI model cost per finished task

item.title: Software Buying as an Operating Skill
item.description: RFP basics, seat waste, who signs, and the three SaaS-management jobs. The stack is the company.
item.author: circuits50capital@circuits.fit (Emilio Santos)
item.content:encoded:
Walk a mid-market close, a warehouse, or a support queue and you are walking a software path. Invoice to cash lives in one product. Exceptions live in a spreadsheet someone swore they would retire. Buying those tools as if they were toner is how you get seven CRMs and one actual process.

Vertice’s Q2 2026 read of licenses it tracks put 65% of SaaS licenses as unused or underutilized (under 50% of purchased seats actually used), up from 62% a year earlier. Fully unused “shelfware” ticked down slightly; underuse did the damage. That is not a reason to fire every tool. It is a reason to stop treating a renewal as a rubber stamp.

RFP basics that survive a demo

Demos are designed to make the happy path look inevitable. Score the unhappy path.

  • What work dies if this tool is down for a day?
  • Show month-end, a chargeback, a warehouse that is offline, a customer who is not in the dropdown — without a services SOW.
  • Who is allowed to add a seat, and how is that logged?
  • What is the exit: export, escrow, or a second vendor already on the bench? If export needs a professional-services ticket, price that ticket now.
  • Which overlapping tool does this retire, and on what date?

If the product cannot show the unhappy path, you are not buying software. You are buying a project. Write the RFP as a process review, not a feature bingo card. A pretty matrix that never names an owner is how overlapping CRMs survive.

A seat that nobody can turn off is not a subscription. It is a tax.

Seat waste

Three piles, not one:

  1. Ghosts — paid seats tied to people who left, or who have not signed in for 90 days.
  2. Overlap — two products doing 30% of the same job. At renewal, one of them is on trial whether the vendor knows it or not.
  3. Underuse — the tool is opened, but most of the purchased capacity is idle. Vertice’s 50% threshold is a blunt instrument. It is still more honest than “we still need it.”

True-down unused seats before the quote locks. “Standard uplift” is often a sales sentence. If it is not in the paper, it is a request. An 8% increase on a tool that replaced two others can be cheap. A 0% increase on a tool nobody opens is still a loss.

Who signs

Three chairs, one meeting: the person who signs, the person who uses it, and the person who would run the export. If one chair is empty, you will renew by default.

IT should not be the only signature on a tool that runs invoice-to-cash. Finance should not be the only signature on a tool that can take the warehouse down. A founder who can add seats from a credit card is how shadow IT becomes the operating system.

Put a rule on new logos: no entry without a retirement plan for an old one, and a named workflow owner. Hire for that, or keep paying for catalogs.

SaaS management categories

The market split in 2026 is not “one platform to own software.” It is three jobs. Mix them up and you will buy a dashboard when you needed a negotiation, or a negotiation when you needed a kill list.

Category Job Usually owned by
Discovery / SaaS management Find the stack, usage, and ghosts (Zylo, Torii, Productiv, and the spreadsheet-plus-IdP version below ~1,000 people) IT / ops
Procurement / negotiation Benchmarks, true-down, the 8% “standard” increase (Vendr, Tropic, Vertice, or a broker who actually reads the order form) Finance / procurement
Operating ownership Named workflow, kill date, unhappy-path RFP. No vendor replaces this The operator who runs the process

Those names are examples of the category, not a ranking and not a recommendation. Below a thousand employees, an export from identity, a pull from accounts payable, and a 90-day last-login report will get you through the first cycle. Above that, you will miss ghosts without a discovery pass. In either case, the operating skill is the owner and the kill date. The software does not buy itself well.

Sources

  • Vertice, unused SaaS applications, Q2 2026

FAQ

Do we need an RFP for every renewal?

You need the unhappy-path questions and a stay / shrink / leave meeting. A 40-page RFP for a $6,000 tool is theater. A Slack poll after the invoice is how overlap survives.

Is unused-seat waste a reason to rip everything out?

No. Vertice’s 65% figure is unused or underused licenses in its dataset, not a law that your stack is 65% wrong. True-down ghosts. Put overlap on trial. Keep the tool that retired hours or another license.

Who is allowed to add a seat?

Someone named, logged, and tied to a workflow. A founder credit card is not a process.

Which SaaS-management product should we buy?

This page does not pick one. Match the category to the job. Discovery is not negotiation. Neither is a substitute for an owner.

Related briefing

  • Software buying is an operating skill
  • How to read a SaaS renewal

item.title: How to Read a SaaS Renewal
item.description: A 90-day pass: seats, overlap, price, and the exit before you answer the increase.
item.author: circuits50capital@circuits.fit (Emilio Santos)
item.content:encoded:
Most renewals fail in month eleven because nobody owns month nine. The vendor sends a quote. Finance asks if you still need it. You say yes because last quarter’s outage is still in memory. That is how overlapping CRMs survive.

Use this as a 90-day pass. Print it. Put a name next to each line.

90 days out

  • Export active seats and last-login dates. A seat that has not signed in for 90 days is not a user. It is a tax.
  • List every other tool that does 30% of the same job. If two products share a workflow, one of them is on trial at renewal, whether the vendor knows it or not.
  • Find the termination and data-export clauses. If export needs a services ticket, price that ticket now.

60 days out

Write one paragraph: what work dies if this tool is down for a day, who can add a seat, and what you would switch to. If you cannot write it, you do not have an owner.

Ask the vendor for the renewal in writing with unit price, volume, and any auto-increase. Verbal “we will take care of you” is not a term.

A renewal without a kill list is a subscription you already lost.

30 days out

Check Pass Fail
Unused seats True-down before the quote locks Paying for last-login ghosts
“Standard” increase The clause is in the paper The increase is a habit
Stay / shrink / leave Finance and the operator in one meeting A Slack poll after the invoice

The only metric

Did this tool retire hours, tickets, or another license? If the answer is a vibe, you are buying a logo. Keep the tool that has a before-and-after number. Cut the one that only has a champion.

Sources

  • CISA and FBI, Secure by Demand Guide, August 2024
  • Regulation (EU) 2023/2854, the Data Act, on EUR-Lex
  • FinOps Foundation, FinOps Framework

The contract terms that matter most

Most renewal leverage comes from a short list of clauses. Find each one in the order form or master agreement before the first vendor call.

  • Renewal date and notice period. Many SaaS contracts renew automatically unless you give notice 30, 60, or 90 days ahead. Miss the window and you negotiate from a weaker position.
  • Price increase terms. Look for a cap on renewal increases. If there is none, ask for one. A cap is a common, reasonable request.
  • Seat true-down. Can you reduce seats at renewal, or only add them? Some contracts allow only increases. Fix that at renewal.
  • Data export and return. Can you export all of your data in a usable format, and how long does the vendor keep it after termination?
  • AI and data-use terms. Many products have added AI features. Check whether new terms allow the vendor to use your data for training, and whether that is opt-in or opt-out.
  • Security artifacts. CISA’s Secure by Demand guide suggests asking whether SSO and security logging are in the base product, and whether the vendor can provide an SBOM. Renewal is when you can ask.

A worked example

Example numbers, not survey data. A team pays $48,000 a year for 120 seats. Usage shows 66 active users in the last 30 days, or 55%. The vendor proposes an 8% increase, to $51,840 for the same 120 seats. At 90 days out, the owner checks a 90-day usage view and finds 72 regular users, so proposes 80 seats to allow for growth. At the current per-seat price of $400, 80 seats cost $32,000. Even if the 8% increase is accepted on the smaller count, the new cost is $34,560, about $17,000 below the vendor’s proposal. The owner also asks for a 5% cap on future increases and a 30-day data-return window. The software renewal scorecard produces this agenda from the same inputs.

Common mistakes

  • Negotiating only price. Terms like caps, true-downs, and exit rights often matter more over three years than a one-time discount.
  • Letting the vendor set the timeline. End-of-quarter pressure is the vendor’s deadline, not yours.
  • Skipping the exit test. If you have never exported your data, you do not know whether you can leave.
  • Ignoring overlap. Check whether another tool you own does the same job. Overlap is the easiest saving.

A note for EU workloads

The EU Data Act has applied since September 12, 2025. For data processing services, which can include SaaS, it sets rules on switching providers and ends switching charges from January 12, 2027. If your vendor serves you in the EU, ask how its exit terms reflect that. This is a question for counsel, not a conclusion.

Before you sign off

  • The renewal date and notice deadline are on the owner’s calendar.
  • Usage is pulled for 30 and 90 days.
  • The price cap, true-down, export, data-return, and AI terms are found and noted.
  • The stay, shrink, or leave meeting has the signer, the user, and the person who would run the export.

FAQ

When should we start?

Ninety days before the date on the order form, not ninety days before the vendor’s “we need a signature this week” email.

What if we missed the true-down window?

Ask anyway. Many vendors will cut unused seats once rather than lose the account. Do not treat a missed window as a law of physics.

Who has to be in the stay / shrink / leave meeting?

The person who signs, the person who uses it, and the person who would run the export. If one of those chairs is empty, you will renew by default.

Is an auto-increase always in the contract?

No. “Standard uplift” is often a sales sentence. If it is not in the paper, it is a request.

Related briefing

  • Software buying is an operating skill
  • The new unit economics of AI-native startups
  • Software renewal scorecard

Rather hand it off? The Renewal Audit reviews up to 25 renewals for a fixed $199 and returns a written report in 5 business days.

item.title: What a cyber insurer will still ask: the controls evidence checklist
item.description: Controls evidence checklist for cyber insurance: for MFA, EDR, backups, privileged access and an incident retainer, the proof to have ready for an underwriter or a claims adjuster, plus a 60-day plan. Renewal budgeting is a separate guide.
item.author: circuits50capital@circuits.fit (Emilio Santos)
item.content:encoded:
Swiss Re’s 2026 cyber view, as reported September 2, still has global premium growing even as rates fall for a fourth year (about −5% in 2026 after −13% in 2025). AM Best, via Insurance Journal, had U.S. prices still cutting in the first quarter and a 2025 loss ratio of 53. Cheap paper does not mean a thin application. Underwriters lag the threat. They do not stop asking the same five things.

The five lines that stall a binder

  1. MFA everywhere that matters — email, VPN, admin, cloud consoles. “Rolling out” is not yes.
  2. EDR that is watched — installed is not monitored. Who gets the 2 a.m. alert?
  3. Backups that are immutable or offline, and restored — a screenshot of a backup job is not a restore test.
  4. Privileged access — who can disable the tools in item 2, and is that logged?
  5. A named incident retainer — counsel and a forensics shop you can call without a procurement cycle.
If you cannot answer those in a staff meeting, you do not have a control program. You have hope.

How to use a soft market

Shop limits if a payments or cloud outage would take a quarter. Put finance and IT in the same room in month nine, not month twelve. Do not skip hygiene to “save” on a premium that already assumes you have it. A cheaper policy written on controls you do not run is a denial at claim time.

Swiss Re also notes many AI-related incidents may already sit inside existing “computer system” wordings, with claims of that flavor still limited. Read the form. Do not assume a model leak into an unlisted vendor is covered because the market is soft.

Control checklist

Control What they ask What fails
MFA On for email, VPN, admin, cloud “Rolling out”
EDR Installed and watched No named on-call
Backups Immutable or offline, restore tested A screenshot of a job
Privilege Who can disable EDR, and is it logged Shared admin
Retainer Named counsel and forensics A vendor list with no contract

What evidence to have ready

A yes on an application is easier to defend when you can show it. For each of the five lines, decide in advance what proof you would hand an underwriter, or a claims adjuster after an incident.

  • MFA. A report from your identity provider showing enforcement on email, remote access, admin roles, and cloud consoles. CISA recommends phishing-resistant MFA, such as FIDO/WebAuthn security keys or PKI-based methods, as the strongest option. Start with administrators.
  • EDR. Coverage percentage across endpoints and servers, and the after-hours escalation list with names.
  • Backups. The date and result of the last restore test. CISA’s #StopRansomware guide recommends offline, encrypted backups that are tested regularly.
  • Privileged access. The list of accounts that can disable security tools, and the log showing that action is recorded.
  • Retainer. Signed engagement letters with counsel and a forensics firm, and whether they are on the insurer’s approved panel.

A 60-day plan before renewal

  1. Day 1 to 10. Pull last year’s application. Mark every answer that is not fully true today.
  2. Day 10 to 30. Close the cheap gaps first: turn on MFA for remaining admin accounts, run a restore test, update the escalation list.
  3. Day 30 to 45. Collect evidence for each line. Store it where finance and IT can both find it.
  4. Day 45 to 60. Review the application with the broker. For anything still open, record it in the risk exception register with an owner and a date, and disclose it accurately. A spreadsheet version is in the Renewal & Risk Operator Pack ($29).

Do not forget payment fraud

The FBI’s Internet Crime Complaint Center reported about $2.77 billion in business email compromise losses in 2024, out of $16.6 billion in total reported losses. Many policies treat social engineering and funds-transfer fraud differently from a network breach, sometimes with lower sub-limits. Ask where a fraudulent vendor bank change would fall, and require a call-back to a number on file before changing payment details. Stop using a voice as approval covers the process.

Before you sign off

  • Every yes on the application has evidence behind it, stored where finance and IT can find it.
  • Open gaps are in the risk exception register with an owner and a date.
  • You know where social engineering and funds-transfer fraud sit in the policy, and the sub-limit.
  • Counsel and forensics contacts are signed and known to the on-call team.

For the budget side, see the 2026 cyber insurance checklist for IT budgets.

Backup tools we would use

Disclosure: links marked “Paid link” may earn Circuit & Capital a commission at no cost to you.

  • Microsoft 365 or Google Workspace: IDrive Cloud Applications Backup, $20 per seat per year on IDrive’s page (checked November 10, 2026), with a 7-day trial. Paid link: we may earn a commission. Microsoft’s own Microsoft 365 Backup, at $0.15 per GiB per month, is the non-affiliate alternative.
  • Laptops and desktops: IDrive Team, from $9.99 a month for 5 computers on a yearly plan. Paid link: we may earn a commission. Backblaze Business Backup, $99 per computer per year, is a good non-affiliate option.
  • Shared team files with version history: pCloud Business. Paid link: we may earn a commission. Synced storage is not a backup by itself, so pair it with one of the above.

Prices and the full comparison: password managers and backup tools for small teams.

Sources

  • Risk & Insurance / Swiss Re, Sept. 2, 2026
  • Insurance Journal / AM Best, July 27, 2026
  • CISA, Implementing Phishing-Resistant MFA (PDF)
  • CISA, #StopRansomware Guide
  • FBI IC3, 2024 Internet Crime Report (PDF)
  • NIST Cybersecurity Framework

FAQ

Does a cheaper premium mean a lighter application?

No. Rates can fall while the questionnaire stays mean. Underwriters lag the threat. They do not stop asking the same five things.

What does “EDR that is watched” mean?

Someone is named, after hours, to the alert. Installed agents with nobody on call are a no.

Do we need a retainer if we have an internal IR team?

You still want counsel and a forensics shop on paper. Internal teams do not replace a call you can make at 2 a.m. without procurement.

Can we skip a control because the market is soft?

Not if you want the claim paid. A cheaper policy written on controls you do not run is a denial later.

Related

  • Cyber insurance got cheaper. The questionnaire did not.
  • Cyber insurance is rewriting the IT budget
  • Risk exception register

item.title: Put an AI cost on one workflow: a 90-day costing method
item.description: For the operator who owns one process: a 90-day method to attach token spend, review time and rework to a single workflow with a definition of done, with a worked example. Reviewing the whole AI budget is a separate guide.
item.author: circuits50capital@circuits.fit (Emilio Santos)
item.content:encoded:
This guide is about one process, not the AI budget. Pick a workflow with a finish line, measure it before and after, and end with a cost per finished unit. The reason to start that small: McKinsey’s 2026 survey, as reported in September, still had only 37% of respondents attributing any EBIT to AI, and about 6% as high performers. Individual productivity is not the same as a cheaper close. This guide is how to stop mixing those two.

Pick a workflow with a finish line

Good: monthly close commentary, support macros, bid/no-bid memos, invoice exceptions. Bad: “make the company more AI-native.” If you cannot name the artifact that is done, you cannot measure time or cost.

Write the current path: who starts it, how long it takes, where it fails, what “done” looks like. That is your baseline. No baseline, no after.

Instrument three costs

  • License or token spend for that workflow only — not the company-wide copilot bill.
  • Human review time after the model drafts. Review is the cost that hides in “we saved time.”
  • Rework when the draft invents a date, a customer, or a covenant.
If the only metric is seats, the organization will buy seats.

90 days, one owner

Cost Count this Do not count this
Tokens or license Spend on this workflow The company-wide copilot bill
Review Minutes after the draft “We feel faster”
Rework Invented dates, names, covenants A demo that went well

Name a manager whose bonus includes cycle time or error rate for that workflow. Put the date on the calendar now. Gartner said in September that only 22% of organizations had scaled AI across multiple business units. You do not need to be in the 22%. You need one number that moved.

If nothing moved, cut the overlapping copilots and keep the model on the one path that has an owner. That is not anti-AI. It is how you keep the next Gartner-sized invoice from becoming the strategy.

A worked example

Example numbers for illustration, not survey data. A finance team writes monthly variance commentary. Today it takes an analyst 6 hours a month at a loaded cost of $80 an hour: $480. The team pilots a model that drafts the commentary.

  • Token cost. About 40 drafts a month across business units. At the prices and token counts the team measured, about $0.70 per draft including retries: $28.
  • Review. The analyst spends 2.5 hours reviewing and editing: $200.
  • Rework. Twice a month, a draft cites the wrong period or invents a driver. Fixing and checking those takes 1 hour: $80.

New monthly cost: $308, against a $480 baseline. A saving of $172 a month, or about 36%. That is real, and much smaller than the “six hours saved” the demo implied. The cost per finished task calculator does the token and review math. The token cost to gross margin tool shows the effect on a product.

How to measure, step by step

  1. Record a baseline for two cycles. Time and errors before the model. Without it, you cannot show a change.
  2. Tag spend to the workflow. Use a separate API key, project, or cost tag so the tokens for this workflow are not mixed into the company total. The FinOps Foundation’s material on AI costs covers allocation methods.
  3. Time review honestly. Ask the reviewer to log minutes for a few weeks.
  4. Count rework. Keep a simple tally of drafts that needed substantial correction, and why.
  5. Compare after 90 days. Report cost, cycle time, and error rate against the baseline. Decide: expand, adjust, or stop.

Reading a price list

Model providers publish per-token prices, usually separate prices for input and output tokens, and sometimes discounts for batch processing or cached input. Anthropic’s pricing page is one example. Prices change, so record the date and the price you actually pay. Output tokens often cost several times more than input tokens, so a workflow that writes long drafts costs more than one that classifies short items.

Common mistakes

  • Counting the company-wide license as the workflow’s cost, which makes small pilots look expensive and large rollouts look free.
  • Leaving out review time.
  • Measuring for one week. Month-end and quarter-end workflows need at least two cycles.

Before you sign off

  • One workflow, one owner, and a finished artifact you can count.
  • A baseline from at least two cycles before the model.
  • Spend tagged to this workflow only.
  • Review minutes and rework tracked, not estimated.
  • A 90-day decision date on the calendar.

Sources

  • Gartner AI spending forecast, May 19, 2026
  • Gartner scaling survey, Sept. 1, 2026
  • McKinsey State of AI 2026
  • FinOps Foundation, FinOps for AI overview
  • Anthropic, pricing: an example of a published per-token price list

FAQ

Why one workflow, not the whole company?

Because a company-wide copilot bill has no definition of done. One artifact you can date is a number. A stack of seats is a vibe.

What counts as review time?

The minutes after the model drafts, before the work is shipped. If a person still has to catch invented dates, that time is cost.

What if nothing moved in 90 days?

Cut the overlapping copilots. Keep the model on the one path that has an owner. Then measure again.

Do we need to be in Gartner’s 22% who scaled AI?

No. You need one number that moved on one workflow.

Related

  • AI spend is not the same as AI return
  • The AI productivity paradox at mid-market companies
  • AI model cost per finished task

item.title: AI Spend Is Not the Same as AI Return
item.description: Gartner sees $2.59 trillion in AI spending this year. McKinsey still finds only a minority of firms attributing EBIT to it.
item.author: circuits50capital@circuits.fit (Emilio Santos)
item.content:encoded:
Update, October 1, 2026. On September 16 Gartner revised the 2026 figure to $2.7 trillion, up 49.5%. The May number below is the forecast this piece used when it ran. The revision is Gartner revised the AI bill.

In May, Gartner forecast worldwide AI spending of $2.59 trillion in 2026, up 47% from 2025. Infrastructure — servers, chips, networks, AI-optimized cloud — is more than 45% of that pile. John-David Lovelock, a Gartner analyst, put the awkward part in plain English: so far the spend is driven by tech vendors and hyperscalers. Enterprises “have yet to really flex their spending potential,” and CIOs still struggle to show a business outcome.

That is the split worth managing. The market is building capacity. Most companies are still buying pilots and calling them strategy.

What the surveys actually say

McKinsey’s 2026 State of AI survey, summarized in early September coverage of the report, found 37% of respondents attributing at least some EBIT impact to AI — roughly unchanged from the prior year. The share of “high performers,” defined as firms that both call the impact significant and attribute at least 5% of EBIT to AI, sat around 6%. Individual workers tell a different story: 80% said AI improved their own productivity; 50% said it helped them make better decisions.

Those two facts can both be true. A faster draft is not a cheaper close. Time saved at the desk does not automatically show up as margin if the workflow, the review step, and the headcount plan do not change.

About 20% of McKinsey respondents said AI operating costs, including tokens, were already constraining use. Most still planned to spend more. Gartner, in a separate September survey, said only 22% of organizations had successfully scaled AI across multiple business units.

A budget that grows 47% while the EBIT share stays flat is not a strategy. It is a bet that the spreadsheet will catch up.

Who is actually paying

The Ramp AI Index, reported by PYMNTS in August, showed how uneven the checkbook is inside the United States. In July the median company spent $11.95 per employee on AI. The top 1% spent a median of $7,400 per employee. Anthropic led paid business adoption in that dataset at 43.5% of U.S. businesses; OpenAI trailed on the latest monthly increment; xAI reached 4% of businesses.

Goldman Sachs, cited in the same PYMNTS piece, found that only 2% of S&P 500 companies quantified AI’s effects in second-quarter earnings. Of that tiny group, 11% cited measurable productivity in coding or support. Median earnings rose 17% at companies that quantified versus 14% at those that did not — a small gap, and not proof of causation. It is a reminder that the firms doing the counting are at least looking.

What to do with the numbers

If you run a mid-market shop, do not copy the top 1% per-employee spend. Copy their habit of attaching a cost to a workflow. Pick one process with a definition of done — close commentary, ticket macros, bid memos — and put a before-and-after number next to the license line. If you cannot show movement in 90 days, you have a subscription, not a deployment.

The Gartner forecast is not wrong because it is large. It is incomplete if you treat it as a mandate to match the industry’s check. Infrastructure companies will keep building. Your job is to make sure the next seat you buy retires an hour, a tool, or a rework loop — not just a slide.

Worked example: one workflow, two review times

“Attach a cost to a workflow” is easier to say than to do, so we ran one through our free token cost to gross margin calculator on November 11, using the tool’s own code. Every number below is an illustrative input, not a vendor’s list price or a real company’s data.

The workflow: support ticket replies at a mid-market firm. Before AI, a reply takes 12 minutes at a loaded cost of $45 an hour, so each reply costs $9.00. That $9.00 goes in the calculator’s “price” field, because it is the cost the AI version has to beat. With AI, a draft uses 3,000 input tokens and 800 output tokens, priced at an illustrative $3 and $15 per million tokens, and the firm handles 1,500 tickets a month.

  • If review takes 6 minutes: token cost about $0.02 per reply, review cost $4.50, a saving of $4.48 per reply, 49.8%, or about $6,719 a month.
  • If review takes 11 minutes, because staff rewrite most drafts: review cost $8.25, a saving of $0.73 per reply, 8.1%, or about $1,094 a month.

In both cases the tool printed “Human review costs more than the tokens.” The model bill was about two cents. The number that decided the result was review time, which is a workflow and training question, not a pricing one. That is the McKinsey gap in miniature: the worker can feel faster while the firm saves little.

Limits: the calculator leaves out license seats, setup time, failed or retried drafts and quality effects, and it does not call a model. A saving per reply is only money if the hours go somewhere: fewer contractor hours, a queue that no longer needs a new hire, or work that was not getting done. Subtract the seat cost for the people involved before you call it a return. For retries and failures, use the AI cost per finished task tool.

Sources

  • Gartner on X, AI spending up 49.5% in 2026, September 16, 2026
  • Gartner on X, AI cost is becoming as important as deployment, September 24, 2026
  • Gartner, “Forecasts Worldwide AI Spending to Grow 47% in 2026,” May 19, 2026
  • Gartner, survey on scaling AI across business units, Sept. 1, 2026
  • McKinsey, “The State of AI: Global Survey 2026” (figures as reported in HPCwire / AIwire, Sept. 2, 2026)
  • PYMNTS, Ramp AI Index and Goldman Sachs earnings note, Aug. 17, 2026

Operator guides: How to tell AI spend from AI return. For one workflow, use token cost to gross margin, then Put an AI cost on one workflow. The September revision is Gartner revised the AI bill.

Follow Circuit & Capital on Bluesky, Facebook and X (@circuitsfit) for new briefings.

item.title: Chip Licenses Keep Moving. The Mid-Tier Still Waits.
item.description: BIS opened a case-by-case window for H200-class chips. Korea tightened AI-chip exports on Sept. 1.
item.author: circuits50capital@circuits.fit (Emilio Santos)
item.content:encoded:
On January 13, 2026, the U.S. Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security said it would review export licenses for Nvidia’s H200, AMD’s MI325X, and similar chips to China on a case-by-case basis, if security conditions are met. That followed a December announcement that those products could ship to approved Chinese customers. The conditions, as BIS described them, include showing that U.S. customers will not lose capacity, that the buyer screens customers, and that the product is independently tested in the United States.

That is a loosening relative to a blanket “presumption of denial.” It is not an open door. Case-by-case means a queue. A queue means a calendar risk for anyone whose revenue depends on a yes.

Read the three conditions as work, not as policy

BIS’s release spells out what an applicant must demonstrate. Each one is a project somebody has to own:

  • No reduction in capacity for U.S. customers. The applicant must show that exporting to China will not reduce global semiconductor production capacity currently available to U.S. customers. That is a supply-allocation argument, and it needs numbers from operations, not a letter from sales.
  • The Chinese purchaser has export compliance procedures, including customer screening. Your customer’s compliance program becomes part of your application. If the buyer cannot show one, the license is weaker before it is filed.
  • Independent third-party testing in the United States to verify performance and security. That adds a lab, a schedule and a cost to every product line that wants to use the window.

The rule took effect on publication in the Federal Register, BIS said. The point for planners is that a policy can open in a day while the work it requires takes a quarter.

The rule moved twice

Reporting in June described a second turn. After the administration dropped the earlier “AI Diffusion Framework” in May, BIS guidance — covered by Al Jazeera and summarized in later research notes — treated license requirements as applying to companies headquartered or parented in China even when they operate outside China. Politico reported in July that license applications were piling up, the Entity List had gone months without additions, and former officials alleged a gap before May 31 guidance closed sales of restricted chips to China-headquartered buyers abroad.

I cannot verify every allegation in that Politico piece from here. What is on the public BIS site is enough for operators: the January H200/MI325X policy exists, and so does a February settlement. Applied Materials and Applied Materials Korea agreed to pay about $252 million to BIS for illegal exports of semiconductor manufacturing equipment to China, the bureau announced February 12. BIS said the amount was twice the roughly $126 million value of the shipments, the maximum allowed by statute. The mechanics of that case are in Chip export controls and the suppliers caught in between.

A license delay is a delivery date. A penalty is a product-line autopsy.

Seoul joined the list

On September 1, South Korea’s Ministry of Trade, Industry and Resources added high-performance AI chips and certain lithography, etching, and deposition equipment to its strategic export-control list. Exporters need ministry approval. Aju Press reported the change implements more than 80 updates from four international regimes, including Wassenaar.

If you sell tools, parts, or packaging into that chain, you now have two governments that can pause a crate. Large equipment makers have export counsel. A $40 million supplier often has a spreadsheet and a freight forwarder.

Treat the license queue as a forecast input

A license that is under review is not revenue, and it is not lost revenue either. It is a timing question, and finance teams should model it that way. BIS runs a public status tool, STELA, that lets an applicant check where an application stands using its application number. If your forecast includes shipments that need a license, someone should be checking STELA on a schedule and reporting the status in the same meeting where the forecast is reviewed.

The same discipline applies to the customer side. Because the January policy asks the buyer to show its own screening, the sales team should know, before a quote goes out, whether the buyer can produce that evidence. A quote that depends on a license the customer cannot support is not a pipeline opportunity. It is a hope with a part number.

What a board should ask

What share of trailing revenue would stall if the top three end-use cases needed a new license tomorrow? Who owns screening — sales or a named compliance lead? Has the bill of materials been split into “ships without a license / needs a license / do not quote”? How many applications are pending, how old is the oldest, and what revenue sits behind them?

What to do this quarter

  • List every pending license with its application number, age, product, customer and the revenue behind it. Check status in STELA monthly.
  • Split forecast revenue into “no license needed,” “license pending” and “license not yet filed.” Report all three.
  • Ask key Chinese and Korean customers for their compliance evidence now, before an application needs it.
  • Budget for U.S. third-party testing if you plan to use the January case-by-case window.
  • Re-screen China-parented customers outside China against the current lists and guidance.

Do not wait for the next headline to draw that map. BIS already showed it will both open a window and fine a household name. Korea made the window smaller for some dual-use gear. The mid-tier does not get a press conference. It gets a denied AES filing.

Sources

  • BIS, “Department of Commerce Revises License Review Policy for Semiconductors Exported to China,” Jan. 13, 2026
  • BIS, Applied Materials $252 million penalty, Feb. 12, 2026
  • BIS on X, Applied Materials settlement, February 12, 2026
  • BIS, STELA license application status tool
  • Politico, “China hardliners take aim at Commerce Department official,” July 8, 2026
  • Aju Press, “Korea adds semiconductors to export control list,” Sept. 1, 2026

The quarter checklist and forecast framing are the desk’s. Policy facts are as stated by the sources above.

item.title: Cyber Insurance Got Cheaper. The Questionnaire Did Not.
item.description: Swiss Re puts 2026 global cyber premium at $16.4 billion with rates still down. The application still wants MFA.
item.author: circuits50capital@circuits.fit (Emilio Santos)
item.content:encoded:
Swiss Re’s latest cyber reinsurance report, covered by Risk & Insurance on September 2, puts global cyber premium on track for $16.4 billion in 2026, growing about 5% a year since 2022. Rates fell for a fourth straight year, but the cut shrank: roughly −13% globally in 2025 versus about −5% in 2026, with the U.S. stabilizing faster than Europe. North America is still about two-thirds of the market at $10.7 billion.

That is a buyer’s tape. It is not a “risk went away” tape.

Losses are creeping while prices fall

AM Best, as reported by Insurance Journal in July, said the U.S. cyber loss ratio in 2025 rose for a second year to 53 — the first time above 50 since the pandemic ransomware spike. Direct premium looked roughly flat after adjusting for a Beazley book moving onshore. Third-party claims were trending up about 30%. The first quarter of 2026 was the eighth straight quarter of U.S. price cuts.

Fitch, in a May monitor, said U.S. cyber premiums had increased after a two-year slide, while losses also rose and the line stayed profitable. Those two houses are not describing identical clocks. One is looking at a 2025 loss ratio and early-2026 rates; the other at a premium rebound in its May sample. For a CFO, the usable sentence is simpler: you can still shop the renewal, and the application will still ask whether backups are immutable and whether MFA is actually on.

A cheaper policy that assumes controls you do not have is not a bargain. It is a denial waiting for a claim.

Where the gap is

Swiss Re’s segment split is the part boards skip. Micro-SMEs and SMEs remain thinly insured (about 5–10% and 10–20% penetration) but are still expected to throw off $4.9 billion in premium this year. Mid-market sits at 40–50% penetration and about $4.1 billion. Large corporates dominate at 60–70% penetration and $7.4 billion — and may be under-limited. Swiss Re’s claims database, as cited in that coverage, shows an average of 10 losses a year above the typical U.S. purchased limit of about $120 million.

If you are a mid-market operator, you are in the layer insurers still want. Use that. Raise limits if a cloud or payments outage would take a quarter. Do not skip the hygiene that the questionnaire already priced in: MFA, EDR that someone watches, tested restores, a named incident retainer.

AI is not a new line item yet

Swiss Re argues AI is amplifying known cyber loss types — faster vulnerability hunts, more convincing phishing — more than inventing a clean new peril. Many AI incidents may already sit inside existing “computer system” wordings. Claims of that flavor are still limited, the report says. That is a reason to read the policy, not a reason to assume you are covered for a model leaking customer data into a vendor you never listed.

Take the rate cut. Keep the controls. Put finance and IT in the same room in month nine of the policy, not month twelve. The cheap years do not last if loss ratios keep walking up while prices walk down.

Worked example: three answers the application will test

To show what “keep the controls” means at renewal, we ran three typical gaps through our free risk exception register on November 11, using the tool’s own scoring code. These are illustrative inputs for a made-up mid-market firm, not a real client or a real policy.

  • MFA. Three cloud admin accounts still without MFA, “rolling out.” Owner: IT lead. Compensating control: admin sign-ins limited to the office network. Funded: yes, amount 0, because turning MFA on costs staff time rather than a purchase. Expiry: December 15. Accepted by: CFO.
  • Backups. File server with a nightly backup job but no restore test this year. Owner: the managed service provider. Funded: yes, 1,200 for a test day. Expiry: December 1. Accepted by: CFO.
  • Retainer. Counsel and forensics not yet under contract. Control type: Other. Owner: CFO. Compensating control: the broker’s panel list on file. Funded: yes, 5,000. Expiry: January 31, 2027. Accepted by: CEO.

The register returned “Not waivable” for the MFA and backup rows, because it treats MFA, backups, EDR and known-exploited vulnerabilities as controls an exception cannot excuse. The MFA row also carried “No funded fix,” and the backup row “Expires in 20 days.” The retainer row returned no flags. Summary: “Not waivable: 2. Rows with a missing owner, expiry, or funded fix, or an expiry inside 30 days: 2.”

Read against the application, two of the five lines in this example are a “no” today, whatever the plan says. That is the answer to give the broker, with the dates.

Now the price side, also illustrative. On an $18,000 expiring premium, a 5% rate cut, in line with Swiss Re’s rough 2026 global figure, saves $900 a year. That is less than the $1,200 this example sets aside for one restore test, and far less than a claim that is disputed because the form said backups were tested. The rate cut is real money. It is not a reason to answer the form optimistically.

Limits: the register flags missing owners, dates and funding. It does not know whether MFA is enforced or a restore works. It also flags a fix with a zero amount as unfunded, which is strict for a fix like MFA that costs only staff time. Record the hours as the amount if that helps the conversation. Rate changes vary by carrier, size and claims history, so use your broker’s number, not a market average.

Sources

  • Risk & Insurance, Swiss Re cyber report coverage, Sept. 2, 2026 (Swiss Re report: Building a sustainable cyber market in the AI era)
  • Insurance Journal, AM Best U.S. cyber market, July 27, 2026
  • Fitch Ratings, “U.S. Cyber Insurance Premiums Increase,” May 27, 2026

Operator guides: Cyber insurance renewal prep for mid-market IT budgets (2026) and What a cyber insurer will still ask. If a public customer is on the policy, the disclosure clock is Before the Form 8-K clock.

item.title: Software Buying Is an Operating Skill
item.description: The stack is no longer an IT catalog. It is how the company actually runs — and most firms still buy it like office supplies.
item.author: circuits50capital@circuits.fit (Emilio Santos)
item.content:encoded:
Walk a mid-market close, a warehouse, or a support queue and you are walking a software path. Invoice to cash lives in one product. Exceptions live in a spreadsheet someone swore they would retire. Escalations live in a chat tool that is not the “system of record.” Buying those tools as if they were toner is how you get seven CRMs and one actual process.

The companies that waste the least money do not have a prettier vendor matrix. They have a named owner for each workflow, a kill date for overlapping seats, and a rule that a new logo cannot enter without a retirement plan for an old one.

Stop scoring demos

Demos are designed to make the happy path look inevitable. Score the unhappy path: month-end, chargebacks, a warehouse that is offline, a customer who is not in the dropdown. If the product cannot show that without a services SOW, you are not buying software. You are buying a project.

A seat that nobody can turn off is not a subscription. It is a tax.

The three questions that belong in procurement

What work dies if this tool is down for a day? Who is allowed to add a seat? What is the exit — export, escrow, or a second vendor already on the bench? If finance cannot answer those, IT will answer them during an outage, which is the expensive way.

Make renewal a product review

Annual renewals are where vendors hide price. Treat them like a product review: usage, overlapping tools, and whether the original problem still exists. A 8% increase on a tool that replaced two others can be cheap. A 0% increase on a tool nobody opens is still a loss.

Software buying is now an operating skill because the company is the stack. Hire for that, or keep paying for catalogs.

The scorecard is the software renewal scorecard. Operator guides: Software buying as an operating skill and How to read a SaaS renewal. If the renewal now includes an agent, the sheet is the agent access limit sheet, then Limit what an agent can touch.

Updated October 2026: why this is a bigger deal now

This note first ran on August 31 as a short operator essay. Since then, two things have made the buying decision heavier. First, more renewals now include AI features or agents that can act inside the product, which changes what you are approving. Our agent access guide covers that. Second, public guidance on what to ask a software vendor has grown. CISA’s 2026 minimum elements for a software bill of materials, covered in SBOM now covers the suite, give buyers a named list to put in a contract.

Why it matters, by role

CFO. Software is a recurring cost that grows quietly. Seats get added and rarely removed. Price increases arrive at renewal, when switching is hardest. The finance lever is timing: decisions made 90 days before renewal are cheaper than decisions made in the last week. How to read a SaaS renewal lays out the 90, 60, and 30-day steps.

CISO. Every new tool is a new place for data, a new identity to manage, and a new vendor to monitor. CISA’s Secure by Demand guide, published with the FBI in August 2024, lists questions buyers can ask before purchase: whether the vendor offers single sign-on and logging in the base product, whether it publishes a vulnerability disclosure policy, and whether it can provide an SBOM. Ask those before the contract, not after the incident.

Founder. Early-stage companies tend to buy tools one at a time, each for a good reason. Two years later, three tools do the same job and nobody can turn any of them off. Name an owner for each workflow early. It costs nothing and saves a cleanup project later.

Operator. You live with the tool after the contract is signed. Ask to see the unhappy path in the demo: month-end, a failed sync, an offline site, an exception that does not fit the dropdown. If the vendor cannot show it, plan for the workaround.

A buying checklist that fits on one page

  1. Name the workflow and the owner. One person, by name, who can say what the tool is for and when it would be retired.
  2. List what it replaces. If nothing is retired, the new tool is additive cost. Write the retirement date for any overlapping tool.
  3. Score the unhappy path. Pick three hard cases from your real operations and ask the vendor to run them.
  4. Ask the security questions. SSO and MFA in the base tier, security logs you can export, a public vulnerability disclosure policy, and an SBOM on request. These come from CISA’s Secure by Demand guide.
  5. Set the seat rule. Who can add seats, and who reviews unused seats each quarter.
  6. Write the exit. Full data export in a documented format, a data-return window after the contract ends, and a notice period you can meet.
  7. Cap the price. A contractual cap on renewal increases. A blank increase clause is the vendor’s option, not yours.

A worked example

The numbers below are illustrative, not survey data. Say a team pays for 120 seats of a tool at $400 per seat per year, or $48,000. In the last 30 days, 66 people logged in. That is 55% use. Before renewal, the owner proposes cutting to 75 seats to leave room for growth. At the same per-seat price, the new cost is $30,000, a $18,000 saving, before any price negotiation. If the vendor also proposes an 8% increase, the right comparison is the new price on 75 seats, not the old price on 120.

Run those inputs through the software renewal scorecard and it flags the seat gap and any missing price cap, and writes the requests for the vendor email.

What to watch next

  • AI features inside renewals. Watch for new clauses on training, data use, and agent actions added to existing products. They change the risk of a tool you already own.
  • EU cloud switching. For EU data processing services, the Data Act ends switching charges on January 12, 2027. Check whether your vendors update exit terms. The detail is in the cloud repatriation note.
  • Vendor security artifacts. More buyers are asking for SBOMs and security logs in the contract. If your vendor cannot provide them, that is information about the vendor.

Sources

This is an operator note. It does not cite a buying survey. The 8% and the seven CRMs are illustrations, not a count.
