item.title: When Compliance Is the Product
item.description: Data residency, audit trails, and model clauses are no longer legal footnotes. They are packaging.
item.author: circuits50capital@circuits.fit (Emilio Santos)
item.content:encoded:
A decade ago, compliance sat in an appendix. Buyers asked for a SOC report, filed it, and went back to features. That order flipped. In regulated and merely nervous companies, the feature that wins is the one that can prove where the data sat, who touched it, and which model was not allowed to see it.

Vendors noticed. Region pins, customer-managed keys, and “no training on your prompts” are now sales motions with list prices. Some of that is real control. Some of it is a checkbox with a surcharge.

Ask where the log lives

An audit trail that lives in the vendor’s cloud in a different country than the workload is a story, not a control. Ask for the region of the logs, the retention you can set, and whether you can export without a professional-services ticket. If the answer is a PDF, you bought theater.

A control you cannot export is a control you do not own.

The model clause is a product decision

“We don’t train on your data” is not one setting. It is training, evaluation, human review, and subprocessors. Map those four. If any one of them is “maybe, in a different product tier,” price that tier as the real SKU.

Policy as a wedge

Export rules, privacy law, and sector guidance will keep splitting the market into “good enough for a startup” and “good enough for a bank.” The second market pays more and moves slower. Builders who ignore it will still sell. Builders who fake it will get a lawsuit with a product name on it.

Treat compliance as packaging only if you can open the box. Otherwise it is a liability with a landing page.

The pages that open the box are the guides: What Article 50 asks a buyer, What belongs in a processor clause, and A one-page AI use rule. Gartner’s September 19 post says EU AI Act literacy requirements are now in effect. That is Gartner’s claim. The timeline is the EU briefing.

Updated October 2026: what moved since August

This note first ran on August 31. Three dated items have moved closer, and they are the reason compliance features now show up on order forms rather than in appendices.

  • EU AI Act transparency. The European Commission’s AI Act Service Desk timeline says the Article 50 transparency rules started to apply on August 2, 2026. For certain generative systems already on the market before that date, the machine-readable marking duty in Article 50(2) has a transition that ends December 2, 2026. The buyer questions are in What Article 50 asks a buyer.
  • EU high-risk dates. The same public timeline records the stand-alone high-risk duties for December 2, 2027 and duties for high-risk systems inside regulated products for August 2, 2028. A vendor that answers a transparency question with a 2027 date is answering a different question. The full timeline is in the EU AI Act briefing.
  • EU Data Act switching. Regulation (EU) 2023/2854, the Data Act, has applied since September 12, 2025. Its cloud-switching chapter covers “data processing services,” and providers may charge only reduced, cost-based switching charges until January 12, 2027. After that date, switching charges are not allowed. That turns “can we leave” from a negotiation into a contract term worth checking.

Why it matters, by role

CFO. Compliance tiers are where list prices climb. Region pinning, customer-managed keys, longer log retention, and a no-training commitment are often sold as an upgrade. If the control is a legal requirement for your business, the upgrade is the real price. Budget for it as the base SKU and stop treating the cheaper tier as the comparison.

CISO. A control you cannot see is a control you cannot attest to. Your auditors and your customers will ask for evidence, not a vendor’s marketing page. A SOC 2 report from the AICPA framework helps, but read its scope and period. A report that covers the hosting layer and not the AI feature you bought does not cover the AI feature.

Founder. If you sell into regulated buyers, these features are not optional extras. They decide whether you get through procurement. Build the export, the log access, and the data-use map before the first bank asks. Faking them costs more later than building them now.

Operator. You inherit whatever the contract says. If the vendor stores logs in a region you cannot use, or deletes them after 30 days, you will find out during an incident. Ask now, while the deal is open.

A checklist for the next renewal

  1. Log location and retention. Which region holds the audit log, how long it is kept, and whether you can set the retention yourself.
  2. Export without a ticket. Can you export logs and data in a documented, machine-readable format from the admin console or an API? If export requires professional services, write the cost down.
  3. The four-part data-use map. For customer data and prompts, ask separately about training, evaluation, human review, and subprocessors. Get each answer in writing and tied to the product tier you are buying.
  4. Processor terms. If the GDPR applies to the data, check that the data-processing addendum covers what Article 28 requires: subject matter, duration, nature and purpose of processing, types of data, sub-processor rules, and deletion or return at the end. What belongs in a processor clause walks through it.
  5. Assurance scope. Ask for the current SOC 2 report and read which systems and which period it covers. Note anything you bought that sits outside that scope.
  6. Exit terms. For EU data processing services, check how the switching and data-export terms line up with the Data Act dates above. For everything else, write the exit into the contract: format, timeline, and who pays.
  7. Price the tier. If any answer above is “only in Enterprise,” price Enterprise as the real cost and compare vendors on that basis.

The software renewal scorecard scores several of these lines, including export, exit clause, subprocessors, and AI training terms, and writes the agenda for the vendor email.

What to watch next

  • December 2, 2026. The Article 50(2) marking transition ends for covered generative systems already on the market. Ask vendors that generate text, images, audio, or video what mark they apply and from which date.
  • January 12, 2027. Data Act switching charges end for data processing services. Expect vendor contract updates before then. Read them.
  • Renewal paperwork. Watch for vendors moving no-training or region commitments from the contract into a policy page they can change. A commitment on a web page is weaker than one in the order form.

Sources

  • Gartner on X, September 19, 2026: Gartner says EU AI Act literacy requirements are now in effect.
  • European Commission, AI Act Service Desk, implementation timeline: Article 50 from August 2, 2026, the December 2, 2026 marking transition, and the high-risk dates
  • Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, the AI Act, on EUR-Lex
  • Regulation (EU) 2023/2854, the Data Act, on EUR-Lex: switching rules for data processing services and the January 12, 2027 end of switching charges
  • Regulation (EU) 2016/679, the GDPR, on EUR-Lex: Article 28 processor terms
  • EDPB Guidelines 07/2020 on controller and processor
  • AICPA, SOC 2 overview

The dates this desk uses are in the EU briefing. This note does not add a literacy procedure.

item.title: The AI Productivity Paradox at Mid-Market Companies
item.description: Tools landed in every department. Output did not. The bottleneck is workflow, not the model.
item.author: circuits50capital@circuits.fit (Emilio Santos)
item.content:encoded:
Walk a mid-market operator through last year’s software budget and you will find a familiar pattern: a generative AI line item that grew faster than any other category, a slide that promised 20% time back, and a quiet admission in the hallway that nobody can find the 20%.

This is not a model-quality problem. Frontier systems write decent first drafts, summarize noisy tickets, and clear the kind of boilerplate that used to clog Monday mornings. The paradox is operational. Companies bought a capability and installed it on top of processes that were never designed to absorb a faster first draft.

Where the hours actually went

The same three sinks show up when finance, IT, and the line compare notes.

First, review replaced production. A junior analyst who used to spend three hours building a memo now spends two hours checking whether the model invented a customer, a covenant, or a date. The calendar still shows a three-hour block because review is harder to batch than drafting. The work got different, not shorter.

Second, pilots never became defaults. Tools live in a browser tab that power users love and everyone else forgets. There is no system of record for “this is how we write a QBR.” Without a default path, you do not get compounding. You get anecdotes.

Third, the metric was vanity. Seat counts and prompt volume look like adoption. They do not tell you whether close, cycle time, ticket resolution, or win rate moved. If the scoreboard is licenses, the organization will buy licenses.

A faster first draft in a broken workflow is a more expensive broken workflow.

The firms that did get the hours back

The exceptions are boring, which is why they work. They picked one workflow with a clean definition of done — monthly close commentary, support macros, bid/no-bid memos — and they changed the standard operating procedure, not just the toolbar.

They also staffed a human owner. Not an “AI committee.” A named manager whose bonus includes cycle time for that workflow. Vendors will not do this for you. Neither will a center of excellence that only runs lunch-and-learns.

What to cut, what to keep

If you cannot point to a before-and-after number in 90 days, you do not have a deployment. You have a subscription. Treat it like any other underperforming SaaS: consolidate tools, kill overlapping copilots, and put the remaining spend next to a process map.

Keep the models. Kill the theater. The productivity story in 2026 will not be won by the company with the most seats. It will be won by the company that rewired the few workflows that actually set the P&L.

Gartner posted on October 1 that most organizations are not yet ready to delegate work to AI agents, and on September 24 that managing AI cost is becoming as important as deploying it. Those posts are the announcement. The pages that tell you what to do start with token cost to gross margin, then the guides: Put an AI cost on one workflow, A one-page AI use rule, and How to tell AI spend from AI return.

Sources

  • Gartner on X, October 1, 2026: most organizations are not yet ready to delegate work to AI agents.
  • Gartner on X, September 24, 2026: managing AI cost is becoming as important as deploying it.

The 20% in the lead is a slide an operator will recognize. It is not a figure from those posts. The three sinks are the desk’s pattern, not a published survey.

item.title: Private Credit Is Quietly Funding the Software Roll-Up
item.description: When public markets froze on multiples, direct lenders stepped in — and started acting like operators.
item.author: circuits50capital@circuits.fit (Emilio Santos)
item.content:encoded:
The software roll-up did not die when growth stocks derated. It changed banks. Instead of a high-multiple listing and a cheap revolver, more platforms are being stitched together with direct lending that looks, on paper, like conservative cash-flow finance and, in practice, like a shadow equity check.

Sponsors still love vertical software: sticky customers, invoice-driven collections, and a story about cutting two CROs after the third add-on. What changed is who is willing to underwrite the next deal when the IPO window is a rumor and banks want amortization.

How big the lender is now

The Federal Reserve’s May 2026 Financial Stability Report puts numbers on it. It defines private credit as loans originated by nonbanks and negotiated bilaterally between borrower and lender, and estimates that, as of the latest data in the second half of 2025, private credit loans came to about $1.4 trillion, or about 10 percent of the total debt of U.S. nonfinancial corporations and about one-third of below-investment-grade debt excluding bank loans.

The same report says something software operators should read twice: the software sector had become the largest sector in private credit portfolios, driven by elevated private equity activity. In other words, the roll-up is not a niche trade inside private credit. It is the center of it.

Why lenders like the collateral

Recurring revenue is easier to model than a factory. Churn shows up in the cohort before it shows up in the borrowing base. That is catnip for credit funds that built teams to read SaaS metrics rather than shipping manifests.

The structure is familiar: unitranche, a loose covenant on leverage, a tighter one on liquidity, and an equity cure. The novelty is operational. Lenders now ask for product-level retention, net revenue retention, and a map of where AI features are bundled versus billed. They are not becoming product managers. They are becoming allergic to “AI” as an EBITDA add-back.

If the add-on cannot share a billing system in 90 days, it is not a synergy. It is a second company.

The sentiment turned on software specifically

The Fed report says investor sentiment toward private credit turned increasingly negative from the middle of 2025, following some high-profile corporate defaults and concerns about the potential for advances in AI to disrupt industries, “particularly software.” That is a notable sentence from a central bank. The collateral that lenders liked because it was sticky is now being questioned because it might be replaceable.

The report also flags stress signals in the loans themselves. Defaults in private credit remained relatively low, but it describes elevated use of payment-in-kind (PIK) provisions — interest paid with more debt rather than cash — as an indication that some borrowers may face repayment difficulties. And new-loan spreads in private credit ticked up, which the Fed attributes to ongoing investor concern over portfolio credit quality.

The funding side has a new weak point

Private credit historically relied on institutional money locked up for 7 to 10 years. The Fed notes that more capital now comes from individual investors through “semi-liquid” vehicles: perpetual-life business development companies (BDCs) and interval funds, together about $241 billion in net assets, or about 20 percent of net assets under management in private credit vehicles. Most perpetual BDCs disclosed an intention to cap redemptions at 5 percent of net asset value per quarter.

According to the report, redemption requests rose in the fourth quarter of 2025 and accelerated in the first quarter of 2026, when a number of funds received requests much larger than 5 percent of NAV; most managers chose to cap at 5 percent. In that quarter, accepted redemptions somewhat exceeded new inflows at perpetual BDCs for the first time since those vehicles were created. The Fed judged the financial-stability risk “limited and manageable,” but warned that continued redemptions and negative sentiment could reduce credit availability for some borrowers, especially riskier ones.

For a software platform that planned its next three tuck-ins on a lender’s appetite, that is the risk that matters. It is not a crisis. It is a slower yes.

The risk that does not fit the CIM

Integration risk is the silent covenant. Two products with similar logos and incompatible data models will not produce the cost takeout in the model. Credit agreements still treat “cost synergy” as a management slide, not a test.

There is also refinancing risk with a software accent. The Fed report notes that debt-servicing capacity is lower among riskier private firms, especially those that rely on floating-rate debt such as leveraged loans and private credit. If rates stay higher for longer, the roll-up that worked at six turns on a lower coupon looks different at the same turns on a coupon that eats the free cash flow that was supposed to fund the next deal.

What to watch

Watch hold periods, not press releases. If platforms start selling divisions instead of adding them, the credit cycle in vertical software has turned. Watch for PIK toggles in amendments, and for lenders putting observers in operating reviews. That is the tell that the fund thinks it bought a business, not a coupon. Watch the semi-liquid funds’ quarterly redemption disclosures; the Fed built its flow data from BDC Form 8-K filings, which anyone can read on SEC EDGAR.

What to do this quarter

  • If you run a sponsor-backed software company: rebuild the covenant model with today’s floating rate and a second case 100 basis points higher. Know the month the liquidity covenant gets tight.
  • Prove integration in billing, not slides. Pick one add-on and put it on the shared billing and identity system. Lenders now ask; have the answer.
  • Separate AI revenue from AI cost. Show which AI features are billed, which are bundled, and what they cost to serve. The token cost to gross margin calculator is a start.
  • If you buy from a roll-up: read the renewal for price-increase caps and assignment clauses before an owner change, using the software renewal scorecard and How to read a SaaS renewal.
  • If you allocate to private credit: ask the manager for software exposure, PIK share and redemption queue as of the last quarter end.

For operators, the implication is simple. The cheap equity era trained founders to grow into a multiple. The private-credit era trains them to grow into a coverage ratio. Those are different companies. See also Software buying as an operating skill.

Sources

  • Federal Reserve Board, Financial Stability Report, May 2026 (PDF): Box 4.1, “Developments in Private Credit,” and Sections 1 and 2 on spreads, PIK use and debt-servicing capacity.
  • Federal Reserve, Financial Stability Report archive
  • SEC EDGAR full-text search, for BDC 8-K and 10-Q filings.

The figures above are the Fed’s. The covenant and integration framing, and the “six turns” example, are desk illustration, not a specific deal.

item.title: Chip Export Controls and the Suppliers Caught in Between
item.description: Policy is written in Washington. The P&L lands on toolmakers, packagers, and the mid-tier vendors nobody briefed.
item.author: circuits50capital@circuits.fit (Emilio Santos)
item.content:encoded:
Export controls are discussed as a duel between capitals. The people who feel them first are often two or three tiers down: the firm that sells filtration, the shop that rebuilds a tool, the distributor that used to treat a license as a formality.

The policy intent is strategic — keep the most advanced compute out of specific end uses and end users. The commercial effect is messier. Demand does not vanish. It reroutes, delays, or shows up as a rush order from a customer who suddenly needs a “compliant architecture.”

The mid-tier problem

Large equipment makers have export teams, outside counsel, and a government-relations slide. A $40 million supplier has a spreadsheet and a freight forwarder. When a rule changes, the large firm pauses shipments and staffs the pause. The small firm discovers the pause when a letter of credit fails.

Classification is the hidden product. Two parts that look identical on a packing list can sit on different sides of a control if one is “specially designed.” Getting that wrong is not a rounding error. It is a denial, a seizure, or a years-long investigation. The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS), the Commerce Department agency that administers the Export Administration Regulations (EAR), publishes its own step-by-step guidance on how to classify an item. Start there before paying anyone to tell you the same thing.

Compliance is now a delivery date, not a legal memo.

What the biggest recent case actually shows

On February 12, 2026, BIS announced a settlement with Applied Materials and Applied Materials Korea. The facts in the bureau’s release are a map of how the mid-tier gets caught, even though the company is not mid-tier:

  • In 2020, the Chinese customer that Applied had been selling ion implanters to was placed on the Entity List, which means a license is needed before shipping it items subject to the EAR.
  • In 2021 and 2022, according to BIS, Applied shipped ion implanters first to its Korean affiliate for assembly and then on to China, without applying for or receiving a license.
  • BIS put the value of the shipments at about $126 million. The penalty of about $252 million is twice the transaction value, which BIS says is the maximum allowed by statute, and the bureau called it the second-highest penalty it has ever imposed.
  • Applied agreed to multiple audits of its export compliance program and annual certifications to BIS, and BIS said the compliance employees and senior trade and production executives responsible are no longer employed there.

Three lessons travel down the supply chain. The routing through an affiliate in a third country did not change the answer. The listing happened years before the violation, so “we were already selling to them” is not a defense. And the cost was not only the fine; it was years of audits and the people.

What operators should actually do

Map end users, not just destinations. A tool sold to a neutral geography can still be a problem if the beneficial owner is on a list. The International Trade Administration publishes the Consolidated Screening List, which combines export screening lists from the Departments of Commerce, State and Treasury, with a free search tool, downloadable files and an API. A company that ships controlled items and does not screen every new customer and every new ship-to against it is choosing not to know. The Entity List itself sits in Supplement No. 4 to Part 744 of the EAR, on the official eCFR.

Build a kill switch in the order book: a deal does not enter production until screening is done, even if sales hates it. Then write it down. BIS publishes guidance on export compliance programs, and the Applied settlement shows the bureau treats the quality of that program as part of the remedy.

Second, assume the rule will move again. Design products with a “good / better / restricted” bill of materials so you are not redesigning under a deadline. That costs engineering time now. It is cheaper than a warehouse of stranded kits.

Third, know the disclosure rule before you need it. Under 15 CFR 764.5, BIS’s Office of Export Enforcement treats voluntary self-disclosure as a mitigating factor, and a deliberate decision not to disclose a significant apparent violation as an aggravating one. The regulation is also clear that disclosure does not guarantee leniency and does not prevent a criminal referral. That is a reason to have counsel identified in advance, not a reason to wait.

The investment read

Controls are a subsidy to whoever can manufacture the substitute inside the fence. They are a tax on whoever’s installed base sat on the other side of it. Read capex announcements with that lens. A new line can be demand. It can also be a political hedge that never earns its cost of capital if the rule is later relaxed — or tightened past the point of the hedge. The January 2026 move to case-by-case review for some advanced chips to China, covered in Chip licenses keep moving, is a reminder that the fence moves in both directions.

For boards of suppliers, the question is not “are we geopolitical.” It is “what percent of trailing revenue would we lose if our top three end-use cases needed a license tomorrow.” If you cannot answer that in a staff meeting, you do not have a control program. You have hope.

What to do this quarter

  • Classify the top 20 SKUs. Record the export classification and the reasoning for each, using BIS’s classification guidance. Flag anything nobody can explain.
  • Screen the customer master. Run every active customer, consignee and ship-to through the Consolidated Screening List. Repeat whenever a list changes, not once a year.
  • Check affiliate routing. List every shipment that goes to an affiliate, integrator or distributor before its final destination, and confirm who the end user is.
  • Write the hold rule. No order enters production without completed screening, signed off by a named compliance owner rather than sales.
  • Pick counsel now. Know who you would call about a possible voluntary self-disclosure before you find a problem.
  • Put the revenue-at-risk number in the board pack. One line: percent of trailing revenue that would need a license if the rule moved.

Sources

  • BIS, “Applied Materials to Pay $252 Million Penalty,” February 12, 2026
  • BIS on X, Applied Materials settlement, February 12, 2026
  • International Trade Administration, Consolidated Screening List
  • eCFR, 15 CFR Part 744 (control policy: end-user and end-use based; Entity List at Supplement No. 4)
  • eCFR, 15 CFR 764.5, Voluntary self-disclosure
  • BIS, Classify your item and BIS, Export Compliance Programs

The case facts are from BIS. The mid-tier framing, the $40 million supplier and the quarter checklist are the desk’s.

item.title: Cyber Insurance Is Rewriting the IT Budget
item.description: Underwriters now ask better questions than some boards. The answers are showing up as line items.
item.author: circuits50capital@circuits.fit (Emilio Santos)
item.content:encoded:
For a decade, cybersecurity spend followed fear and vendors. Then the insurance market tightened, deductibles jumped, and the renewal packet started to look like an audit. CFOs noticed. The questionnaire was shorter than the strategy deck and meaner about specifics: multifactor everywhere, immutable backups, endpoint detection that is actually watched, a list of who can disable it.

That packet is now one of the more honest IT planning documents in the building. If you cannot get coverage — or you can, but only with a deductible that would wreck a quarter — the control is not optional. It is priced.

From “best practice” to “condition”

MFA on email used to be a talking point. It is now a condition of many policies. So are privileged-access management, tested restores, and a named incident-response retainer. Companies that treated those as a 2028 project discovered they were a 2026 premium.

This is not the insurer being kind. It is the insurer refusing to subsidize the same ransomware script twice. The side effect is useful: it gives the CISO a budget argument that does not depend on a scare story.

The cheapest control is the one that keeps the policy from becoming a brochure.

Where the money actually moves

Watch the mix, not the top line. Identity, backup, and detection are taking share from sprawling “platform” deals that cannot be mapped to a yes/no question on a form. Training still gets funded because underwriters ask about it, even when operators privately doubt the click-through course.

Also watch who owns the relationship. If the broker sits only with finance, IT will be surprised by a control they cannot implement in 30 days. If IT owns it alone, finance will be surprised by the premium. The companies that renew cleanly put both in the room in month nine, not month twelve.

The limit of the model

Insurance is not a substitute for security, and a completed questionnaire is not a mature program. Controls that please an underwriter can still fail a determined attacker. Use the form as a floor. Do not confuse it with a strategy.

Still, as a capital-allocation device, the market is doing something boards failed to do: it is forcing a short list. In a world of infinite tools, a short list is a gift.

Operator guides: Cyber insurance renewal prep for mid-market IT budgets (2026) and What a cyber insurer will still ask.

Updated October 2026: cheaper policies, same questions

This note first ran on August 19. Since then, the market has kept softening. Our September note, Cyber got cheaper. The questionnaire did not., covers the rate figures and their sources. The short version for budget owners: lower premiums have not removed the control questions. A cheaper policy written on controls you do not actually run can still fail at claim time.

The threat side has not eased. The FBI’s Internet Crime Complaint Center (IC3) reported $16.6 billion in losses reported to it in 2024, a 33% increase from 2023. Business email compromise alone accounted for about $2.77 billion of reported losses. In December 2024 the FBI also warned that criminals use generative AI to make fraud more convincing and to run it at larger scale.

Why it matters, by role

CFO. The insurance application is a short list of controls the market is willing to price. Use it in budget planning. If a control on the form is not in place, the cost shows up somewhere: a higher deductible, an exclusion, a denied claim, or a project you fund in a hurry.

CISO. The form gives you a budget argument that finance already accepts. Map each question to an owner and evidence. “We have MFA” should mean you can show where it is enforced, including email, remote access, admin accounts, and cloud consoles.

Founder. Smaller companies often buy cyber cover because a customer contract requires it. Read what the customer asked for: limit, deductible, and which coverages. Then read the application questions before you answer them. An inaccurate answer is a bigger risk than a higher premium.

Operator. Restores, alert monitoring, and admin account reviews are operations work. If the form says they happen, they need to happen on a schedule, with someone assigned.

The controls that keep coming up

Insurers write their own forms, so wording varies. The controls below line up with public guidance from CISA and NIST, which is a useful way to check that the form is asking for real security and not only paperwork.

  1. Phishing-resistant MFA. CISA’s fact sheet on implementing phishing-resistant MFA identifies FIDO/WebAuthn authenticators and PKI-based methods as the strongest options. Start with email, remote access, and administrators.
  2. Backups you have restored. CISA’s #StopRansomware guide recommends maintaining offline, encrypted backups and regularly testing them. A backup job that has never been restored is an assumption.
  3. Endpoint detection that someone watches. Write down who receives the alert outside business hours.
  4. Privileged access. List who can disable security tools and whether that action is logged.
  5. Incident response plan and contacts. The #StopRansomware guide recommends a plan that is exercised. Know which counsel and forensics firm you would call, and whether the insurer requires its panel.
  6. Payment change verification. Given the business email compromise numbers above, require a call-back to a number already on file before changing vendor bank details. See Stop using a voice as approval.

A planning calendar

  • Month 9 of the policy year. Finance, IT, and the broker review last year’s application. Mark every answer that is not fully true today.
  • Month 10. Fund or schedule the gaps that are cheap to close. Write down the ones that will stay open and why.
  • Month 11. Collect evidence: MFA coverage reports, a recent restore test, the alert escalation list.
  • Month 12. Submit an application you can defend line by line.

The detailed lists are in two guides: the 2026 cyber insurance checklist for IT budgets and What a cyber insurer will still ask. If a control will not be in place by renewal, record it in the risk exception register with an owner and an expiry date.

What to watch next

  • AI-related wording. Watch for new exclusions or endorsements that mention AI, deepfakes, or social engineering. Read where a voice-cloning fraud would fall.
  • Evidence requests. Some underwriters ask for scans or reports, not just yes or no answers. Be ready to show proof.
  • Pricing turns. Soft markets end. Controls you add now will matter more when rates rise again.

Sources

This note does not cite a premium, a deductible, or a loss ratio. The measured market note is Cyber got cheaper. The questionnaire did not.

item.title: The New Unit Economics of AI-Native Startups
item.description: Gross margin is no longer a software story. Token costs, evals, and human review decide who scales.
item.author: circuits50capital@circuits.fit (Emilio Santos)
item.content:encoded:
Classic SaaS trained a generation of founders to treat gross margin as a solved problem. Hosting was cheap, support was a ratio, and the 80-point margin was a personality trait. AI-native products broke that habit. The cost of goods sold now moves with every user action, every retry, and every time a human has to catch the model being confidently wrong.

Investors still want software multiples. The P&L is starting to look like a hybrid of software and services — except the “service” is a GPU bill that does not sleep, plus a review queue that does.

Three cost lines that matter

Inference. Caching, smaller models for easy tasks, and not sending the entire history on every turn are the difference between a toy and a business. If your architecture is “always call the biggest model,” you do not have architecture. You have a demo.

Evaluation. Quality is a cost center. Offline evals, production traces, and the people who read the traces. Skip this and you will “save” money until a customer files a ticket that is really a lawsuit.

Human review. The dirty secret of many “autonomous” products is a queue in Manila, Austin, or Eastern Europe. That is fine if it is designed. It is fatal if it is a surprise at 40% of tickets.

Price the 95th-percentile conversation, not the median demo.

The vendors publish the levers. Use them.

Model providers now document pricing mechanisms that change unit cost by large factors, and most of them reward architecture rather than negotiation.

Prompt caching. Anthropic’s documentation says cache reads are billed at 10 percent of the base input-token price for most models, with lower multipliers for some, while writing to the five-minute cache costs 25 percent more than base input. A product that resends the same long system prompt, policy document or codebase on every call is paying full price for text the provider will discount by an order of magnitude — if the request is structured so the repeated part comes first and stays identical.

Batch processing. OpenAI’s Batch API documentation describes a 50 percent cost discount compared with its synchronous APIs, with a 24-hour completion window and separate, higher rate limits. Anything that does not need an answer while the user waits — nightly summarization, document classification, back-filling embeddings, evaluation runs — is a candidate. Half price on a third of your volume is a real margin line.

Model routing. Providers publish tiered price sheets in which smaller models cost a fraction of the flagship. Routing easy requests to the cheaper tier and escalating only on low confidence is the inference equivalent of not sending every support ticket to the most senior engineer.

Prices and multipliers change, so link to the vendor’s live pricing page in your own cost model and re-check it each quarter rather than hard-coding last year’s number.

Pricing has to follow the cost shape

Seat-based pricing on a variable-cost product is how you fund your power users with your idle ones until the power users eat the company. Usage tiers, hard caps, and product design that makes the expensive path rare are not “growth hacks.” They are survival.

The OWASP Top 10 for LLM applications lists “unbounded consumption” as a security risk: uncontrolled inference that degrades service or runs up cost. That framing is useful for finance teams. A missing rate limit is not only an abuse vector; it is an open-ended cost of goods sold.

The winning teams instrument contribution margin per workspace the way 2015 companies instrumented net retention. If a customer is beloved and negative, they are not a logo. They are a leak.

A simple way to measure it

Pick one unit the customer recognizes — a resolved ticket, a reviewed contract, a generated report. For a sample of real ones, add up four numbers: model tokens billed (input, cached input and output separately), retrieval and tool calls, evaluation and logging cost, and minutes of human review at a loaded hourly rate. Divide by the price the customer pays for that unit. Do it for the median case and for the 95th percentile. The gap between those two numbers is usually where the pricing problem lives.

What “good” looks like

A path to 70%+ gross margin after the product has routing, caching, and a review policy — not on day one. A sales team that is not allowed to waive usage caps without finance. A roadmap that treats model spend as a first-class constraint, the way mobile teams treated battery.

The companies that fail will look busy. They will ship features. They will have impressive demos. They will not know, to the dollar, what a conversation costs. In this market that is not a rounding error. It is the business.

What to do this quarter

  • Price one unit end to end. Use Put an AI cost on one workflow and the AI cost per task tool. Report median and 95th percentile.
  • Turn on caching where prompts repeat. Restructure the longest repeated prefix so it can be cached, then compare the invoice a month later.
  • Move non-interactive work to batch. List every job that does not need a live answer and test it on a batch endpoint.
  • Add hard caps. Per-workspace spend limits and alerts, with a named owner for the alert.
  • Put margin per workspace on the dashboard. Feed it into the token cost to gross margin calculator and review the bottom ten accounts monthly.

Gartner posted on September 24 that a shift in AI pricing, from seats and consumption toward coding agents, makes cost management as important as deployment. The post is the claim. The worksheets above are the response.

Sources

  • Gartner on X, September 24, 2026: a shift toward coding agents makes cost management as important as deployment.
  • Anthropic, Prompt caching documentation: cache reads at 10% of base input price for most models; five-minute cache writes at 1.25x.
  • OpenAI, Batch API guide: 50% cost discount versus synchronous APIs, 24-hour completion window.
  • OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications, 2025: LLM10, Unbounded Consumption.

The margin lines in this note, including the old 80-point habit and the path toward 70%, are desk framing. They are not measurements from these sources.

item.title: Cloud Repatriation: When the Bill Becomes the Strategy
item.description: Finance is pulling workloads home. Engineering is discovering that “home” is a product decision, not a protest.
item.author: circuits50capital@circuits.fit (Emilio Santos)
item.content:encoded:
The cloud argument of the 2010s was elasticity. The cloud argument of the mid-2020s is the invoice. Steady-state workloads — the ones that run every hour of the quarter — do not need a burst story. They need a unit cost. When that unit cost is higher than a colo row plus a small platform team, finance starts using the word “repatriation,” which is a polite way to say “we are moving it.”

This is not a morality play about hyperscalers. It is a matching problem. Some products are still perfect for the public cloud: spiky demand, global footprint, managed data stores you do not want to staff. Others were lifted and shifted in a hurry and never earned their keep.

The bill is a map

If you cannot say which service, which team, and which product own the top twenty lines, you are not ready to move anything. You are ready to argue. FinOps that only produces dashboards is theater. FinOps that can attach a cost to a SKU can choose.

Egress and data gravity do more damage than compute. The workload looks cheap until you try to leave, at which point the architecture reveals it was a hotel, not a house.

Repatriation without an ownership model is just a more expensive outage.

What actually comes home

Batch analytics, predictable inference, and stateful systems with clumsy data gravity are the usual candidates. Customer-facing apps with a global edge usually stay. The hybrid is the real destination: reserved cloud for the bursty surface, owned capacity for the furnace.

People are the constraint. A company that outsourced operations cannot “bring it home” without hiring, and hiring is slower than a board slide. The successful moves staff the platform team first, migrate a boring workload second, and only then hold a press quote.

How to decide

Run a twelve-month fully loaded comparison: cloud list minus real discounts, versus colo, hardware, staff, and the cost of being wrong. Include the feature you will not get — managed failover, a global backbone — as a product risk, not a rounding error.

If the savings only appear if nobody leaves the company, the savings are fictional. If they survive two resignations and a bad disk year, you have a strategy.

Operator guides: When cloud repatriation is a finance decision, not an engineering slogan and The cloud shared-responsibility checklist. The second one is written from Amazon’s page. Do not paste it onto Azure or Google.

Updated October 2026: leaving got cheaper on paper

This note first ran on August 14. One argument for staying in a public cloud has always been the cost of leaving, especially data transfer fees. Several facts on that point are worth having in front of you before any repatriation discussion.

  • Provider exit waivers. In January 2024, Google Cloud announced it would waive data transfer fees for customers migrating off Google Cloud. In March 2024, AWS announced free data transfer out to the internet for customers moving data out of AWS, subject to its process and conditions. Both require you to ask, and both have terms. Read them before you plan.
  • EU Data Act. Regulation (EU) 2023/2854 has applied since September 12, 2025. For data processing services, providers may charge only reduced, cost-based switching charges until January 12, 2027. After that date, switching charges are not allowed.
  • UK competition review. The UK Competition and Markets Authority published the final decision of its cloud services market investigation on July 31, 2025. It recommended that the CMA prioritise strategic market status investigations into Microsoft and AWS under its digital markets powers.

None of this makes a move cheap. Migration labor, parallel running, and new hardware cost far more than a one-time transfer for most companies. What has changed is that “we can never leave” is a weaker argument than it was.

Why it matters, by role

CFO. Repatriation is a capital decision dressed as an engineering one. It trades operating expense for capital expense and staff. Insist on a fully loaded comparison over at least twelve months, and ask what happens to the savings if two key engineers leave.

CISO. Moving out of a public cloud moves security work to you. Under AWS’s shared responsibility model, AWS secures the infrastructure that runs its services, and the customer secures what it puts in the cloud. Leave, and the building, the hardware, and the network become yours too. The shared responsibility checklist lists who patches what today.

Founder. Early on, the cloud is almost always the right answer. The question becomes real when a steady workload is large enough that its monthly bill would pay for a small platform team. Until then, spend the effort on cost tagging so you know which product drives the bill.

Operator. You will run the parallel environment during migration. Plan for months of double cost and double on-call, not a weekend cutover.

A twelve-month comparison template

Fill both columns with your own numbers. Do not use a vendor’s savings calculator as the only input.

LineStay in cloudMove to owned or colo capacity
Compute and storageCurrent bill after real discounts and commitmentsHardware, spread over its expected life, plus colo space and power
Network and transferOngoing egressCarrier circuits, plus one-time exit transfer if no waiver applies
PeopleCurrent cloud operations staffPlatform team, on-call, hardware support contracts
MigrationNoneEngineering time, parallel running, testing
Lost servicesNoneManaged databases, failover, global network you must replace or give up
RiskPrice changes at renewalHardware failure, staff turnover, capacity planning errors

The FinOps Foundation’s framework is a good reference for building the cloud column honestly: allocate costs to teams and products first, then compare.

What to watch next

  • January 12, 2027. The Data Act’s end of switching charges for EU data processing services. Watch how providers update EU contract terms.
  • CMA follow-up. Whether the CMA opens strategic market status investigations into the two providers named in its recommendation, and what conduct requirements follow.
  • AI infrastructure. GPU capacity is the newest version of the same rent-versus-own question. Our note on AI infrastructure impairment covers the risk of owning hardware that ages fast.

Sources

  • AWS, Shared Responsibility Model, the page behind the shared-responsibility checklist
  • AWS News Blog, free data transfer out to the internet when moving out of AWS, March 2024
  • Google Cloud blog, eliminating data transfer fees when migrating off Google Cloud, January 2024
  • Regulation (EU) 2023/2854, the Data Act, on EUR-Lex: switching charges reduced until, and banned from, January 12, 2027
  • UK CMA, cloud services market investigation: final decision published July 31, 2025
  • FinOps Foundation, FinOps Framework

This note does not cite a repatriation survey. The twelve-month comparison is a method, not a published savings figure.

item.title: Six Questions Every Board Should Ask About Generative AI
item.description: Most decks still sell possibility. Directors need a control framework that survives the next vendor cycle.
item.author: circuits50capital@circuits.fit (Emilio Santos)
item.content:encoded:
Boards have been briefed. They have seen the demo. They have approved a budget large enough to be visible and small enough to be deniable. What they often have not done is interrogate the company like owners. Generative AI is not a single project. It is a class of operational risk that happens to look like a product.

Here are six questions that fit in a committee packet. If management cannot answer them in plain language, you do not have a program. You have a vendor relationship. Each question below comes with what a good answer looks like, so a director can tell the difference between a plan and a slide.

1. Where does customer data go, in fact?

Not the policy PDF. The actual path: which tools, which regions, which logs, which subprocessors, which “improvement” toggles are on by default. If the answer is “we think legal signed off,” keep asking.

A good answer is a one-page data-flow diagram per approved tool, with the contract clause that governs retention and training next to each arrow. A weak answer is a list of vendor logos. The OWASP Top 10 for large language model applications, the most widely used public checklist of LLM security failures, lists sensitive information disclosure and system prompt leakage as separate risks. That is a useful prompt for the committee: ask management which of those ten items it has tested, and who ran the test.

2. What decision is the model allowed to finish?

Drafting a memo is not the same as issuing a credit decision, a medical summary, or a support refund. Draw the line in writing. Ambiguity here is how you get a headline.

The same OWASP list names “excessive agency” as its own risk: a system that is granted more permissions or autonomy than the task needs. Agents make this concrete. If a tool can send an email, change a record, or move money, the board should know which approvals sit between the model and the action. A good answer names the actions that always need a human, the ones that never do, and the log that proves which happened.

3. Who is accountable when it is wrong?

A committee is not an owner. Name a role, a review path, and a kill switch. If the only answer is “the vendor’s SLA,” you have outsourced judgment you still own.

The NIST AI Risk Management Framework, released January 26, 2023, organizes the work into four functions: govern, map, measure and manage. “Govern” comes first for a reason. It covers roles, policies and accountability, and NIST’s Generative AI Profile (NIST AI 600-1, released July 26, 2024) extends the framework to risks specific to generative systems. A board does not need to adopt the framework wholesale. It does need management to say which function each owner covers, and which gaps nobody owns yet.

Possibility is a sales word. Permission is a board word.

4. What is the unit cost at the volume we claim?

Seats are not economics. If the plan assumes infinite cheap tokens, the plan is a wish. Ask for the cost of one completed task — one ticket closed, one contract reviewed, one claim triaged — at today’s volume and at the volume in the business case. Then ask what happens to that number if usage triples and the vendor changes its price sheet.

The OWASP list includes “unbounded consumption” as a security risk, which is a polite way of saying a runaway loop or an abusive user can turn into a bill. A good answer includes a spending cap, an alert, and a named person who gets the alert.

5. What do we stop doing?

If nothing is retired — no overlapping copilots, no legacy process, no headcount plan that changes — this is additive spend. Additive spend needs a higher proof than “everyone else is doing it.”

Ask for the list of tools that overlap. Most companies that have run a year of pilots own more than one assistant, more than one transcription tool and more than one “AI feature” bundled into an existing renewal. A good answer pairs each new line item with a contract that ends, a process that changes, or a metric that should move.

6. How will we know in 90 days?

Pick one or two operating metrics, not a sentiment survey. Cycle time, error rate, cost per ticket, win rate. Put the date on the calendar now. Boards that skip this will still be watching demos next summer.

A good answer includes the baseline as of today. Without a baseline, every result after launch looks like an improvement.

A note for boards with European exposure

The EU Artificial Intelligence Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689) is not only a concern for model builders. Its general provisions, including the Article 4 duty on providers and deployers to take measures to ensure a sufficient level of AI literacy among staff who operate AI systems, have applied since February 2, 2025. Other obligations phase in later under the regulation’s own timetable. If the company deploys AI in the EU, the board should ask counsel which obligations already apply, which are coming, and which product lines they touch. Our longer read on that is What the EU AI Act still applies.

What to do this quarter

  • Put the six questions on one agenda. Send them to management two weeks before the meeting and ask for written answers, not a presentation.
  • Ask for the tool inventory. Every approved AI tool, its owner, the data it touches and the contract that governs it. The AI agent inventory and access map is a free template.
  • Get one unit cost. Choose one workflow and price it end to end with Put an AI cost on one workflow and the token cost to gross margin calculator.
  • Adopt a one-page rule. A short use policy that staff can actually read beats a long one they cannot. Start from A one-page AI use rule.
  • Limit agent permissions. Use the agent access limit sheet and Limit what an agent can touch before any agent is allowed to act without a human.
  • Set the 90-day review date. Write down the baseline metric and the date it will be checked.

None of this is anti-AI. It is pro-fiduciary. The technology is real. So is the ability of organizations to confuse motion with return.

Gartner posted on October 1 that most organizations are not ready to delegate work to an agent. Use that as the board’s opening, then hand them the page.

Sources

  • Gartner on X, October 1, 2026: most organizations are not yet ready to delegate work to AI agents.
  • NIST, AI Risk Management Framework: released January 26, 2023; the page also records the July 26, 2024 release of the Generative AI Profile.
  • NIST AI 600-1, Generative Artificial Intelligence Profile (PDF)
  • OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications, 2025 edition: includes sensitive information disclosure, excessive agency, system prompt leakage and unbounded consumption.
  • Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, the Artificial Intelligence Act, on EUR-Lex

The six questions and the “good answer” tests are the desk’s. The sources above are cited for the specific facts attributed to them.

item.title: Retail Media Networks Are Eating the Digital Ad Market
item.description: Closed-loop purchase data beat the open web. The next fight is over who owns the aisle.
item.author: circuits50capital@circuits.fit (Emilio Santos)
item.content:encoded:
For twenty years the open web sold attention and inferred intent. Retailers already had the receipt. Once they built the pipes to auction that receipt back to brands — onsite search ads, offsite audiences, in-store screens — a new media company appeared inside companies that used to think of themselves as grocers and category killers.

This is why retail media keeps taking budget from both linear TV and the old display stack. Attribution is not a science experiment when you can see the cart. Brands will overpay for a clean story. Retailers will take the overpay and call it high-margin revenue, because it is.

The product is the closed loop

Onsite sponsored search is the core: high intent, ugly creative, excellent conversion. Offsite is the land grab — using loyalty data to follow the shopper onto other apps. In-store is the slow build: screens, shelf labels, receipts. Each layer has different ops. Only the first is mature at most chains.

The strategic risk is concentration. If a handful of retailers become the default path to the basket, brand.com and the open web become a branding tax. That is already the conversation in CPG holding companies, even when the public numbers still look diversified.

The aisle was always media. We just started invoicing it like media.

What brands should demand

Incrementality, not last-click theater. Clean-room access, not a PDF of “insights.” A path to creative that is not ten SKUs fighting in a search box. And a hard look at whether the retailer is also a competitor launching a private label next to the ad you just bought.

Agencies that only know social auctions will struggle. The buying motion looks more like trade promotion plus programmatic, which is a sentence that should frighten anyone with a clean org chart.

The publisher lesson

Independent publishers cannot copy Walmart’s receipt. They can copy the discipline: first-party relationships, honest measurement, and inventory that is scarce enough to price. Retail media’s rise is a reminder that ads follow data gravity. If your site has no gravity — no habit, no identity, no reason to return — you will rent attention at declining rates.

That is the uncomfortable mirror for an ad-supported briefing like this one. The work has to be worth a habit. The rest is slots.

Updated October 2026: the measurement standard is the story

This note first ran on August 10. The point that has held up best is the one about measurement. Retail media is sold on the promise that the retailer can see the sale. The industry now has a public standard for how that should be measured, and buyers should use it.

In January 2024, the Interactive Advertising Bureau (IAB) and the Media Rating Council (MRC) published final Retail Media Measurement Guidelines, after a draft for public comment in September 2023. The guidelines cover data collection and quality checks, audience measurement, viewable impressions, invalid traffic, attribution windows, incrementality testing, reporting, and in-store digital screens. The IAB and IAB Europe have also published separate in-store retail media definitions and guidelines. The working group included retailers, brands, agencies, and measurement firms.

Why it matters, by role

CFO. Retail media often sits between two budgets: trade promotion, which finance knows how to audit, and media, which it often does not. Decide which budget it comes from and apply that budget’s controls. If it is trade spend with a media label, it should still have to show an effect on sales that would not have happened anyway.

Founder. For a young consumer brand, sponsored search on a large retailer can be the fastest way to be found. It can also become a toll you pay forever. Track how much of your revenue on that retailer depends on ads. If the share keeps rising, the retailer has more pricing power over you each quarter.

Operator. Retail media ties ads to inventory. If you advertise a product that is out of stock, you pay for clicks that cannot convert. Connect the ad schedule to your stock feed, or at least check it weekly.

CISO. Clean rooms and audience sharing move customer data between companies. Ask what data leaves your systems, under which contract, and who can query it. A clean room is a control only if you know its rules.

What to ask a retail media network

  1. Incrementality. Which method does the network use to show that sales would not have happened anyway? The IAB/MRC guidelines describe randomized controlled tests, synthetic controls, matched-market tests, and modeled approaches. Ask which one, and ask for the methodology in writing.
  2. Attribution window. How many days after an ad view or click does a sale count? Longer windows produce bigger numbers. Make sure you compare networks on the same window.
  3. Invalid traffic. How is non-human or invalid traffic filtered, and is that filtering audited?
  4. Viewability. For display and video, what counts as a viewable impression? For in-store screens, how is exposure measured?
  5. Reporting granularity. Can you see results by product, by placement, and by new versus repeat customer, or only a summary?
  6. Data access. What can you take away from a clean room, and what stays with the retailer?
  7. Conflicts. Does the retailer sell a private-label product in the same category? If so, how are placement and data walls handled?

A simple test you can run

If the network cannot offer a controlled test, run a crude one yourself. Pick a set of comparable products or regions. Pause ads on half for a few weeks and keep the other half running. Compare sales. This is less rigorous than the methods in the guidelines, and seasonality and promotions can distort it. It is still better than accepting attributed sales as incremental sales.

What to watch next

  • Audited measurement. Whether networks have their measurement audited against MRC standards, and say so in their sales materials.
  • In-store screens. In-store media is the least mature layer. Watch how exposure is counted before paying premium prices for it.
  • Concentration. Whether a few retailers keep gaining share of brand budgets. That shifts pricing power away from brands and toward the retailers that own the checkout.

For the finance side of judging any spend by its return rather than its reported activity, see AI spend is not the same as AI return. The method transfers.

Sources

This is an operator note. It does not cite an ad-market forecast or a retailer’s filing.

  • Media Rating Council, Standards and Guidelines: lists the IAB/MRC Retail Media Measurement Guidelines, January 2024 (PDF)
